en: The country of Ṭakka (磔迦國) is over ten thousand *li* in circuit; it borders the Vipāśā River to the east and faces the Sindhu River to the west. The capital city of the country is over twenty *li* in circuit. The land is suitable for non-glutinous rice and produces much winter wheat; it yields gold, silver, brass, copper, and iron. The climate is hot, and the land is subject to many windstorms. The customs of the people are violent and wicked, and their speech is vulgar and obscene. Their clothing is bright white, consisting of so-called *kauśeya* (silk) garments, *chaoxia* (morning glow) robes, and the like. They have little faith in the Buddhadharma and mostly serve the heavenly deities. There are ten *saṃghārāma*s and several hundred *deva* temples. In the past, this country had many charitable houses to provide for the poor and needy, where medicine or food was distributed; with such provisions for their sustenance, travelers were never in want.
From here, the northern route extends for one thousand eight or nine hundred li; the path is perilous, crossing mountains and traversing valleys, until one reaches the country of Lāhula (洛護羅國).

As for the boundaries of its territory, they may be described. The realm of the Five Indias (五印度) measures more than 90,000 li in circumference. On three sides it borders the great sea, and in the north it rests against the Snow Mountains (Himālaya). It is broad in the north and narrow in the south, shaped like a half-moon, with the land divided into more than seventy countries. The climate is exceptionally hot, and the ground is often damp with springs. To the north, mountains and ridges rise in succession, and the hills are of saline-alkaline soil; to the east, the plains are fertile and moist, and the cultivated fields are rich and productive; in the south, the vegetation is lush and flourishing; and in the west, the land is stony and barren. This is the general situation, which can be briefly stated.

Within a radius of two hundred li around the great city, the people of that land call it the Land of Blessedness (Kurukṣetra). According to the records of former times, the Five Indias were once ruled by two kings; their territories bordered each other and were subject to mutual invasions, with wars never ceasing. The two rulers conspired together, wishing to decide the matter through a decisive battle to determine the victor and bring peace to the populace. The common people were all resentful and would not follow the kings' commands. The kings thought that it is difficult to plan the beginning of an undertaking with the masses, but that the divine can move living beings and authority can establish merit. At that time, there was a Brahman known for his great talent; the king secretly presented him with a gift of silk and ordered him into the rear palace to compose a sacred text, which was then hidden in a mountain cave. As time passed, the trees grew to the size of a man’s embrace. The king sat in court and told his ministers: "Because of my lack of virtue, I unworthily occupy this high position; yet the Emperor of Heaven has looked down upon me and granted me a spiritual book in a dream, which is now located on a certain mountain, hidden on a certain ridge." Thereupon, he issued an order to search for it, and the book was found beneath the mountain forest. The officials offered congratulations, and the masses were joyful; it was proclaimed far and near, so that all might hear and know of it. Its general purport was: "Life and death are without bounds, and the cycle of transmigration is endless; sentient beings are submerged and drowning, with no way to save themselves. I, through a marvelous stratagem, shall cause them to depart from all suffering. Now, this royal city and its surroundings of two hundred li were a land of blessings and merit in the ages of former emperors. As the years and months have been extremely long, the inscriptions and records have been obliterated; living beings do not realize this and have consequently sunk into the sea of suffering. If they are drowning and not saved, what is to be said of it?" "All you sentient beings, if you die facing the enemy in battle, you will be reborn among humans; if you slaughter many of the innocent, you will receive the blessings and joys of heaven; and if obedient grandsons and filial sons who serve their elderly parents travel through this land, they shall obtain infinite blessings. With so little effort yielding such great merit, how could you let this advantage slip away? Once you lose this human body, the three paths (the three lower realms of existence) are dark and obscure. Therefore, let all living beings each apply themselves to their practice!" Thereupon, the people all engaged in battle, viewing death as a return home. The king then issued an order to recruit the brave and fierce; the two kingdoms joined in battle, and the piled-up corpses were like dense grass. Down to the present day, skeletal remains are scattered across the fields; as the events took place in ancient times, the human bones are of a massive size. Local custom passes down the name of this place as the Land of Blessings (Kurukṣetra). Four or five li to the northwest of the city, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). The bricks are all a yellowish-red color and are very bright and clean. Inside is one *dou* of the Tathāgata’s relics, which emit light from time to time and manifest many divine wonders.

The country of Lampāka (濫波國) is over a thousand *li* in circuit. To the north, it has the Snow Mountains at its back, and on the other three sides, it borders the Black Range (黑嶺). The capital city of the country is over ten *li* in circuit. For several hundred years, the royal lineage has been extinct, and powerful men have contended for strength, leaving the country without a great sovereign; only recently has it become a dependency of the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). The land is suitable for non-glutinous rice and produces much sugarcane; although trees are numerous, they yield little fruit. The climate is gradually becoming warmer, with light frost but no snow. The customs of the country are prosperous and joyful, and the people are fond of singing and chanting; however, their dispositions are timid and weak, their hearts are deceitful, and they engage in mutual deception and mockery, lacking any sense of deference. Their physical stature is small, and their movements are restless. They mostly wear white cotton cloth and their attire is bright and decorative. There are more than ten monasteries with few monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Mahayana. There are several dozen *deva* temples, and the followers of heterodox paths are very numerous.
The capital city of the country (Lanpo 濫波國) is more than ten li in circuit.
The capital city of the country of Nagarahāra (那揭羅曷國) is more than twenty li in circuit.

Two li to the east of the city is a stūpa over three hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It is constructed of piled stone rising prominently, with exquisite carvings and a unique design; it is the place where the Bodhisattva Śākya (釋迦菩薩) encountered the Buddha Dīpankara (然燈佛), spread out his deerskin garment, and laid down his hair to cover the mud, thereby receiving his prediction. Although aeons have passed and the world has been destroyed, this trace has not vanished. On certain fast days, the heavens rain down various flowers, and the populace, vying in their devotion, perform offerings. To its west is a saṃghārāma with few monks. Further to the south is a small stūpa; this is the site where the mud was once covered, which King Aśoka built in this secluded spot to avoid the main road. Inside the city are the old foundations of a great stūpa. I have heard from the records of the ancients that there was once a Buddha tooth here, which was tall, broad, and magnificent. Now that the tooth is gone, only the old foundations remain. Beside it is a stūpa over thirty feet high. Local tradition says, without knowing its origin, that it descended from the sky and established its base here. Since it was not made by human hands, it possesses many spiritual marvels. More than ten li to the southwest of the city is a stūpa marking the spot where the Tathāgata, traveling through the air from Central India to convert beings, descended; the people of the country, moved by admiration, built this spiritual foundation. Not far to its east is a stūpa where the Bodhisattva Śākya once encountered the Buddha Dīpankara and purchased flowers.

Traveling over eight hundred *li* east from the Yamunā River, one reaches the source of the Ganges River (Gaṅgā), which is three or four *li* wide; where it flows southeast into the sea, it is over ten *li* wide. The color of the water is a deep blue, and the waves flow vast and wide. Although there are many spiritual anomalies, they do not harm living beings. Its taste is sweet and delicious, and fine sand flows along with the current. According to the records of the local customs, it is called the "water of merit." Even if one has accumulated sins and transgressions, bathing in it removes them. Those who hold life lightly and drown themselves are reborn in heaven and receive blessings; those who cast their remains into it after death do not fall into the evil paths; and by splashing the waves and agitating the current, the souls of the departed obtain salvation.  At that time, the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆菩薩) from the country of Siṃhala (執師子國) had deeply penetrated the true reality and attained the nature of all phenomena. Pitying these foolish people, he came here to guide and instruct them. At that time, men and women had all gathered, young and old alike, and were splashing the waves and agitating the current on the riverbank. The Bodhisattva Deva, mingling with them to draw the water, lowered his head and pushed the water in the opposite direction, his behavior differing from that of the crowd. A non-Buddhist asked, "Why are you acting so strangely, sir?" The Bodhisattva Deva replied, "My parents and relatives are in the country of Siṃhala. I fear they are suffering from hunger and thirst, and I hope to provide them with relief from afar." The non-Buddhists said, "You are mistaken, sir! You have not thought this through and are performing this act in vain. Your home and country are far away, separated by vast mountains and rivers; to splash this water here to relieve their hunger there is like walking backward to try and reach a destination in front—it is unheard of." The Bodhisattva Deva replied, "If those burdened by sins in the dark paths of the afterlife can still receive the benefit of this water, why should it not reach those separated by mountains and rivers?" At that time, the various non-Buddhists (外道), realizing that they were defeated by his logic, abandoned their false views, accepted the true Dharma, reformed themselves, and wished to follow his teachings.

Traveling over twenty *li* southwest of the city to a small rocky ridge, there is a monastery with lofty halls and multi-storied pavilions, constructed from piled stones. The courtyards and buildings are desolate, and there are absolutely no monks. In the center is a *stūpa* over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Southwest of the monastery is a deep, precipitous ravine with a waterfall flowing down and cliffs standing like walls. On the stone wall of the eastern cliff is a large cave, which is the dwelling place of the dragon Gopāla (瞿波羅龍). The entrance path is narrow, the cave is dark and gloomy, the cliff rocks drip with moisture, and the path is wet with the remaining flow. In the past, there was a shadow of the Buddha, shining as if it were his true form, with all the marks and characteristics complete, appearing just as if he were present. Since recent times, people have not been able to see it fully; even if they do see it, it is only indistinctly. Those who pray with utmost sincerity and have a spiritual response may see it clearly for a moment, but it cannot last long. Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the world, this dragon was a cowherd who supplied milk and curds to the king, but he failed to present them properly. Having been reprimanded, he harbored resentment in his heart; he then used gold coins to buy flowers to offer to a *stūpa* of prediction, wishing to become a wicked dragon to destroy the country and harm the king. He then rushed to the stone wall and threw himself to his death. Consequently, he resided in this cave and became a great dragon king, intending to emerge from the cave to fulfill his evil vow. Just as this thought arose, the Tathāgata perceived it. Compassionate toward the people of this country who were about to be harmed by the dragon, he exercised his supernatural powers and arrived from Central India. When the dragon saw the Tathāgata, his poisonous intent ceased; he accepted the precept against killing and vowed to protect the True Dharma. The dragon then requested the Tathāgata, "May you always reside in this cave, and may your holy disciples constantly receive my offerings." The Tathāgata replied, "I am about to enter nirvana, but I shall leave my shadow for you and send five arhats to constantly receive your offerings. Even when the True Dharma has faded away, this practice shall not cease. If your poisonous heart should flare up in anger, you should look upon the shadow I have left behind; because of its compassionate nature, your poisonous heart will cease. In this Bhadrakalpa, the World-Honored Ones who are yet to come will also have compassion for you and will all leave their images behind."  Outside the entrance of the Shadow Cave (佛影窟), there are two square stones. On one of the stones is the footprint of the Tathāgata, where the wheel mark is faintly visible and light occasionally shines forth. To the left and right of the Shadow Cave are many stone chambers, all of which are places where the various holy disciples of the Tathāgata entered into meditative concentration. In the northwest corner of the Shadow Cave is a stūpa, which marks the place where the Tathāgata used to walk. Beside it is a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. Not far from this is a stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata manifested and expounded the True Doctrine, and where he spoke of the aggregates and realms. To the west of the Shadow Cave is a large flat rock where the Tathāgata once washed his kaṣāya robe, and the faint traces of its pattern are still visible.

Thirty-some *li* southeast of the city, one arrives at the city of Haḍḍa (醯羅城). It is four or five *li* in circumference, with steep and rugged defenses, and flower groves and ponds that are bright, fresh, and clear as mirrors. The people living in the city are honest, simple, and possess upright faith. There is a multi-storied pavilion with painted beams and vermilion pillars. In the second story of the pavilion is a small stupa made of the seven precious substances, in which the crown bone of the Tathāgata is placed. The bone is one foot and two inches in circumference, with distinct hair pores, and its color is yellowish-white; it is contained in a precious casket and placed inside the stupa. Those who wish to know the signs of their good or evil karma mix incense powder with clay and press it onto the crown bone; according to the response of their merit, the patterns appear clearly. There is another small stupa made of the seven precious substances to store the Tathāgata’s skull bone, which is shaped like a lotus leaf and is the same color as the crown bone; it is also kept sealed within a precious casket. There is another small stupa made of the seven precious substances containing the Tathāgata’s eyeball, which is as large as a *nā* (crabapple) fruit, brilliant and transparent, shining through from inside to out; it is also kept sealed within a precious casket. The Tathāgata’s *saṃghāṭī* (monastic robe) is made of fine *nü* (a type of fine cotton or wool fabric), its color is yellowish-red, and it is kept in a precious casket; as the years have been long, it is slightly damaged. The Tathāgata’s *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) has rings made of white iron and a shaft made of sandalwood; it is kept in a precious tube. Recently, a king heard that all these objects were things the Tathāgata had personally used in the past, and relying on his power, he forcibly took them away. Once they arrived in his own country, he placed them in the palace where he resided, but before even twelve days had passed, when he sought them, they were already lost; upon further searching, they had already returned to their original place. These five sacred sites possess many spiritual wonders, and the king of Kapiśa (迦畢試國) has appointed five pure-practitioners (brahmacārins) to provide incense and flowers in service to them. Pilgrims coming to pay their respects arrive in an unbroken succession. The pure-practitioners, desiring to pursue emptiness and tranquility, and considering that wealth is something people value, have provisionally established a schedule of fees to put an end to the clamor and confusion. The general outline is as follows: those who wish to see the Tathāgata’s skull bone must pay a tax of one gold coin; if they wish to take an impression, they must pay a tax of five gold coins; for the remaining items, there is a graded schedule of fees. Although the fees are heavy, the number of those coming to pay their respects only increases. To the northwest of the multi-storied pavilion is a stūpa, which is also very tall and displays many spiritual wonders; if a person touches it with a finger, it immediately begins to shake, its very foundations tilt and move, and its bells ring in harmony.

In the northwest territory of the kingdom, on the east bank of the Ganges (gaṅgā) River, lies the city of Mayūra (摩裕羅城), which is over twenty li in circuit. The inhabitants are prosperous, and the city is encircled by clear streams; it produces brass, rock crystal, and precious vessels. Not far from the city, bordering the Ganges River, there is a great deva temple with many miraculous manifestations. Within it is a pond with stone-lined banks, replenished by water diverted from the Ganges; the people of the five Indias call it the Gate of the Ganges (Gaṅgādvāra), a place for generating merit and expiating sins. Constantly, hundreds of thousands of people from distant regions gather here to bathe. Benevolent kings have established charitable hostels here, stocked with fine food and stored with medicines, to bestow gifts upon the widowed and solitary, and to provide for the orphaned and destitute.
Some say that it flows underground and emerges at Jishi Mountain (積石山), being the current of the Sītā River (徙多河) and the source of the river of China.
The great capital city of the country is called Puruṣapura (布路沙布邏), and it is over forty li in circuit.

From the Black Ridge (Heiling) onwards, all are customs of the Hu. Although they are grouped with the Rong peoples, they are divided into distinct tribes with demarcated borders, and for the most part, they are settled inhabitants. They build walled cities and devote themselves to agriculture and animal husbandry. By nature, they value wealth and property, while their customs hold benevolence and righteousness in low regard. There is no ritual in marriage, and no order of precedence between the noble and the base; the words of women are heeded, while men occupy a subordinate position. Upon death, they cremate the remains, and there is no fixed period for mourning. They scarify their faces and mutilate their ears, cut their hair and rend their garments, and slaughter herds of livestock to sacrifice to the spirits of the dead. On auspicious occasions they wear white garments, while for mourning they dress in black. These are the general customs and practices, briefly outlined here; their differing administrations and unique regulations will be described separately according to each region. The customs of India are discussed in the final record.

Inside the royal city, to the northeast, there is an old foundation; it was formerly the precious pedestal of the Buddha’s alms bowl. After the Tathāgata entered nirvana, the bowl drifted to this country, where it was formally worshipped for several hundred years; it then circulated through various countries and is now in Persia (Pārśva). Eight or nine li to the southeast of the city, there is a Pippala tree (卑鉢羅樹) over a hundred feet high, with wide-spreading branches and leaves that provide a dense shade. The four Buddhas of the past have already sat beneath it, and images of these four Buddhas still exist there today. During the Bhadrakalpa, the nine hundred and ninety-six Buddhas will all sit there as well. Deities guard and protect it, and its spiritual influence is secretly bestowed. The Śākya Tathāgata once sat under this tree facing south and told Ānanda: "Four hundred years after I pass away, a king will appear in the world named Kaniṣka; not far to the south of this spot, he will erect a stūpa, and a great portion of the relics of my bones and flesh will be gathered within it."

The kingdom of Agni (阿耆尼國) is over six hundred *li* from east to west and over four hundred *li* from south to north. The kingdom’s capital city is six or seven *li* in circumference. It is backed by mountains on all four sides, and the roads are perilous and easy to defend. Streams flow around it, and water is diverted to irrigate the fields. The soil is suitable for growing non-glutinous millet, broomcorn millet, winter wheat, fragrant jujubes, grapes, pears, crabapples, and various other fruits. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs of the people are simple and honest. Their writing system is modeled on that of India, with slight modifications. Their clothing is made of felt and coarse wool; they cut their hair short and do not wear headcloths. For currency, they use gold coins, silver coins, and small copper coins. The king is a native of the country; he is brave but lacks strategy, and he is fond of boasting of his own achievements. The country lacks a strict code of conduct, and the laws are not well-regulated. There are more than ten monasteries with over two thousand monks, who study the Sarvāstivāda (說一切有部) school of the Hīnayāna. Since their scriptural teachings and Vinaya discipline follow those of India, the students study them using the original texts. Their conduct and adherence to the Vinaya are pure, clean, and diligent. However, they consume the three kinds of "pure meat," remaining attached to the gradual teachings.
The capital city of the country of Agni (阿耆尼國) is six or seven li in circuit. It is backed by mountains on all four sides, and the roads are precipitous and easy to defend.

In front of a divine shrine (devalaya) north of a city on the eastern border of the kingdom, there is a large dragon pond. The various dragons change their forms to mate with mares, and thus produce dragon-colts that are fierce and difficult to tame. It is only the offspring of these dragon-colts that can be broken and ridden, which is why this country produces many fine horses. According to the accounts of the ancients, in recent times there was a king named Golden Flower (Suvarṇapuṣpa), whose administration and teachings were enlightened and discerning, and he moved a dragon to serve as his mount. When the king was about to pass away, he touched the dragon’s ear with his whip, whereupon it submerged and disappeared, remaining hidden to this day. There are no wells in the city, so the people draw water from that pond. The dragons transform into men and mate with the women; the children born of this are brave and swift, able to outrun galloping horses. Through this gradual intermingling, the people have all become of dragon lineage, relying on their strength to act tyrannically and refusing to obey the king’s commands. The king then colluded with the Turks to slaughter the people of this city, executing both young and old until not a single soul remained. The city is now desolate, and human habitation has ceased.

To the south of the Pippala tree is a stupa built by King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王). Four hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, King Kaniṣka ascended the throne and ruled over Jambudvīpa. He did not believe in merit or demerit and slighted the Buddha’s Dharma. While hunting in the marshes, he encountered a white rabbit; the king personally gave chase, but it suddenly vanished at this spot. He saw a young cowherd among the trees making a small stupa three feet in height. The king asked, "What are you doing?" The cowherd replied, "Long ago, the holy wisdom of Śākya Buddha prophesied: 'A king will appear who shall build a stupa on this excellent site, and many of my bodily relics will be gathered within it.' Your Majesty’s holy virtues were cultivated in the past, your name matches the ancient prophecy, and your divine merit and superior fortune are destined for this very moment; therefore, I have come ahead to alert and inspire you." Having said this, he suddenly disappeared. Hearing these words, the king was filled with joy and reverence. Reflecting on his name and the Great Sage’s prior prophecy, he developed true faith and deeply respected the Buddha’s Dharma. Around the small stupa, he built a stone stupa, wishing to use his power to cover it completely. Yet, as he increased the height, the small stupa always emerged three feet above it. Only when the height exceeded four hundred feet—with the base standing one and a half li in circumference and a five-tiered foundation one hundred and fifty feet high—was he finally able to cover the small stupa. The king, rejoicing at this auspicious event, further erected twenty-five tiers of gilded copper rings above it, and placing one hu of the Tathāgata’s relics within them, he performed offerings in this manner. No sooner was the construction finished than he saw the small stupa protruding halfway out from beneath the southeast corner of the great foundation. The king was displeased and cast it away; it then lodged halfway within the stone base under the second tier of the stupa, while another small stupa emerged once more at its original location. The king then withdrew and sighed, saying: "Alas, human efforts are easily misguided, but divine merit is difficult to conceal. When supported by the holy and spiritual, what can anger achieve?" Having felt shame and fear, he confessed his fault and returned. Those two stupas are still present today; those who are afflicted with illness and wish to pray for recovery apply incense and scatter flowers, and with sincere devotion take refuge, most of them obtaining a cure. To the south of the stone steps on the eastern face of the great stupa, two stupas are carved, one three feet high and the other five feet high, their design and shape modeled after the great stupa. Two Buddha images are also fashioned, one four feet high and the other six feet high, imitating the seated image with crossed legs under the Mahā-bodhi tree; when the sunlight shines upon them, the golden color glitters brilliantly, and as the shadows gradually shift, the stone patterns appear dark blue. I have heard from the elders that several hundred years ago, there were golden ants in the crevices of the stone base, the large ones like fingers and the small ones like grains of wheat, which followed one another to gnaw at the stone wall, the patterns appearing as if carved and inlaid with gold sand, forming these images, which are still present today. On the southern side of the stone steps of the great stūpa (大窣堵波) there is a painted Buddha image sixteen feet high; from the chest upward it appears as two bodies, but from the chest downward it is joined into one. I have heard from the elders that in the beginning, there was a poor man who supported himself by manual labor and, having obtained one gold coin, wished to have a Buddha image made. He went to the place of the stūpa and said to a painter, "I now wish to depict the exquisite features of the Tathāgata (如來), but I have only one gold coin, which is insufficient to reward your labor; I have long cherished this desire but am burdened by worry, being constrained by my poverty." At that time, the painter, perceiving his utmost sincerity, did not speak of the price but promised to complete the work. Later, there was another man whose circumstances were the same as the former; he brought a gold coin and requested that an image of the Buddha be painted. The painter then accepted the money from both men, sought out excellent pigments, and painted a single image for them both. When the two men came on the same day to pay their respects, the painter pointed to the one image, showed it to them, and said, "This is the Buddha image you commissioned." The two men looked at each other, as if they had some misgivings. The painter, knowing their doubts in his heart, said to the two men, "Why are you so long in thought? Whatever I have received, I have not diminished by even a hair's breadth. If these words are not false, the image will surely manifest a divine transformation." Before his voice had ceased, the image manifested a miracle: the bodies separated and their shadows intertwined, and the light of the image shone brilliantly. The two men were convinced and filled with faith and joy. More than a hundred paces to the southwest of the great stupa (mahāstūpa), there is a white stone Buddha image eighteen feet high, standing and facing north; it possesses many divine signs and frequently emits light. At times, people have seen the image go out at night to walk, circumambulating the great stupa. Recently, a group of thieves intended to enter and commit theft, but the image went out to meet them; the band of thieves was terrified and retreated, and the image returned to its original place, standing as before. Because of this, the group of thieves reformed and renewed themselves, traveling through the towns and villages to tell everyone, far and near. To the left and right of the great stupa, there are hundreds of small stupas arranged like fish scales. The Buddha images are adorned with the utmost craftsmanship, and extraordinary fragrances and strange sounds are sometimes heard; divine immortals and sages are occasionally seen circumambulating them. Regarding this stupa, the Tathāgata prophesied that it would be burned seven times and rebuilt seven times, at which point the Buddhadharma would come to an end. The records of the ancients state that it has already been built and destroyed three times. When I first arrived in this country, I happened to encounter a great fire, and I saw it being constructed, though it was not yet completed.

More than forty *li* to the north of the deserted city, nestled against a mountain slope and separated by a river, are two monasteries; both are named Cakuri (昭怙釐), distinguished as the Eastern and Western respectively. The ornamentation of the Buddha statues almost surpasses human craftsmanship. The monks are pure and austere, truly diligent and earnest. In the Buddha hall of the Eastern Cakuri Monastery, there is a jade stone over two feet wide, yellowish-white in color and shaped like a sea clam. Upon it is a footprint left by the Buddha, measuring one foot eight inches in length and over six inches in width. On some fast days, it emits a brilliant light. Outside the west gate of the great city, on both sides of the road, there are standing statues of the Buddha, each over ninety feet tall. In front of these statues is the site where a great assembly is held every five years. Every year, during the several tens of days around the autumnal equinox, the monks of the entire country gather here. From the king down to the officials and commoners, all set aside worldly affairs to observe fasts and precepts, receive scriptures, and listen to the Dharma, forgetting their fatigue throughout the day. The various monasteries adorn their Buddha statues, polishing them with precious gems and decorating them with brocades and silks, then loading them onto palanquins; these are called "processional images." Numbering in the thousands, they gather like clouds at the assembly site. On the fifteenth and the last day of every month, the king and his ministers deliberate on state affairs, consulting with eminent monks before making proclamations.

Traveling northwest from the country for more than three hundred li, one crosses a stony desert and reaches the Ice Mountains (凌山, *Língshān*). This is the northern plateau of the Pamir Range (葱嶺, *Cōnglǐng*), where the waters mostly flow eastward. Snow accumulates in the mountain valleys, remaining frozen throughout the spring and summer; although it occasionally thaws, it soon freezes over again. The path is dangerous and obstructed, and the cold winds are bitter and fierce. There are many disasters caused by violent dragons that harass travelers. Those who travel this road must not wear reddish-brown clothing, carry calabashes, or shout loudly. If there is the slightest violation, disaster is witnessed immediately. Violent winds erupt, blowing sand and raining stones; those who encounter them perish, and it is difficult to survive.

Beside the great city, overlooking the Ganges (殑伽河) River, is Mount Īraṇa (伊爛拏山), which breathes forth mists and clouds that obscure the sun and moon. From ancient times to the present, immortals and sages have followed one another to dwell here in meditation, and there is now a deva temple that still observes the traditional rites. In the past, the Tathāgata also resided here, extensively expounding the wonderful Dharma for the sake of devas and humans.

Traveling northwest from the Clear Lake (Qingchi) for over five hundred li, one arrives at the city of the Suyab River (素葉水城). The city is six or seven li in circumference, where merchants from various Hu countries live together. The soil is suitable for millet, wheat, and grapes, though trees are sparse. The climate is windy and cold, and the people wear garments of felt and coarse wool. To the west of Suyab, there are several dozen isolated cities, each with its own established leader; although they do not take orders from one another, they are all subject to the Turks (突厥).

One hundred forty or fifty li to the east of the city, south of the Ganges (gaṅgā), water surrounds a solitary islet with lofty and precipitous cliffs; atop it stands a deva temple where the deity manifests many miracles. Chambers have been carved into the cliffs and water channeled to form ponds; with its flowery groves, exotic trees, massive rocks, and perilous peaks, it is an abode for the benevolent and wise, so beautiful that visitors forget to return. In the mountains and forests of the country's southern border, wild elephants and fierce beasts roam in herds numbering in the thousands.

From the city of the Suyab River (素葉水城) to the kingdom of Kesh (羯霜那國), the region is named Sogdiana (窣利), and the people are also called by this name. Their script and language are named accordingly. The origins of their script are simple, consisting of only twenty-odd letters which generate further words through combination; their use has gradually expanded until they possess rudimentary written records. They read their texts vertically and pass them down from teacher to pupil without interruption. They wear garments of felt and coarse wool, and dress in furs and fine cotton, with narrow and tight-fitting clothing. They trim their hair to expose the crown or shave it off entirely, and bind their foreheads with colored silk. They are tall and imposing in stature but timid in disposition. Their customs are frivolous and deceitful; they often act with guile and are generally avaricious. Fathers and sons calculate profit against each other, regarding wealth as the measure of nobility and making no distinction between the virtuous and the base. Although some possess vast wealth, their clothing and food are coarse and simple. Those who labor in the fields and those who pursue profit are mixed in roughly equal halves.

Traveling more than four hundred *li* westward from the city of Suyab (素葉城), one arrives at the Thousand Springs (千泉). The Thousand Springs is an area over two hundred *li* square, with the Snow Mountains (雪山) to the south and level land on the other three sides. The soil and water are fertile and moist, and the trees are sparse and spreading; in the month of late spring, the various flowers are like brocade. There are a thousand springs and ponds, which is how it earned its name. The Khan of the Turks (突厥可汗) comes here every year to escape the summer heat. Within the area are herds of deer, many of which are adorned with bells and rings; they are tame and familiar with people, and do not easily take fright or run away. The Khan cherishes and admires them, and has issued an order to his subordinates that anyone who dares to kill or harm them shall be executed without pardon. Therefore, these herds of deer are able to live out their natural lives.

In the northern border, not far from the Ganges (殑伽河; gaṅgā) River, there is a large high terrace built of piled bricks and stones. Its foundation is broad and lofty, featuring exquisite carvings, and all around its sides are engraved images of various holy beings, with the forms of the Buddha and the devas distinctly rendered.

Traveling one hundred and forty or fifty li westward from the Thousand Springs (千泉), one arrives at the city of Talas (呾邏私城). The city is eight or nine li in circumference, and Hu merchants from various countries live there together. The suitability of the soil and the sequence of the seasons are much the same as in Suyab (素葉).

Traveling southward for more than ten *li*, there is a small isolated town (小孤城) of over three hundred households. The inhabitants were originally people of the Middle Kingdom (中國人) who were captured by the Turks (突厥) in the past; later, they gathered their compatriots together to jointly defend this town and settled within it. In their clothing and deportment, they have come to resemble the Turks, yet in their speech and manners, they still retain those of their original country.

From here, traveling southwest for more than two hundred li, one arrives at the city of Baishui (White Water). The city is six or seven li in circumference. The produce of the land and the suitability of the climate are even superior to those of Talas (呾邏私).

More than twenty li to the west of the city is the Vāśibhā Monastery (跋始婆僧伽藍). Its courtyards and buildings are spacious and open, and its terraces and pavilions are lofty. There are more than seven hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahayana teachings; most of the eminent scholars and renowned monks of East India reside here. Not far to its side is a stupa (窣堵波) built by King Aśoka. This is the place where, in the past, the Tathāgata spent three months preaching the Dharma for the devas and humans; on fast days, it sometimes emits a brilliant light. To its side are the sites of the sitting and walking meditation paths of the four Buddhas. Not far from here is another shrine (精舍; Skt. mūla-gandha-kuṭī), in which is an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. Its spiritual insight is all-revealing and its divine responses are manifest, so that people from far and near fast and pray before it.

Traveling southwest for more than two hundred li, one arrives at the city of Gongyu (恭御城). The city is five or six li in circumference. The plains and marshes are rich and fertile, and the forests are lush and luxuriant.
To the east, it borders the Yaxartes River (葉河). The Yaxartes River originates from the northern source of the Onion Mountains (葱嶺), flows to the northwest, and is vast, turbid, turbulent, and swift.
To the northeast of here, in a valley by the shore of the great sea, is the kingdom of Śrīkṣetra (室利差呾羅國).

Traveling westward from here for more than a thousand li, one reaches the country of Sutrūṣṇa (窣堵利瑟那國). The country of Sutrūṣṇa is fourteen or fifteen hundred li in circuit. To the east, it borders the Yaxartes River (葉河). The Yaxartes River originates from the northern source of the Onion Mountains (葱嶺), flows toward the northwest, and is vast, turbid, turbulent, and swift. The products of the soil and the customs of the people are the same as those of the country of Chāch (赭時國). It has its own king and is subject to the Turks (突厥).

From here, going northwest, one enters the Great Sandy Desert (大沙磧), where there is absolutely no water or grass. The roads are vast and indistinct, and the boundaries are difficult to discern; one must look toward the great mountains (pravaragiri) and seek out scattered bones to know the direction and mark the path traveled.
The capital city of the country (Samarkand 颯秣建國) is more than twenty li in circuit; it is extremely strategic and secure, and is densely populated.

From here, traveling southwest for over five hundred li, one reaches the country of Chorasmia (貨利習彌伽國). The country of Chorasmia lies along both banks of the Oxus River (縛芻河); it is twenty to thirty li from east to west and over five hundred li from south to north. The agricultural products and customs are the same as those of the country of Vadi (伐地國), though the language differs slightly.

Traveling southeast through the mountains for more than three hundred *li*, one enters the Iron Gate (Tämir qapïɣ). The Iron Gate is flanked by mountains on both sides that are extremely steep and precipitous; although there is a narrow path, it is fraught with obstructions, and the stone walls on both sides are the color of iron. Gate leaves have been installed and reinforced with iron clamps, and many iron bells are suspended from the door panels; because of its strategic peril and strength, it was given this name.

Following the course of the Vakhsh River (縛芻河) downstream to the north, one arrives at the country of Tirmidh (呾蜜國). The country of Tirmidh is over six hundred *li* from east to west and over four hundred *li* from south to north. The capital city of the country is over twenty *li* in circumference; it is long from east to west and narrow from south to north. There are more than ten monasteries and over one thousand monks. Regarding the various *stūpas*—which are what were formerly called *futu* (浮圖), and also called *tūpa* (鍮婆), *tāpa* (塔婆), *sītūpō* (私鍮簸), or *sǒudǒupō* (藪斗波), all of which are corruptions—as well as the venerable images of the Buddha, they possess many miraculous manifestations and are spiritually responsive.

To the east, one arrives at the country of Cagayāna (赤鄂衍那國). The country of Cagayāna is more than four hundred li from east to west and over five hundred li from south to north. The capital city of the country is more than ten li in circumference. There are five sanghārāmas (伽藍), and the number of monks is very small.

To the east, one reaches the country of Kharūn (忽露摩國). The country of Kharūn is over one hundred *li* from east to west and over three hundred *li* from north to south. The capital city of the country is over ten *li* in circumference. Its king is a Xisu Turk. There are two monasteries and over one hundred monks.

To the southwest, bordering the Vakhsh River (縛芻河), one reaches the country of Kuwayāna (鞠和衍那國). The country of Kuwayāna is more than two hundred *li* from east to west and over three hundred *li* from south to north. The capital city of the country is more than ten *li* in circumference. There are three monasteries and more than one hundred monks.

To the east, one reaches the country of Wakhsh (鑊沙國). The country of Wakhsh is more than three hundred li from east to west and over five hundred li from north to south. The capital city of the country is sixteen or seventeen li in circuit.

To the east, one arrives at the country of Khuttal (珂咄羅國). The country of Khuttal is over one thousand li from east to west and over one thousand li from north to south. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circumference.

From the country of Hu (*γwar*) to the southeast lie the countries of Khasta (闊悉多國) and Antarava (安呾羅縛國); the accounts of these are recorded in the narrative of the return journey. To the southwest of the country of Hu is the country of Baghlān (縛伽浪國).

To the southwest of the country of Hu (活國) is the country of Baghlān (縛伽浪國). The country of Baghlān is over fifty li from east to west and over two hundred li from south to north. The capital city of the country is over ten li in circumference.
To the south, one reaches the country of Rūb-Simingān (紇露悉泯健國). The country of Rūb-Simingān is over one thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit.

To the northwest, one arrives at the country of Khulm (忽懍國). The country of Khulm is over eight hundred li in circuit. The capital city of the country is five or six li in circuit. There are more than ten sanghārāmas (伽藍), and the community of monks numbers more than five hundred.

To the west, one arrives at the country of Bākhl (縛喝國). The country of Bākhl is more than eight hundred *li* from east to west and more than four hundred *li* from north to south. To the north, it borders the Vaxšu River (縛芻河). The capital city of the country is more than twenty *li* in circuit, and people all call it the "Little Rājagṛha." Although the city is fortified, it has very few inhabitants. The produce of the land is extremely abundant, and the various flowers of land and water are difficult to enumerate fully. There are more than one hundred monasteries and over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
The country of Jumadha (銳秣陀國) is fifty or sixty li from east to west and over one hundred li from south to north. The capital city of the country is over ten li in circuit.

Proceeding southwest, one reaches the country of Gūzgān (胡寔健國). The country of Gūzgān is more than five hundred *li* from east to west and over one thousand *li* from north to south. The capital city of the country is more than twenty *li* in circumference. There are many mountains and rivers, and it produces excellent horses.

Proceeding northwest, one reaches the country of Ṭālaqān (呾剌健國). The country of Ṭālaqān is over five hundred li from east to west and fifty or sixty li from south to north. The capital city of the country is over ten li in circumference. To the west, it borders on the frontiers of the country of Pārs (波剌斯國).

Traveling south from the country of Bactria (縛喝國) for over one hundred li, one arrives at the country of Gachi (揭職國). The country of Gachi is over five hundred li from east to west and three hundred li from north to south. The capital city is four or five li in circuit; the land is stony and barren, with a succession of hills and mounds. There are few flowers or fruits, but much pulse and wheat. The climate is cold and severe, and the customs of the people are fierce and violent. There are more than ten monasteries and over three hundred monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school. To the southeast, one enters the Great Snow Mountains (Mahāhimavat), where the valleys are deep and the mountains high, and the peaks and cliffs are treacherous. Wind and snow follow one another, and even in midsummer, it remains frozen; accumulated snow fills the valleys, and the paths are difficult to traverse. Mountain spirits and demons act with violent malice, and bands of robbers roam freely, making murder their occupation.

After traveling more than six hundred li, I left the borders of the country of Tukhāra (都貨邏國) and arrived at the country of Bāmīyāna (梵衍那國). The country of Bāmīyāna is more than two thousand li from east to west and over three hundred li from north to south; it is situated in the midst of the Snow Mountains. The people rely on the mountain valleys and build their settlements according to the terrain. The capital city of the kingdom rests against a cliff and spans a valley, measuring six or seven li in length, with high rocks at its back to the north. There is winter wheat, but few flowers or fruits; it is suitable for animal husbandry, and there are many sheep and horses. The climate is cold and harsh, and the customs are rugged and fierce; the people mostly wear garments of leather and wool, which is appropriate for their environment. Their writing, customs, and use of currency are the same as those of the country of Tukhāra. Their language is slightly different, but their appearance and manners are largely the same. Their sincere faith is especially greater than that of neighboring countries. From the Three Jewels above down to the hundred spirits below, there is none to whom they do not offer their sincerity, exhausting their hearts in reverence. For merchants traveling to and fro, the heavenly spirits manifest auspicious signs or show ominous changes to seek blessings and merit. There are several dozen monasteries and several thousand monks, who follow the Lokottaravāda school (說出世部) of the Lesser Vehicle.

In a mountain nook to the northeast of the royal city, there is a standing stone statue of the Buddha, one hundred and forty or fifty feet high; its golden color is dazzling, and its precious ornaments are brilliant. To the east is a monastery, which was built by a former king of this country.
To the east of the monastery is a standing statue of the Buddha Śākyamuni (釋迦佛) made of brass, over one hundred feet high; its parts were cast separately and then joined together to form the whole.

In a monastery two or three li east of the city, there is a reclining statue of the Buddha entering nirvana, over a thousand feet long. Whenever the king holds a Great Quinquennial Assembly (pañcavārṣika) here, he gives away everything from his wife and children down to the national treasures; once the state treasury is exhausted, he offers himself as a gift, and his officials and subordinates then pay ransom to the monks to redeem him, considering such practices to be their primary duty.
From here, traveling east, one enters the Snow Mountains (Himavat), crosses over the Black Range (Kṛṣṇagiri), and reaches the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國).

From here, traveling east, one enters the Snow Mountains (Himālaya), crosses the Black Range (Paropamisos), and arrives at the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). The country of Kāpiśī is over four thousand li in circuit; it has the Snow Mountains at its back to the north and is bordered on three sides by the Black Range. The capital city of the country is over ten li in circuit. The land is suitable for grain and wheat, and produces many fruits and trees; it yields fine horses and saffron. Rare goods from various regions are mostly gathered in this country. The climate is cold and windy; the people’s nature is violent and rough, their speech is vulgar, and their marriage customs are chaotic. Their writing is largely the same as that of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國), though their customs, language, and manners of instruction are quite different. They wear garments of wool and clothing made of leather and felt. For currency, they use gold coins, silver coins, and small copper coins, the standards and designs of which differ from those of other countries. The king is of the Kṣatriya caste; he is wise and resourceful, brave and fierce by nature, and his might intimidates the neighboring regions, ruling over ten or more countries. He loves and nurtures his subjects and reveres the Triple Gem. Every year, he commissions a silver Buddha image eighteen feet high and holds a Great Quinquennial Assembly (Pañcavārṣika) to provide for the poor and destitute and bestow alms upon widowers and widows. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas, with more than six thousand monks, who mostly study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. The stūpas and saṃghārāmas are lofty, spacious, vast, and pure. There are several dozen deva temples and over one thousand followers of heterodox paths; some go naked, some smear themselves with ash, and some wear garlands of skulls as crowns.

Three or four li to the east of the great city, at the foot of the northern mountain, there is a large monastery with over three hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). According to the records of former times, King Kaniṣka of the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) once extended his prestige to neighboring countries and his influence to distant regions. He mobilized his army to expand his territory as far as the east of the Pamirs (葱嶺), and the vassal states west of the river, fearing his might, sent hostages to him. Having received the hostage princes, King Kaniṣka treated them with special courtesy and provided them with different residences according to the seasons: in winter they stayed in the various states of India, in summer they returned to the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國), and in spring and autumn they resided in the country of Gandhāra. Because the hostage princes had residences for these three seasons, a monastery was built for each; this monastery is the one built for their summer residence. Therefore, on the walls of the various buildings, the hostage princes are depicted, their appearance and attire quite similar to those of the Middle Kingdom (China). After they were able to return to their own countries, they kept their former residences in their hearts, and although separated by mountains and rivers, they did not cease their offerings. Thus, the present community of monks, whenever the time comes for the entry into or the conclusion of the summer retreat, holds grand Dharma assemblies to pray for blessings and cultivate merit for the sake of the hostage princes, a practice that has continued without interruption to the present day. Beneath the right foot of the statue of the Great Spirit King, located to the south of the east gate of the monastery’s Buddha hall, there is treasure buried in the ground, hidden there by the hostage princes. The inscription regarding this says: "When the monastery falls into disrepair, take this to restore it." Recently, a frontier king, greedy and fierce, heard that this monastery contained much hidden treasure and drove out the monks. Just as he was about to begin the excavation, the figure of a parrot on the crown of the Divine King vigorously flapped its wings and cried out in alarm, causing the earth to shake; the king and his soldiers fell back in terror and collapsed, and only after a long time could they rise, whereupon they apologized for their offense and returned home. On the northern ridge of the monastery there are several stone chambers, which are the places where the hostage princes practiced meditation. Within them are hidden many miscellaneous treasures, and beside them is an inscription, guarded by a yakṣa. Whenever anyone wished to open them and take the treasures within, this yakṣa would manifest various forms through supernatural power—appearing as a lion, a python, a fierce beast, or a poisonous insect—showing great wrath in these strange forms, so that no one dared to attempt an excavation. On a great mountain ridge (Skt. pravaragiri) two or three li to the west of the stone chambers, there is a statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara; if someone prays with utmost sincerity to see him, the Bodhisattva emerges from the statue in a wondrous physical form to comfort the practitioner.

Thirty-some *li* southeast of the great city, one arrives at the Rāhula (曷邏怙羅) monastery. Beside it is a *stūpa* over one hundred feet high. On days of fasting, it sometimes emits a bright light. From the crevices in the stone of the inverted-bowl structure, black fragrant oil flows out, and in the quiet of the night, sounds of music are sometimes heard. According to ancient records, it was built in the past by Rāhula, a high minister of this country. After the work was completed, someone spoke to him in a dream, saying, "The *stūpa* you have built does not yet contain any relics. Tomorrow morning, someone will offer one; you should request it from the king." At dawn, he entered the court and made his request, saying, "Unaware of my own mediocrity, I dare to make a petition." The king asked, "What is it that you desire?" He replied, "There is someone who will offer something today; I hope for your grace to bestow it upon me." The king said, "Very well." Rāhula stood waiting at the palace gate, watching for the arrival. Soon, a man appeared carrying a relic casket. The minister asked, "What do you intend to offer?" The man replied, "Buddha relics." The minister said, "I will guard them for you; you should first report this to the king." Fearing that the king would prize the relics and regret his previous favor, Rāhula hurried to the monastery and climbed the *stūpa*. Moved by his utmost sincerity, the stone inverted bowl opened of its own accord. He placed the relics inside and rushed out so quickly that his clothes were caught. The king sent men to pursue him, but the stone had already closed. Therefore, black fragrant oil flows from its crevices.

Two hundred and more *li* northwest of the royal city, one arrives at the Great Snowy Mountain (Mahāhimavat). On the summit of the mountain is a pool; those who pray for rain or for clear weather have their wishes fulfilled according to their requests. According to ancient records, there was formerly an arhat in the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) who regularly received offerings from the nāga king of this pool. Every day at the midday meal, he would use his supernatural powers to sit upon his rope bed and travel through the void. His attendant, a novice (śrāmaṇera), secretly clung to the underside of the rope bed and hid himself. When the time for the meal arrived, the arhat departed; upon reaching the nāga palace, he discovered the novice. The nāga king then invited them both to stay for the meal. The nāga king served the arhat with heavenly nectar, while he served the novice with human food. Once the arhat had finished his meal, he expounded the essential teachings of the Dharma for the nāga king. The novice, as was his custom, washed the bowls for his master. Finding leftover grains in the bowl and being astonished by their fragrance, he immediately gave rise to an evil vow, resenting his master and feeling anger toward the nāga: "May all the power of my merit manifest now, that I may cut off this nāga’s life and become the king myself." At the moment the novice made this vow, the nāga king already felt a headache. The arhat spoke words of instruction and exhortation, and the nāga king apologized for his faults and blamed himself; however, the novice remained resentful and did not follow the instruction to forgive. Once they had returned to the monastery (saṃghārāma), the novice made a vow with utmost sincerity. Due to the power of his merit, he died that very night and was reborn as a great nāga king. Fierce and impetuous, he came to enter the pool, killed the former nāga king, occupied the nāga palace, took possession of his retinue, and assumed control over his life. Because of his former vow, he stirred up violent storms and rain, uprooting trees and intending to destroy the monastery. At that time, King Kaniṣka, feeling puzzled, inquired about the matter, and the arhat explained everything to the king. The king then established a monastery (saṃghārāma) for the nāga at the foot of the Snow Mountains and erected a stupa (stūpa) over one hundred feet high. The nāga, harboring his former resentment, proceeded to stir up wind and rain. The king was intent on universal salvation, while the nāga, fueled by the poison of his anger, committed acts of violence, causing the monastery and the stupa to be destroyed six times and rebuilt seven times. King Kaniṣka, ashamed that his work was not being completed, wished to fill in the nāga’s pool and destroy his dwelling; he immediately mobilized his troops and arrived at the foot of the Snow Mountains. At that time, the nāga king, feeling deep fear, transformed himself into an old brahmin, knocked on the king’s elephant, and remonstrated, saying: "Great King, you have cultivated good roots in the past and planted many superior causes, which has enabled you to become a human king to whom all submit. Why, then, do you contend with a nāga today? A nāga is merely an animal, a base and vile species, yet he possesses great power and cannot be contested by force. Riding the clouds and driving the wind, treading on the void and walking on water—these are things not controlled by human power; how could they be objects of the king’s wrath? If the king now mobilizes the entire nation to fight against a single nāga, then if you win, the king will gain no prestige for subduing a distant foe, and if you lose, the king will suffer the shame of being defeated by an unworthy opponent. For the sake of the king’s own interests, it would be best to withdraw the troops." King Kaniṣka did not follow this advice. The nāga then returned to the pool, and with a sound like rolling thunder, violent winds uprooted trees, sand and stones fell like rain, clouds and fog obscured the light, and the army’s horses were terrified. The king then took refuge in the Triple Gem and prayed for protection, saying, "By virtue of the many blessings I cultivated in past lives, I became a king of men, deterring powerful enemies and ruling over Jambudvīpa; that I am now humiliated by this dragon beast is truly due to my meager merit. May all the power of my merit manifest at this moment." Immediately, great smoke and flames arose from his two shoulders; the dragon retreated, the wind grew still, and the clouds and fog rolled away. The king ordered his army to each carry one stone to fill the dragon pool. The dragon king transformed back into a Brahmin and entreated the king again, saying, "I am the dragon king of that pool; fearing your majesty, I submit to you. May the king have compassion and forgive my past offenses. The king nurtures and protects all living beings; why would you inflict harm upon me alone? If you kill me, both you and I will fall into the evil realms; you will be guilty of taking a life, and I will harbor a heart of resentment and enmity—karmic retribution is clear, and good and evil are manifest." The king then made a clear covenant with the dragon, stating that if there were any further offenses, he would certainly not forgive them. The dragon said, "Because of my evil karma, I have received a body as a dragon. The nature of a dragon is fierce and evil, and I cannot control myself; if a heart of anger arises, I may forget what has been stipulated. Now that the king is establishing a monastery (saṃghārāma), I dare not destroy it. I will send one person to keep watch on the mountain ridge; if black clouds arise, they must strike the ghaṇṭā (gong) urgently. When I hear that sound, my evil heart will cease." The king thereupon renovated the monastery and built a stūpa, and the practice of watching for clouds continues to this day without interruption. According to the records of predecessors, there is more than one *sheng* of the Tathāgata’s bone and flesh relics inside the stūpa, and the miraculous events associated with them are difficult to describe in detail. Once, smoke suddenly rose from within the stūpa, followed shortly by fierce flames. The people of the time thought the stūpa had been reduced to ashes, but after gazing at it for a long while, the fire died down and the smoke vanished. Then, the relics were seen like a banner of white pearls, circling the central pillar and winding upwards to the edge of the clouds before whirling back down.

Inside the Old Royal Monastery (Jiuwang Jialan) on the south bank of the great river to the northwest of the royal city, there is a tooth of the Bodhisattva Śākya from his childhood, over an inch long. To the southeast of this monastery is another monastery, also named Old Royal, which possesses a piece of the Tathāgata’s skull bone over an inch wide; its color is yellowish-white, and the hair pores are distinct. There is also hair of the Tathāgata, the color of which is dark blue, spiraling to the right, drawn out to over a foot in length, and curled to about half an inch. Regarding these three items, whenever the six fast days arrive, the king and his ministers scatter flowers in offering. To the southwest of the Skull Bone Monastery is the Old Queen’s Monastery (Jiuwangfei Jialan), in which there is a gold and copper stūpa over a hundred feet high. According to local tradition, there is more than a *sheng* of the Buddha’s relics inside this stūpa. On the night of the fifteenth day of every month, it emits a circular light that illuminates the dew basin, shining continuously until dawn, at which point the light gradually withdraws into the stūpa.

The kingdom of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國) is over four thousand li in circuit; to the north, it has the Snow Mountains at its back, and on three sides, it is bordered by the Black Range (黑嶺). The kingdom’s great capital city is over ten li in circuit.

Traveling over fifty li to the northwest of the stūpas of Brahmā and Indra, there is a stūpa where the Śākya Tathāgata converted the Mother of Demon Children (Hārītī) and caused her to cease harming people; therefore, it is the custom of this country to offer sacrifices to her when praying for offspring.
Traveling two hundred-odd li southeast from the place where the Bodhisattva Śyāmaka (商莫迦) was harmed, one arrives at the city of Varusa (跋虜沙城).

More than twenty *li* to the northeast of the city of Varusa (跋虜沙城), one arrives at the mountain of Daṇḍaloka (彈多落迦山). On the ridge there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, where Prince Sudāna (蘇達拏) once lived in seclusion. Not far to its side is a stūpa where the prince gave his son and daughter as a gift to a brahmin; the brahmin beat the children, and their blood stained the ground, so that even now the plants and trees there still bear a crimson hue. In the crags is a stone chamber, the place where the prince and his consort practiced meditation. In the valley, the branches of the forest trees hang down like curtains; these are all places where the prince used to roam and rest in the past. Not far to its side is a stone hut, which is the dwelling place of an ancient *ṛṣi*.

Traveling over a hundred *li* to the northwest from the rishi’s hut and crossing a small mountain, one reaches the great mountain (Pravaragiri). On the southern side of the mountain is a monastery with few monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna. Beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. This is the place where the One-Horned Rishi (Ekashṛṅga-ṛṣi) formerly resided. The rishi was seduced and led astray by a courtesan, causing him to lose his supernatural powers, and the courtesan then rode upon his shoulders to return to the city.

Fifty-some *li* to the northeast of the city of Varusa (跋虜沙城), one arrives at Mount Cong (崇山). On the mountain, there is a blue stone image of the wife of Maheśvara (大自在天), who is the goddess Bhīmā (毘摩天女). According to local tradition, this celestial image appeared there naturally. Because it is highly miraculous, there are many who come to pray; people from all the countries of India, whether noble or humble, gather here from far and near to seek blessings and make vows. For those who wish to see the form of the celestial deity, if they are sincere and single-minded and fast for seven days, some may obtain a vision, and most of their prayers are fulfilled. At the foot of the mountain, there is a temple of Maheśvara where ash-smearing heretics (塗灰外道) perform their ritual worship.

Traveling one hundred and fifty li southeast from the Bhīmā temple (毘摩天祠), one reaches the city of Udakahāṇḍa (烏鐸迦漢荼城), which is over twenty li in circuit and borders the Sindhu River (信度河) to the south. The inhabitants are wealthy and happy, precious goods are accumulated in abundance, and rare curiosities from all quarters are mostly gathered here.

The country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國) is over five thousand li in circuit. Mountains and valleys are contiguous, and rivers and marshes connect with the plains. Although grain is sown, the land is not very fertile. There are many grapes but little sugarcane; the land produces gold and iron and is suitable for saffron; the forests are lush, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The cold and heat are temperate, and the winds and rains follow their proper seasons. The people are timid and cowardly, and their customs are deceitful. They are fond of learning but do not achieve success, and they make incantations their professional skill. They mostly wear white cotton cloth and have few other types of clothing. Although their language differs, it is largely the same as that of India. Their writing and etiquette are quite similar. They highly esteem the Buddhadharma and revere and believe in the Mahāyāna. Along the banks of the Śubhavastu River (蘇婆伐窣堵河), there were formerly one thousand four hundred monasteries, most of which are now desolate. Formerly there were eighteen thousand monks, but now they have gradually decreased. They all study the Mahāyāna and make silent meditation their occupation; they are skilled at reciting the texts but have not yet fathomed their profound meanings. Their moral conduct is pure, and they are especially skilled in incantations. Regarding the traditions of the Vinaya rules, there are five schools: first, the Dharmaguptaka; second, the Mahīśāsaka; third, the Kāśyapīya; fourth, the Sarvāstivāda; and fifth, the Mahāsāṃghika. There are more than ten deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. There are four or five fortified cities, and their king usually governs from the city of Mangala (瞢揭釐城). The city is sixteen or seventeen li in circuit and is densely populated.
There are four or five fortified cities, and the king mostly governs from the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城). The city is sixteen or seventeen li in circuit, and the inhabitants are numerous and prosperous.
Along the banks of the Śubhavastu River (蘇婆伐窣堵河), there were formerly one thousand four hundred monasteries, most of which are now desolate.

Traveling two hundred and fifty or sixty *li* northeast from the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), one enters a great mountain and reaches the Apalāla (阿波邏羅) Dragon Spring, which is the source of the Śubhavastu (蘇婆伐窣堵) River. The stream flows to the southwest; it contains ice during the spring and summer, and at dusk, the flying spray resembles snow, with the snowflakes shimmering in five colors and radiating light in all directions.  As for this dragon, in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was born in the human realm with the name Gangi (殑祇); he was deeply skilled in sorcery and restrained evil dragons from causing torrential rains, so the people of the country relied on him to store surplus grain. The inhabitants and the masses, feeling gratitude and cherishing his virtue, taxed each household one *dou* of grain to present to him. After many years had passed, there were some who defaulted on their payments. Gangi became angry and vowed to become a poisonous dragon, violently unleashing wind and rain to damage the crops. After his life ended, he became the dragon of this pool. The spring flows with white water, damaging the land's productivity.  The Śākya Tathāgata, governing the world with great compassion, took pity on the people of this country for suffering this unique disaster and descended to this place, desiring to convert the violent dragon. He had the Vajrapāṇi (執金剛神) strike the mountain cliff with his vajra; the Dragon King was terrified and emerged to take refuge. Hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, his mind became pure and he attained faith and enlightenment. The Tathāgata then commanded him not to damage the crops. The dragon said, "Everything I eat depends on the harvest from the people's fields. Now, having received the holy teaching, I fear it will be difficult to sustain myself; I request to collect grain stores once every twelve years." The Tathāgata, in his encompassing compassion, took pity and granted this. Thus, even now, the country suffers the calamity of white water once every twelve years.

More than thirty *li* to the southwest of the Apalāla (阿波邏羅) Dragon Spring, on a large flat rock on the northern bank of the river, there is a footprint trodden by the Tathāgata. Its measured length varies according to the merit of the person, for this is where the Tathāgata left his mark when he departed after subduing this dragon. Later generations piled stones upon it to construct a chamber, and people from far and near gather there to make offerings of flowers and incense.
Going more than thirty li downstream, one reaches the rock where the Tathāgata washed his clothes, where the patterns of the kaṣāya robe are as distinct as if they had been engraved.

Not far from its side is the great stūpa of Soma (蘇摩). In the past, when the Tathāgata was Indra (帝釋), there was a time of pestilence in the world. Taking pity on all sentient beings, he transformed his body into a Soma snake; all who ate of it were restored to health and comfort.

Traveling sixty or seventy li southwest of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), on the east bank of a great river, there is a stūpa over sixty feet high, which was built by King Uttarasena (上軍王). Formerly, when the Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he told the great assembly: "After my nirvāṇa, King Uttarasena of the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國) should be given a share of the relics." When the various kings were about to measure out the shares, King Uttarasena arrived late, and consequently, there was talk of slighting him. At that time, the assembly of devas and men reiterated the words of the Tathāgata’s final charge, so he was allowed to participate in the distribution; he carried them back to his own country and reverently constructed this to honor them.

By the bank of the great river beside the stupa, there is a large rock shaped like an elephant. Formerly, when King Uttarasena (上軍王) was returning with the relics carried by a great white elephant, the elephant suddenly stumbled and fell upon reaching this spot, and consequently died; it then turned into stone, and a stupa was built right beside it.
The capital city of the kingdom is more than ten li in circuit.

More than seventy li to the northwest of the great city is the pond of the Dragon King Elāpattra (醫羅鉢呾羅), which is over a hundred paces in circumference. Its water is clear and pure, and multicolored lotus flowers bloom there together in diverse hues. This dragon is the one who, in the time of the Buddha Kāśyapa, was a bhikṣu that damaged an elāpattra tree. Therefore, when the people of that land now pray for rain or clear weather, they must go to the pond together with a śramaṇa; when he snaps his fingers and offers words of comfort, their wishes are invariably fulfilled.

Traveling over thirty li southeast from the Dragon Pond and entering between two mountains, there is a stupa (stūpa) built by King Aśoka (無憂王), over a hundred feet in height. It is the prediction of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni that when the future World-Honored One Maitreya (慈氏世尊) appears in the world, there will naturally be four great treasure troves, and this sacred site is one of them. According to ancient records, whenever an earthquake occurs and all the mountains shake, the area for a hundred paces around the treasure remains perfectly still without any quivering. Some foolish men once attempted to dig it up recklessly, but the earth shook and they all fell prostrate. Nearby is a monastery (saṃghārāma), which is severely dilapidated and has long been devoid of monks.
The capital city of the country (Siṃhapura 僧訶補羅國) is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit; it rests against the mountains and occupies the ridges, making it steep, precipitous, and strategically secure.

Not far to the south of the city is a stupa (stūpa), which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Its ornamentation is damaged, but miraculous manifestations occur there in succession. Beside it is a monastery (saṃghārāma), which is empty and without monks.

Forty or fifty li to the southeast of the city, one reaches a stone stupa built by King Aśoka, which is over two hundred feet high. There are more than ten ponds surrounding it on the left and right, with banks carved from stone in various shapes and kinds. The clear water surges and flows, gurgling and splashing; dragons, fish, and other aquatic creatures swim deep within their underwater grottoes, while lotus flowers of four colors cover the clear pools. A hundred kinds of fruit trees grow in abundance, flourishing together in different colors; the woods and ponds reflect one another, truly a place for recreation. Beside it is a monastery, long since devoid of monks. Not far from the side of the stupa is the place where the original teacher of the white-robed heretics realized the principles he sought and first preached his doctrine; there is now a memorial mark there, and a deva temple has been built beside it. His followers practice austerities, diligent day and night, without a moment of rest. The doctrine preached by their original teacher largely steals the meaning of the Buddhist sutras, establishing methods according to their own kind and imitating the rules and rituals. The elders are called bhikṣu (苾芻), and the juniors are called śrāmaṇera (沙彌). Their deportment and monastic discipline are quite similar to the Buddhist laws. They differ only in that they retain a small amount of hair, go naked, or, if they do wear clothing, it is white, which serves to distinguish them from other sects. Their image of the heavenly teacher is surreptitiously modeled after the Tathāgata; the clothing is different, but the auspicious marks are no different.

To the north of the site of the body-sacrifice, there is a stone stūpa over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It is carved with extraordinary craftsmanship and often illuminates with divine light. Small stūpas and various stone niches, numbering in the hundreds, surround this sacred precinct; those who suffer from illnesses are often cured after circumambulating it. To the east of the stone stūpa is a monastery (saṃghārāma) with more than a hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna teachings.

From here, traveling east for more than fifty li, one reaches the mountain of Vyāsa (孤山). There is a monastery (saṃghārāma) there with over two hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. Flowers and fruits are abundant, and the springs and ponds are as clear as mirrors. Beside it is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which marks the spot where the Tathāgata in the past converted an evil yakṣa, commanding him to cease eating meat.
The capital city of the country faces a great river to its west; it measures twelve or thirteen li from north to south and four or five li from east to west.

More than ten *li* southeast of the new city, north of the old city, and on the sunny side of the great mountain (Pravaragiri), there is a monastery with over three hundred monks. In its stupa is a Buddha’s tooth, about an inch and a half long and yellowish-white in color, which sometimes emits light on fast days. In the past, when the Kṛtīya (訖利多) race destroyed the Buddha’s Dharma, the monks dispersed, each living where they found it convenient. There was one śramaṇa who traveled through the various regions of India to observe and pay homage to the sacred sites, expressing his utmost sincerity.
