Later, hearing that his home country had been pacified, he set out on his return journey. He encountered a herd of elephants moving across the marshes, rushing about and roaring thunderously. Seeing this, the śramaṇa climbed a tree to avoid them. At that time, the elephants rushed together, vied with each other to suck up pond water to soak the roots of the tree, and then collectively pushed and dug at it until the tree finally toppled over. Having captured the śramaṇa, they carried him on their backs into a great forest, where a sick elephant lay suffering from a sore; it led the monk's hand to the afflicted spot, which had been pierced by a piece of withered bamboo. The śramaṇa then pulled out the bamboo, applied medicine, tore his robe, and wrapped the elephant's foot. Another large elephant brought a golden casket and gave it to the sick elephant, who, upon receiving it, passed it to the śramaṇa; when the śramaṇa opened the casket, he found it contained a Buddha’s tooth. The elephants surrounded him, and the monk had no way to leave. The next day at the time of the midday meal, they each brought exotic fruits to serve as his meal. After he had eaten, they carried the monk out of the forest, and only after traveling several hundred *li* did they set him down, whereupon each knelt in worship and departed. The śramaṇa reached the western border of the country and crossed a rapid river; when he reached midstream, the boat was on the verge of capsizing. Those sharing the boat said to one another, "The cause of this boat's impending disaster is this śramaṇa; he must possess a relic of the Tathāgata, and the dragons covet it." The boatman searched and indeed found a Buddha’s tooth. Then the śramaṇa held up the Buddha’s tooth and, looking down, said to the dragon, "I now entrust this to you, and shall return before long to take it back." He did not cross the river, but turned the boat back and departed; looking at the river, he sighed and said, "Because I lack the arts of subdual, I have been deceived by a dragon beast!" He went again to India to learn the methods for subduing dragons. After three years, he returned to his own country; when he reached the riverbank and set up an altar, the dragon then held up the casket of the Buddha’s tooth and presented it to the śramaṇa. The śramaṇa took it back and, at this saṃghārāma (伽藍), performed offerings.
More than ten li to the southeast of the new city, to the north of the old city, and on the southern slope of the great mountain (Pravaragiri), there is a monastery with over three hundred monks.

Fourteen or fifteen li to the south of the monastery, there is a small monastery containing a standing statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩). For those who vow to fast until death with the intention of seeing the Bodhisattva, he manifests his marvelous physical body from within the statue.

More than ten li to the east of the Buddha-tooth monastery, among the cliffs of the northern mountains, there is a small monastery where the great master of shastras Skandhila (索建地羅) once composed the *Abhidharma-prakaraṇa-pāda-śāstra* (眾事分毘婆沙論). In the small monastery there is a stone stūpa over fifty feet high, which contains the bodily relics of an arhat. Previously, there was an arhat whose physical form was immense, and all that he ate was equal to that of an elephant. The people of the time ridiculed him, saying, "You only know how to eat your fill; how could you understand right from wrong?" When the arhat was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he told the people, "I shall soon attain the state of no-remainder; I wish to speak of the wonderful Dharma that I have personally realized." When the people heard this, they mocked one another, yet they all gathered together to observe his success or failure. Then the arhat said to the people, "I will now tell you the original cause and condition. Prior to this life, I received the retribution of an elephant's body in East India, where I lived in the king's inner stable. At that time, there was a śramaṇa in that country who traveled far to India to search for the scriptures and treatises of the holy teachings. The king took me and gave me to the śramaṇa to carry the Buddhist scriptures, and in this way, I arrived here. Not long after, I died. By virtue of the merit accumulated through carrying the scriptures, I was born as a human. Furthermore, blessed with remaining fortune, I donned the dyed robes early and diligently sought liberation, never resting, until I attained the six supernatural powers and severed the desires of the three realms. However, regarding what I eat, the residual habit remains; I always restrain myself, eating only one-third of what I once did." Although there was this account, people still did not believe it. He then ascended into the void, entered the fire-light samādhi (火光定), and smoke and flames issued from his body as he entered parinirvāṇa; his remaining bones fell to the ground, and a stūpa (窣堵波) was erected over them.

Traveling one hundred forty or fifty li west of the city, to the north of a great river and the south of a mountain, one reaches a Mahāsāṃghika monastery (大眾部伽藍) with over a hundred monks. In the past, the Master of Śāstras Bodhila (佛地羅論師) composed the Mahāsāṃghika work *Tattvasaṃcaya Śāstra* (集真論) here.

Traveling southeast from the great city for more than one hundred *li*, one arrives at the city of Navadevakula (納縛提婆矩羅城). It is situated on the eastern bank of the Ganges (殑伽河) and measures more than twenty *li* in circumference. Flowery groves and clear ponds reflect one another. To the northwest of the city of Navadevakula, on the east side of the Ganges, there is a temple to a deva, with multi-storied pavilions and terraced platforms, featuring extraordinary workmanship and unique construction. Five *li* to the east of the city, there are three monasteries (saṃghārāma) sharing the same wall but having different gates, with over five hundred monks who all study the Hīnayāna Sarvāstivāda school. Two hundred paces in front of the monasteries, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. Although the base has collapsed and sunk, it is still over one hundred feet high; this is the place where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for seven days. Inside it are relics that occasionally emit light. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Three or four *li* to the north of the monasteries, bordering the bank of the Ganges, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. Formerly, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here for seven days, at which time five hundred hungry ghosts (preta) came to the Buddha’s presence, heard the Dharma, attained understanding, and, abandoning their ghost bodies, were reborn in heaven. Beside the stūpa of the preaching of the Dharma are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Beside that, there is also a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata.

In the city there is a temple to a deity, adorned and resplendent, with many varied manifestations of spiritual power. According to its scriptures, this place is a supreme site for sentient beings to cultivate merit; to donate a single coin at this temple yields merit exceeding a gift of a thousand gold pieces elsewhere. Furthermore, those who treat life lightly and end their existence within the temple receive heavenly bliss and joy, eternal and inexhaustible. In front of the temple hall stands a large tree with luxuriant branches and dense foliage, where a man-eating ghost (piśāca) has made its home; consequently, many skeletal remains lie scattered around it. When people come to this temple, they invariably throw away their lives, being both intimidated by perverse doctrines and enticed by the deity; from antiquity to the present, this erroneous practice has continued without change. Recently, there was a Brahmin, a son of a noble clan, who was magnanimous, wise, perceptive, and highly talented; he came to the temple and said to the crowd: "It is difficult to guide and transform those with crooked customs and base minds; I shall first join them in their actions and then lead them to conversion." Having ascended the tree, he looked down and said to his friends: "I am about to die. What I once considered a deception is now proven true; heavenly beings and celestial music are in the sky to receive me, and I shall abandon this base form to follow them to a superior realm." He immediately sought to cast himself down to end his life, and though his friends remonstrated with him, his resolve did not waver. He spread out his clothes all around beneath the tree, and when he threw himself down, he remained unharmed and his body was preserved. After a long while he regained consciousness and said: "I only saw various deities in the sky summoning me; this was the lure of evil spirits, not the attainment of heavenly bliss."

To the east of the great city, where two rivers meet, the area is over ten *li* wide; the land is high and dry, covered with fine sand. From ancient times to the present, whenever kings and noble families have wished to perform acts of charity, they have all come to this place to distribute gifts without measure, and thus it is called the Grand Arena of Almsgiving (Mahādānapīṭha). The current King Śīlāditya (戒日王) continues the traditions of his predecessors and is devoted to the practice of charity; he accumulates wealth for five years and then, in a single day, empties his stores, gathering a vast quantity of precious goods at this arena. On the first day, a large statue of the Buddha is installed and adorned with various gems, and the most exquisite and rare treasures are offered to it. Next, offerings are made to the resident monks; then to the assembly present; then to those of high talent and profound learning, and those of broad knowledge and many skills; then to the disciples of non-Buddhist sects and those who live in seclusion; and finally to the widowed, the orphaned, the solitary, and the poor and destitute. Every kind of precious object is prepared and the finest foods are exhausted; in this graded order, everyone is provided for. Once the treasury is emptied and all clothing and ornaments are exhausted, he gives away the lustrous pearl in his topknot and the various necklaces on his body one after another, without the slightest regret. Having completed the distribution, he declares: "How joyful! All that I possessed has now been deposited into the indestructible treasury of the Vajra." Following this, the kings of various countries each offer him precious garments, and within ten days, his treasury is filled once again. At the confluence of the rivers to the east of the Grand Arena of Almsgiving, several hundred people drown themselves every day. The local custom holds that those who wish to be reborn in heaven should abstain from food and drown themselves at this spot, for by bathing in the middle of the current, their sins and defilements will be eradicated. For this reason, people from distant foreign lands flock here, fasting for seven days before ending their lives. As for the mountain apes and wild deer, they roam in groups along the riverbank; some return after washing in the current, while others fast until they die. During the great almsgiving of King Śīlāditya (戒日王), there was a macaque that lived by the riverbank, remaining alone under a tree, isolating itself and fasting, until it died of starvation after several days. Therefore, the various non-Buddhist ascetics (外道) who practice austerities plant tall pillars in the river. At the approach of dawn, they climb them, grasping the top of the pillar with one hand and one foot while stepping on a side peg, with the other hand and foot suspended and stretched out into the void, held straight without bending. They crane their necks and stare with wide eyes, watching the sun as it rotates to the right, and only when dusk falls do they descend. There are dozens of such followers who, hoping through this diligent suffering to escape the cycle of birth and death, have never slackened for several decades.

Traveling over seven hundred li through a great forest to the northeast of the dragon cave and crossing the Ganges (gaṅgā) River, one arrives at the city of Kāśapura (迦奢布羅城), which is over ten li in circuit and whose inhabitants are wealthy and happy. Beside the city is an old monastery of which only the foundations remain; this is the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla once subdued the heretics. A former king of this country supported heterodox views and wished to destroy the Buddha-dharma while venerating the heretics. From among the heretics, he summoned a master of treatises who was intelligent, brilliant, and well-versed in subtle mysteries to compose a fallacious and heterodox work of one thousand stanzas, totaling thirty-two thousand words, to slander the Buddha-dharma and establish his own sect as the orthodox one. Thereupon, he summoned the assembly of monks and ordered them to engage in a debate. If the heretics were victorious, the Buddha-dharma was to be destroyed; if the assembly of monks were not defeated, they were to cut out their tongues in atonement. At that time, the monks, fearing defeat, gathered and discussed the matter, saying, "The sun of wisdom has already set, and the bridge of the Dharma is about to be destroyed. The king sides with the heretics; how can we oppose them? With the situation as it is, what plan can we devise?" The assembly was silent, and no one could offer a suggestion. The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, though young in years, was eloquent, wise, and widely learned, with a character of great breadth. He spoke out in the midst of the assembly, saying, "Although I am not clever, I ask to present a brief proposal. It is truly appropriate that I should quickly respond to the king's command. If I win the high debate, it will be a spiritual blessing; if I am defeated in the inquiry, it will be attributed to my tender age. In this way, there will be an explanation whether I advance or retreat, and the Dharma and the Sangha will be without fault." Everyone said, "This is acceptable." He followed his plan, immediately responded to the king's command, and ascended the debate seat. The non-Buddhist (tīrthika) then laid out his main points, modulating his tone and meaning, and recited his own tenets, waiting for the opponent to raise objections. The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (護法) accepted his words and laughed, saying, "I have already won! Will you recite them in reverse order? Or will you recite them in a confused manner?" The non-Buddhist was taken aback and said to him, "Do not be arrogant. If you can repeat the words in their entirety, that will be victory; accept the text as it is, and then explain its meaning." Dharmapāla then followed his intonation and recited the text and its meaning; his phrasing and logic were not in error, and his tone and rhythm were without discrepancy. Upon hearing this, the non-Buddhist wanted to cut out his own tongue. Dharmapāla said, "Cutting the tongue is not an apology; changing one's views is repentance." He then preached the Dharma for him, and his heart became faithful and his mind enlightened. The king abandoned his heterodox path and followed and honored the true Dharma. Beside the place where Dharmapāla subdued the non-Buddhist, there is a stupa (窣堵波) built by King Aśoka (無憂王); although its foundation has subsided, it is still over two hundred feet high. This is where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for six months. Nearby are the traces of his walking meditation (caṅkrama) and a stupa containing his hair and nails.

Three or four li to the northwest of the monastery, one reaches the Wood of Regained Sight (Andhavana). There are traces of the Tathāgata’s walking meditation and places where various sages practiced concentration, all marked by trees and designated by stūpas. In the past, there was a band of five hundred bandits in this country who ran amok in the villages and acted lawlessly throughout the cities and states. King Prasenajit (勝軍王) captured them, gouged out their eyes, and abandoned them in the deep forest. The bandits, tormented by suffering, cried out in supplication to the Buddha. At that time, the Tathāgata was in the Jetavana Monastery (逝多精舍); hearing their cries of grief, he felt great compassion, and a gentle, cooling breeze blew medicinal herbs from the Snow Mountains into their eyes, whereupon their sight was immediately restored. Upon seeing the World-Honored One standing before them, they conceived the resolve for enlightenment, bowed in joyful worship, and departed after casting down their staves, which then took root there.

More than sixty li to the northwest of the great city, there is an ancient city; this was the birthplace of the Buddha Kāśyapa (迦葉波佛) during the Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years. To the south of the city is a stūpa, which marks the place where he first met his father after attaining perfect enlightenment. To the north of the city is a stūpa containing the entire-body relics of the Buddha Kāśyapa. Both were built by King Aśoka (無憂王).

Traveling over fifty *li* south of the city, one reaches an ancient city containing a *stūpa*; this was the birthplace of the Buddha Krakucchanda (迦羅迦村馱佛) during the Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was sixty thousand years. Not far to the south of the city is a *stūpa* marking the place where he met his father after attaining full enlightenment. To the southeast of the city is a *stūpa* containing the relics of that Tathāgata’s remains. In front of it stands a stone pillar over thirty feet high, on top of which is carved the image of a lion, with an inscription on the side recording the events of his *parinirvāṇa*; it was erected by King Aśoka (無憂王).

Traveling more than thirty li northeast from the city of Krakucchanda Buddha (迦羅迦村馱佛), one reaches an ancient great city. Inside it is a stupa; this is the native city of Kanakamuni Buddha (迦諾迦牟尼佛) from the time in the Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was forty thousand years. Not far to the northeast is a stupa, which is the place where, having attained perfect enlightenment, he converted his father. To the north of this is a stupa containing the relics of that Tathagata’s physical body. In front of it stands a stone pillar over twenty feet high, with the image of a lion carved on top and an account of his nirvana inscribed on the side, erected by King Aśoka (無憂王).

More than forty li to the northeast of the city, there is a stūpa marking the place where the Prince sat in the shade of a tree, watched the plowing of the fields, and practiced meditation, thereby attaining freedom from desire. When King Śuddhodana (淨飯王) saw the Prince sitting in the shade of the tree, having entered into tranquil meditation, while the sunlight shone brightly yet the shadow of the tree did not move, he knew in his heart that the Prince was spiritually holy, and he cherished and respected him all the more.  To the northwest of the great city, there are several hundred thousand stūpas; these are the places where the Śākya clan were slaughtered. After King Virūḍhaka (毘盧釋迦王) had conquered the Śākyas, he took their kin captive, obtaining ninety-nine million nine hundred thousand people, all of whom he put to death. The piled-up corpses were like a thicket, and the flowing blood formed a pond. The devas, wishing to warn the hearts of men, gathered the remains and buried them.  To the southwest of the place where the Śākyas were slaughtered, there are four small stūpas; these are the places where four Śākya men resisted the army. Originally, when King Prasenajit (勝軍王) ascended the throne, he sought a marriage alliance with the Śākyas. The Śākyas, despising him as not being of their own kind, deceitfully gave him the daughter of a servant, yet they betrothed her with great ceremony. King Prasenajit established her as his principal queen, and she gave birth to a son, who was King Virūḍhaka.  When Virūḍhaka wished to go to his maternal uncles to request instruction and pursue his studies, he arrived south of this city and, seeing a new lecture hall, stopped his carriage to rest inside. When the Śākyas heard of this, they drove him out, cursing him: "You base-born slave, how dare you occupy this hall! This hall was built by the Śākyas, intended for the Buddha to reside in." After Virūḍhaka ascended the throne, he sought to avenge this former humiliation, so he raised an army and marched to this place to encamp his troops. Four members of the Śākya clan, who were personally plowing the fields, immediately resisted them; the invading army retreated and dispersed, and the four men then entered the city. Their clansmen, believing that as descendants of a Universal Monarch (cakravartin) and sons of the Dharma King, they should not have dared to commit acts of violence or heartlessly kill others, felt they had disgraced the clan; consequently, they severed ties with them and sent them into distant exile. After the four men were expelled, they fled north to the Snow Mountains; one became the king of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國), one the king of Bāmīyān (梵衍那國), one the king of Himatala (呬摩呾羅國), and one the king of Śami (商彌國). Their dynasties passed down the throne for generations, and their lineage remained unbroken.

Three or four li to the south of the city is a Nyagrodha (尼拘律) forest, where there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). This is the place where the Śākya Tathāgata, having attained perfect enlightenment, returned to his home country to see his royal father and preach the Dharma. When King Śuddhodana (淨飯王) learned that the Tathāgata had already subdued the army of Māra and was traveling about to teach and guide others, his heart was filled with longing and he wished to pay his respects. He then commanded a messenger to invite the Tathāgata, saying: "Formerly you promised that upon attaining Buddhahood, you would return to your place of birth. These words are still in my ears; the time has come for you to arrive." The messenger reached the Buddha and fully conveyed the king's intent. The Tathāgata replied: "Seven days from now, I shall return to my place of birth." The messenger returned and reported this to the king. King Śuddhodana then ordered his officials and subjects to sprinkle and sweep the roads and to gather flowers and incense, and he went out forty li with his ministers to wait for the carriage and welcome him.  At that time, the Tathāgata was with the great assembly, surrounded by the eight Vajra-warriors, led by the Four Heavenly Kings, with Indra (帝釋) and the devas of the Desire Realm attending on the left, Brahmā (梵王) and the devas of the Form Realm attending on the right, and the congregation of bhikṣus following behind. As the Buddha stood among the assembly, he was like the moon reflecting among the stars; his majestic power moved the three realms, and his radiance surpassed the seven luminaries as he walked through the void to reach his birth country. After the king and his ministers had finished paying their respects, they all returned to the city together and stayed at the Nyagrodha (尼拘盧陀) monastery. Not far to the side of this is a stūpa, which is where the Tathāgata sat facing east under a large tree and accepted the golden-threaded monastic robe from his aunt. Next to this stūpa is another, where the Tathāgata converted the eight princes and five hundred members of the Śākya clan. Inside the east gate of the city, on the left side of the road, there is a stūpa where, in the past, the Bodhisattva Prince Sarvārthasiddha (一切義成) practiced various arts. Outside the gate is a temple of Īśvara (自在天); inside the temple is a stone image of the deity in a towering, rising posture, which is the temple the Prince entered while still in his swaddling clothes. When King Śuddhodana (淨飯王) was escorting the Prince back from the country of Lumbinī (臘伐尼國), they passed by this celestial temple on their way. The King said, "This temple is known for its many spiritual manifestations; whenever the children of the Śākya clan seek protection here, their prayers are always answered; we should take the Prince there to pay his respects." At that time, the wet nurse carried the Prince into the temple, and the stone image of the deity rose to greet the Prince. Once the Prince had left, the image returned to its seated position. Outside the south gate of the city, on the left side of the road, there is a stūpa where the Prince competed in arts with the other Śākyas and shot through iron drums.

More than thirty *li* to the southeast from here is a small *stūpa*. Beside it is a spring with water as clear as a mirror. This is where the prince competed in strength and skill with the other Śākyas; when the arrow left the string, it pierced the drums, passed through the target, and buried its feathers in the pool, causing a clear stream to gush forth. Popular tradition calls it the Arrow Spring (Śarakūpa). Those who suffer from illnesses are often cured by drinking from it or bathing in it. People from distant lands take the mud home and, according to their afflictions, moisten it to apply to their foreheads; through the secret protection of the divine spirits, most of them are healed.

Traveling eighty or ninety *li* northeast from the Arrow Spring (Śarakūpa), one arrives at the Lumbinī Grove (臘伐尼林). There is a bathing pool of the Śākya clan, clear and bright as a mirror, with various flowers blooming in profusion. Twenty-four or twenty-five paces to its north is an Aśoka tree (無憂華樹), now withered and dry, which is the place where the Bodhisattva was born. The Bodhisattva was born on the eighth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the eighth day of the third month; the Sthavira school, however, says it was on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the third month. To the east is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), the place where the two dragons bathed the prince. After the Bodhisattva was born, he walked seven paces in each of the four directions without assistance and declared, "In the heavens above and on earth below, I alone am the honored one. From this time forward, the cycle of birth is at an end." Wherever his feet stepped, a large lotus flower emerged. Two dragons leaped forth and remained in the void, each spitting out water—one cold and one warm—to bathe the prince. To the east of the stūpa marking the bathing of the prince are two clear springs, beside which two stūpas were built at the spot where the two dragons emerged from the earth. After the Bodhisattva was born, his relatives and kin all rushed about, seeking water for washing and bathing. In front of the Lady, two springs gushed forth, one cold and one warm, which were then used for the bathing. The stūpa to the south is the place where Śakra Devendra (天帝釋) received the Bodhisattva. When the Bodhisattva first emerged from the womb, Śakra Devendra knelt and received the Bodhisattva with a wondrous heavenly garment. Next are four stūpas, which are the places where the Four Heavenly Kings (Caturmahārāja) held the Bodhisattva. After the Bodhisattva was born from the right side, the Four Great Heavenly Kings received the Bodhisattva with a golden-colored fine cotton cloth and placed him on a golden table. They approached the Lady and said, "The Lady has given birth to this blessed child; it is truly a cause for rejoicing. Even the gods are joyful, how much more so should the people of the world be?"

Not far from the side of the stupa where the Four Heavenly Kings (Caturmahārāja) held the prince, there is a great stone pillar with the figure of a horse on top, which was erected by King Ashoka (Aśoka). Later, due to a thunderbolt caused by an evil dragon, the pillar was broken in the middle and fell to the ground. Beside it is a small river flowing southeast, which the local people call the Oil River. After Queen Māyā (Māyādevī) had given birth, the gods manifested this pond, its water glossy and pure, intending for the Queen to bathe in it to remove the wind-related infirmities. It has now changed into water, yet its current remains greasy.

Crossing the river more than three hundred paces to the north of the city, there is a stupa, which is the place where the Tathāgata (如來) was cremated. The ground is now yellow and black, the soil mixed with ash and charcoal; if one requests with utmost sincerity, one may obtain relics. When the Tathāgata entered into extinction, humans and devas were moved by grief; they made a coffin of the seven treasures and wrapped his body in a thousand layers of fine cotton, offered incense and flowers, and set up banners and canopies. The Malla (末羅) people then bore the hearse in a procession, with guides in front and followers behind, crossing the Gold River to the north, where they filled it with fragrant oil, piled up much scented wood, and set it ablaze. Two layers of the cotton did not burn: one that was closest to the body and one that covered the outermost layer. In order to distribute the relics for all sentient beings, only the hair and nails remained intact and undamaged. Beside the place of cremation is a stupa, marking the spot where the Tathāgata revealed his two feet to Mahākāśyapa (大迦葉波). When the Tathāgata’s golden coffin had been lowered and the fragrant wood piled up, the fire would not ignite, and the assembly was filled with alarm. Aniruddha (阿泥𢫫陀) said, "We must wait for Kāśyapa." At that time, Mahākāśyapa, with five hundred disciples, came from the mountain forests and arrived at the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城). He asked Ānanda, "Can the body of the World-Honored One still be seen?" Ānanda replied, "It is wrapped in a thousand layers of fine cotton, enclosed in heavy coffins, and the fragrant wood has already been piled up; the cremation is about to take place." At that moment, the Buddha, from within the coffin, revealed his two feet; upon the wheel-marks, a strange color was visible. He asked Ānanda, "Why is there this color?" He replied, "When the Buddha first entered parinirvāṇa, humans and devas were overcome with grief, and the tears of the multitude splashed and stained it, causing this strange color." Kāśyapa paid homage, circumambulated, and offered praises; the fragrant wood ignited spontaneously, and a great fire blazed fiercely. Thus, when the Tathāgata entered extinction, he emerged from the coffin three times: first, he extended his arm to ask Ānanda about the path; next, he sat up to preach the Dharma for his mother; finally, he revealed his two feet to show them to Mahākāśyapa. Beside the place where he revealed his feet is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is the site where the eight kings divided the relics. In front of it, a stone pillar was erected, inscribed with an account of the event. After the Buddha had entered nirvāṇa and the cremation was completed, the kings of eight countries arrived with their fourfold armies and dispatched a straightforward Brahmin to say to the Mallas of Kuśinagara (拘尸力士), "The Teacher of gods and men has entered extinction in this country; therefore, we have come from afar to request a share of the relics." The Mallas replied, "The Tathāgata descended in his majesty to this lower realm; he has extinguished the bright guide of the world and we have lost the compassionate father of all living beings. The relics of the Tathāgata should naturally be worshipped by us alone; you have wearied yourselves on the road in vain, for you shall never obtain them." At that time, the various great kings requested them with humble words, but since they were not granted, they said again, "If polite requests are not followed, the might of our armies is not far off." The straightforward Brahmin spoke aloud, "Reflect! The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One patiently cultivated merit and goodness throughout vast kalpas, as I presume you have all heard; it is not appropriate for you now to seek to oppress one another. Since the relics are here, they should be divided into eight equal portions so that each may receive them for worship; why go so far as to raise troops?" The Mallas followed his words and immediately measured the relics, intending to divide them into eight portions. Śakra (帝釋) said to the kings, "The heavens should have a share; do not rely on force to compete." The Nāga kings Anavatapta (阿那婆答多), Mucilinda (文隣), and Elāpattra (醫那鉢呾羅) also proposed, "Do not exclude us. If it comes to force, the masses are no match for us." The straightforward Brahmin said, "Do not clamor and contend; it is proper to divide them together." He immediately made three portions: first for the devas, second for the Nāga host, and third to remain among humans, which the eight kingdoms then subdivided. The devas, Nāgas, and human kings were all moved to sorrow.

The country of Vārāṇasī (婆羅痆斯國) is over four thousand li in circumference. The capital city of the country borders the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) River to the west; it is eighteen or nineteen li long and five or six li wide. The houses are arranged like the teeth of a comb, the inhabitants are prosperous, families possess vast wealth, and their rooms are filled with rare goods. The people are gentle and respectful by nature, and the customs value diligent study; many believe in non-Buddhist paths, and few respect the Buddha-dharma. The climate is temperate, cereal crops are abundant, fruit trees grow luxuriantly, and the grasses are lush and thick. There are more than thirty saṃghārāmas with over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Sthavira-Saṃmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are over one hundred deva temples with more than ten thousand followers of other paths, most of whom worship Maheśvara; some cut their hair, others wear it in a topknot, they go naked without clothing and smear their bodies with ash, diligently practicing austerities to seek liberation from birth and death. Within the great city are twenty deva temples with multi-storied terraces and shrines made of carved stone and ornamented wood, shaded by luxuriant forests and encircled by clear streams; there is a brass statue of the deity nearly one hundred feet tall, solemn and majestic as if it were alive.

To the northeast of the great city, on the west bank of the Vāraṇā River (婆羅痆河), there is a stūpa over one hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In front of it stands a stone pillar, as bright and fresh as a mirror, with a lustrous surface like flowing liquid, in which the image of the Tathāgata (如來) frequently appears.

Traveling northeast from the Vārāṇasī River for more than ten li, one arrives at the Deer Park Monastery (Mṛgadāva 鹿野伽藍). The grounds are divided into eight sections, enclosed by a continuous wall, with multi-storied halls and pavilions of exquisite architectural splendor. There are one thousand five hundred monks, all studying the teachings of the Hīnayāna Sāmmitīya school. Within the great enclosure is a temple (mūla-gandha-kuṭī 精舍) over two hundred feet high, topped with a golden *āmra* fruit in relief; it has a stone foundation and steps, with brick niches arranged in tiers surrounding it in hundreds of levels, each containing a golden Buddha image in relief. Inside the temple is a brass statue of the Buddha, equal in size to the Tathāgata’s body, in the posture of turning the wheel of the Dharma.

To the southwest of the *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) is a stone *stūpa* built by King Aśoka (無憂王); although its foundation has collapsed, it still remains one hundred feet high. In front of it stands a stone pillar, over seventy feet high. The stone is as lustrous as jade and as clear as a mirror; those who pray with sincere devotion may see various images reflected within it, and at times, signs of good and evil are revealed to the observer. This is the place where the Tathāgata, having attained perfect enlightenment, first turned the wheel of the Dharma. Not far to its side is a *stūpa* marking the spot where Ājñātakauṇḍinya (阿若憍陳如) and the others, seeing the Bodhisattva abandon his ascetic practices, ceased to attend upon him and came here to practice meditation by themselves. Beside it is a *stūpa* marking the place where five hundred *pratyekabuddhas* entered *nirvāṇa* together. There are also three *stūpas* marking the sites where the three past Buddhas sat and walked in meditation.

To the west of the monastery enclosure is a clear pond, more than two hundred paces in circumference, where the Tathāgata once bathed. Further west is a large pond, one hundred and eighty paces in circumference, where the Tathāgata once washed his utensils. Further north is a pond, one hundred and fifty paces in circumference, where the Tathāgata once washed his robes. All three of these ponds are inhabited by dragons. Their water is deep and its taste is sweet; it is clear, pure, and bright, and it neither increases nor decreases. If someone with an arrogant mind washes in these ponds, the Kumbhīra (金毘羅) beasts often harm them; if one is deeply respectful, one may draw and use the water without fear. On a large square rock beside the robe-washing pond, there are traces of the Tathāgata’s robes; the patterns are clear and bright, as if carved or engraved, and the faithful often come here to make offerings. If heretics or wicked people step lightly upon this stone, the dragon king in the pond immediately stirs up wind and rain. Not far from the pond is a stūpa, marking the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the bodhisattva path, was a six-tusked elephant king; a hunter, coveting his tusks, disguised himself in a monk’s robe and lay in wait with a drawn bow, but the elephant king, out of respect for the robe, broke off his tusks and gave them to him. Not far from the place where the tusks were broken is a stūpa, marking the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the bodhisattva path, felt pity for the world’s lack of propriety and manifested as a bird. Together with a monkey and a white elephant, he asked here who had first seen the Nyagrodha (尼拘律) tree. Each recounted their experiences, and they established seniority accordingly. Through this, the influence of the teaching gradually spread, people learned the order of precedence, and both the ordained and the laity took refuge. Not far from its side, in a great forest, there is a stūpa marking the place where the Tathāgata, in the past, while he and Devadatta (提婆達多) were both deer kings, settled a matter. Formerly, in this great forest, there were two herds of deer, each numbering more than five hundred. At that time, the king of this country was hunting in the plains and marshes. The Bodhisattva deer king came forward and petitioned the king, saying: "Your Majesty is hunting across the plains, setting fires and loosing flying arrows. All my followers will lose their lives this morning; in a few days they will rot and stink, serving no purpose as food. I wish to arrange a rotation to deliver one deer each day. Your Majesty will have fresh meat for your meals, and I will prolong our lives for a little while." The king approved his words, turned his carriage around, and returned. The two herds of deer took turns delivering their lives. In Devadatta’s herd, there was a pregnant doe whose turn it was to die; she said to her king, "Although I am due to die, my unborn child’s turn has not yet come." The deer king replied angrily, "Who does not treasure their own life!" The doe sighed and said, "My king is inhumane; death is not far off." She then went to report her emergency to the Bodhisattva deer king. The deer king said, "How sorrowful is the heart of a compassionate mother, whose kindness extends even to her unborn child! I will now take your place." He then went to the king’s gate. People on the road passed the word along, calling out, "That great deer king is now entering the city." The city dwellers and commoners all rushed to watch. When the king heard of it, he thought it was not true. The gatekeeper reported it to the king, and the king then believed it. He said, "Why has the deer king come so suddenly?" The deer said, "There is a doe who is due to die, but her fetus has not yet been born; my heart cannot bear it, so I venture to offer my own body in her stead." Upon hearing this, the king sighed and said, "I am a human with the body of a deer, while you are a deer with the body of a human." Thereupon, he released all the deer and no longer required them to forfeit their lives, designating that forest as a sanctuary for the deer; thus, it was called the Forest Given to the Deer (Mr̥gadāva). The name "Deer Park" originated from this.

Going two or three li east from the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva), one reaches a stūpa. Beside it is a dried-up pond, more than eighty paces in circumference, known as "Life-saving" (Jīvitatrāṇa) and also called "Hero" (Vīra). According to the local records: several hundred years ago, there was a hermit who built a hut and lived in seclusion beside this pond. He was extensively learned in the arts and had mastered the ultimate divine principles, being able to turn rubble into jewels and change the forms of humans and animals, yet he was not yet able to ride the winds and clouds or join the company of the immortals. He examined the diagrams and studied the ancients, seeking further for the arts of immortality. The formula stated: "Immortality is the art of long life. If one wishes to seek this study, one must first settle one's resolve and build an altar more than one zhang in circumference. Command a man of mettle, renowned for his loyalty and courage, to hold a long sword and stand at the corner of the altar, holding his breath and remaining silent from dusk until dawn. The seeker of immortality shall sit in the center of the altar, hand resting on the long sword, chanting divine incantations, withdrawing his vision and turning his hearing inward; by daybreak, he shall ascend to immortality. The sharp sword he holds will turn into a precious blade; he will soar through the void and tread upon the air, reigning over the company of immortals, and with the sword in hand, he will command, and all he desires will be fulfilled, without decline or aging, without sickness or death." Having obtained this formula for immortality, the man traveled in search of a man of mettle, but despite seeking for many years, he could not find anyone to satisfy his wish. Later, in the city, he encountered a man wailing as he walked along the road. The hermit observed his appearance and was greatly delighted; he approached him and asked with concern, "Why are you so aggrieved and wounded?" The man replied, "I am poor and destitute, and I labor to support myself." His master had recognized his worth and placed deep trust in him, promising that when five years were completed, he would be rewarded with a heavy bounty. Consequently, he endured toil and hardship, forgetting his suffering. As the five years were about to conclude, he made a single mistake, and for this he was not only whipped and humiliated but also received nothing. "With this weighing on my heart, who is there to pity my grief?" The hermit bade him travel together, and they arrived at a thatched hut. By the power of his arts, the hermit conjured a spread of food and drink; afterwards, he ordered him to bathe in the pond, dressed him in new clothes, and presented him with five hundred gold coins, saying, "When these are exhausted, come and ask for more; pray do not treat me as an outsider." From that time on, the hermit repeatedly bestowed heavy gifts upon him, secretly performing acts of kindness to stir his heart. The hero (烈士) repeatedly sought to offer his life in service to repay the one who understood him. The hermit said, "I have sought a hero for many years; fortunately we have met, and your singular appearance matches the prophecies. I have no other motive; I only wish for you to remain silent for a single night." The hero replied, "I would not even refuse death, so how could I not merely hold my breath?" Thereupon, they set up an altar, received the immortal method, and followed the instructions to perform the rites, sitting and waiting for the sun to set. After dusk, each attended to his duties: the hermit recited divine incantations, while the hero gripped his sharp blade. When it was almost dawn, he suddenly let out a cry. At that moment, fire descended from the sky, and smoke and flames billowed like clouds. The hermit quickly pulled the man into the pond to escape the danger. Afterwards, he asked, "I warned you to remain silent; why did you cry out in alarm?" The hero replied, "After receiving your instructions, when midnight came, I fell into a trance-like dream, and strange transformations began to arise." I saw my former master come in person to comfort and thank me; moved by his great kindness, I restrained myself and did not respond. He became furious and killed me. I entered the intermediate state (antarābhava) and, looking back at my corpse, sighed with regret, yet I still wished to remain silent throughout my lives to repay his great virtue. I was then reborn into a great Brahmin family in South India; from conception to birth and through all manner of hardships, I bore your grace and virtue in mind and never made a sound. Even when I reached the stages of schooling, capping, marriage, mourning my parents, and fathering a son, I always remembered your past kindness and endured in silence, though my kinsmen and relatives all found it strange. When I was over sixty-five years old, my wife said to me, "You must speak! If you do not speak, I shall kill your son." At that moment, I thought that since I had already passed through a lifetime and was now old and frail, this young son was all I had; therefore, I stopped my wife to prevent her from killing him. That is why I let out this cry." The hermit said, "It is my fault! This was the harassment of a demon." The hero, moved by gratitude but grieved that the task was not accomplished, died in a fit of indignation. Because he escaped the disaster of fire, it is called the Life-Saving Pond; because he died out of gratitude, it is also called the Hero's Pond (烈士池). West of the Hero's Pond is the Three-Beast Stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the bodhisattva path, burned his body. At the beginning of the kalpa, in this wilderness, there lived a fox, a rabbit, and a monkey who lived together in harmony despite their different species. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, wishing to test the one practicing the bodhisattva path, manifested his spirit as an old man and said to the three beasts, "Are you three well and at peace?" "Are you free from fear and alarm?" They replied, "We roam through lush grasses and wander in dense forests; though of different species, we share the same joy, and are both peaceful and happy." The old man said, "I have heard that you two or three are deeply affectionate and close in spirit, and forgetting my own old age and infirmity, I have sought you out from afar. Now, I am truly hungry and weak; what do you have to offer me for food?" They replied, "Please stay here a while; we will personally hasten to seek some." Thereupon, with one heart and humble intent, they went their separate ways to search. The fox went along the riverbank and caught a fresh carp in its mouth, while the ape went among the forest trees and gathered rare flowers and fruits; they both returned to the spot and presented them together to the old man. Only the hare returned empty-handed, leaping about to the left and right. The old man said to them, "In my view, you are not in harmony. The ape and the fox share the same intent and each exerted their minds, yet only the hare returned empty-handed, offering nothing at all. Judging by this, the truth is clear." Having heard this derisive remark, the hare said to the fox and the ape, "Gather plenty of firewood and grass, for I am about to do something." The fox and the ape raced to do so, carrying grass in their mouths and dragging wood; once they had piled it high, the fierce flames were about to blaze. The hare said, "O Benevolent One, my body is lowly and base, and what I sought was difficult to achieve; I venture to offer my humble self to provide this one meal." Having finished speaking, it entered the fire and immediately died. At that time, the old man resumed his form as Śakra (帝釋), cleared away the embers to collect the remains, and after sighing in grief for a long while, said to the fox and the ape, "How could it have come to this! I am moved by its heart and shall not let its traces vanish; I will entrust it to the lunar disk to be passed down to future generations." Therefore, everyone says that the hare in the moon has existed from that time onward. People of later times built a stūpa at this site.

Traveling southeast from the Aviddhakarṇa (阿避陀羯剌拏) Monastery for more than one hundred li, one crosses the Gaṅgā (殑伽) River to the south and arrives at the town of Mahāsāla (摩訶娑羅邑). The inhabitants are all of the Brahman caste and do not follow the Buddha-dharma. However, when they see a śramaṇa, they first inquire about his learning; only when they know he possesses a retentive memory do they then pay him deep respect.

To the north of the Ganges (Gaṅgā) River, there is a temple of Nārāyaṇa (那羅延天祠). It has multi-storied pavilions and tiered terraces, which are vast and exquisitely adorned. The images of the various devas are carved from stone; the craftsmanship exhausts human ingenuity, and their spiritual responses are difficult to fathom.

Traveling more than thirty *li* east of the Nārāyaṇa (那羅延天祠) temple, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, more than half of which has sunk into the ground. In front of it stands a stone pillar over two *zhang* high, topped with the figure of a lion and inscribed with a record of the subduing of demons. Formerly, there were demons of the wilderness at this place who, relying on their great power, devoured human flesh and blood, harming living beings and committing the most extreme atrocities. The Tathāgata, pitying the living beings who were meeting untimely deaths, used his supernatural powers to convert the demons, leading them to take refuge with reverence and bringing them into order with the precept against killing. The demons accepted his teaching and followed him in his rounds. Thereupon, they raised a stone to invite the Buddha to sit, wishing to hear the true Dharma and sincerely vowing to protect and uphold it. From that time onward, non-believers vied with one another to push and move the stone seat placed by the demons, but even with thousands of people, none could budge it. Dense forests and clear ponds surround the base; those who come near it are all filled with fear. Not far from the place of the subduing of the demons are several *saṃghārāma*s; although many are in ruins, there are still monks residing there, all of whom follow and study the teachings of the Mahāyāna.

From here, traveling southeast for over a hundred li, one arrives at a stūpa whose foundation has already collapsed and sunk, with the remaining portion standing several tens of feet high. Formerly, after the Tathāgata had entered extinction, the great kings of the eight nations divided the relics. The Brahmin who measured the relics smeared the inside of a vessel with honey to distribute the portions to the various kings. The Brahmin then took the vessel and returned home; having obtained the relics that adhered to it, he built a stūpa and placed the vessel inside, hence it was named accordingly. Later, King Aśoka (無憂王) opened it to take the relic vessel and rebuilt it into a great stūpa; occasionally on fast days, it radiates a brilliant light.

Five or six li to the northwest of the palace city, one arrives at a monastery where the community of monks is small and studies the teachings of the Hīnayāna Sāmmitīya school. Beside it is a stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra (毘摩羅詰經) and where the elder’s son Ratnākara (寶積) and others offered precious parasols. To its east is a stūpa where Śāriputra and others attained the fruit of the non-learner (aśaikṣa).

To the southeast of the place where Śāriputra (舍利子) attained the fruit, there is a stūpa built by the king of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐). After the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, a former king of this country received a share of the relics and respectfully constructed this monument. The *Record of India* (印度記) states: "Originally, there was one *hu* of the Tathāgata’s relics here; King Aśoka (無憂王) opened it and took out nine *dou*, leaving only one *dou* behind." Later, another king wished to open it again and had just begun the work when the earth shook, so he dared not open it.

To the northwest of this there is a stūpa, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Beside it is a stone pillar, fifty or sixty feet high, with the figure of a lion fashioned on top. To the south of the stone pillar is a pond, which was dug for the Buddha by a troop of monkeys. In the past, the Tathāgata once resided here. Not far to the west of the pond is a stūpa, the place where the monkeys took the Tathāgata’s bowl and climbed a tree to gather honey; not far to the south of the pond is a stūpa, which is the place where the monkeys offered honey to the Buddha; in the northwest corner of the pond, there still remains an image of a monkey.

Three or four *li* to the north of the monastery is a *stūpa*, marking the spot where humans and non-humans followed the World-Honored One and stood still as the Tathāgata was proceeding to the country of Kuśinagara (拘尸那國) to enter *parinirvāṇa*. Not far to the northwest is a *stūpa*, marking the spot where the Buddha last gazed upon the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐城). Not far to its south is a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍), with a *stūpa* built in front, marking the site of the Āmrapālī-vana (菴沒羅女園) which she held and offered to the Buddha. Beside the Āmrapālī-vana is a *stūpa*, marking the place where the Tathāgata announced his *nirvāṇa*. Formerly, the Buddha was here and said to Ānanda, "Those who have attained the four bases of psychic power (*catvāraḥ ṛddhi-pādāḥ*) are able to remain for an aeon. The Tathāgata now, how long shall he remain?" In this way he asked three times, but Ānanda did not respond, for he was deluded by the heavenly Māra. Ānanda rose from his seat and went into the forest to meditate in silence. At that time, Māra came to request the Buddha, saying, "The Tathāgata has been in the world teaching and transforming for a long time; those who have been saved from transmigration are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The joy of extinction—now is the time for it." The World-Honored One placed a small amount of soil on his fingernail and said to Māra, "Is the soil of the earth more, or is the soil on my fingernail more?" He replied, "The soil of the earth is more." The Buddha said, "Those whom I have saved are like the soil on my fingernail, while those who have not been saved are like the soil of the great earth. Three months from now, I shall enter *nirvāṇa*." Hearing this, Māra was joyful and withdrew. Ānanda suddenly had a strange dream while in the woods and came to report it to the Buddha, saying: "While I was in the woods, I dreamed of a great tree with luxuriant branches and leaves and dense shade; a violent wind suddenly arose and scattered it until nothing remained. Could it be that the World-Honored One is about to enter extinction? My heart is filled with fear, so I have come to ask." The Buddha told Ānanda: "I told you before that you were obscured by Māra and did not request me to remain at the proper time. The Demon King urged me to enter *nirvāṇa* early, and I have already granted him the date; this dream is the sign of that."  Not far from the place where he announced the time of his *nirvāṇa* is a *stūpa* (窣堵波), which is the place where the thousand sons saw their parents. Long ago, there was a *ṛṣi* (仙人) living in seclusion in a rocky valley. In the second month of spring, while he was bathing in a clear stream, a doe followed him to drink and was moved to give birth to a girl. Her appearance was superior to others, but her feet resembled those of a deer. The *ṛṣi* saw her, took her in, and raised her. Later, he ordered her to seek fire. When she reached the hermitage of another *ṛṣi*, lotus flowers appeared in the tracks where her feet stepped. That *ṛṣi* saw this and, deeply amazed, ordered her to walk around his hermitage before she could obtain the fire. The deer-girl followed his instructions, obtained the fire, and returned.  At that time, King Brahmadatta (梵豫王) was hunting and saw the flowers. He followed the tracks to search for their source, was delighted by their strangeness, and took her back with him in his carriage. A physiognomist predicted that she would give birth to a thousand sons. The other wives heard of this and all began to plot against her. When the months and days were full, she gave birth to a single lotus flower. The flower had a thousand petals, and on each petal sat a son. The other wives slandered her, all claiming it was an inauspicious omen, and threw them into the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) river, where they drifted away with the waves. King Ujjayana (烏耆延王) was sightseeing in the lower reaches of the river when he saw a yellow cloud-like canopy floating on the waves; he took it and opened it to find a thousand sons, whom he nursed and raised until they grew up to possess great strength. Relying on his thousand sons, he expanded his territory in all directions, and riding on the momentum of his military victories, he was about to invade this country. At that time, King Brahmadatta (梵豫王) heard of this and was filled with great fear; his military strength was no match for them, and he could think of no solution. At that moment, the Deer Woman (鹿女) knew in her heart that they were her sons, so she said to the King: "Now that the invaders are at our borders and the people are divided, I, your humble servant, in my simple loyalty, can defeat the powerful enemy." The King did not believe her and remained deeply worried and afraid. The Deer Woman then ascended the city tower to await the arrival of the invaders. The thousand sons led their troops and completely surrounded the city, whereupon the Deer Woman called out to them, "Do not commit such a rebellious act! I am your mother, and you are my sons." The thousand sons replied, "What is this absurd talk?" The Deer Woman pressed her two breasts with her hands, and the milk flowed out in a thousand streams; moved by their natural bond, the milk entered each of their mouths. Thereupon, they took off their armor and returned to their lineage, released their weapons and returned to their kin; the two countries rejoiced together, and the common people were at peace. Not far from where the thousand sons returned to their lineage is a stūpa (窣堵波), which marks the old site where the Tathāgata (如來) once walked. He pointed it out to the assembly and said, "In the past, I returned to my lineage here and saw my relatives. If you wish to know who the thousand sons are, they are the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa (賢劫)." To the east of the place where he narrated his former lives, there is an old foundation upon which a stūpa (窣堵波) is built. It occasionally glows with light, and prayers offered there are sometimes granted; these are the remains of the multi-storied lecture hall where the Tathāgata (如來) preached the *Samantamukha-dhāraṇī* (普門陀羅尼) and other sūtras. Not far from the side of the lecture hall is a stūpa containing the relics of half of Ānanda’s body. Not far from here are several hundred stūpas, and though one might wish to determine their exact number, it has never been known; this is the place where a thousand Pratyekabuddhas (獨覺) entered into extinction (寂滅). Within and surrounding the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐), there are numerous sacred sites, which are difficult to enumerate in full. The old ruins at these scenic and strategic locations stand as thick as fish scales, but as the years have suddenly changed and the seasons have rapidly shifted, the forests have been destroyed and the ponds have dried up; only decayed stumps and remaining traces are left to be examined in detail.

Traveling fourteen or fifteen *li* to the southeast of the city, one reaches a great stūpa, which is the place where the seven hundred sages and saints performed the second council. One hundred and ten years after the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, there were *bhikṣus* in the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐國) who had strayed from the Buddha-dharma and were practicing the disciplinary rules erroneously. At that time, the Elder Yaśoda was residing in the kingdom of Kosala (憍薩羅國), the Elder Sambhūta was residing in the kingdom of Mathurā (秣兔羅國), the Elder Revata was residing in the kingdom of Sahajāti (韓若國), the Elder Sālha was residing in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, and the Elder Kubjashobhita was residing in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra (娑羅梨弗國). These great *arhats* had attained mastery of mind, were keepers of the *tripiṭaka*, had attained the three knowledges, possessed great renown, were known to the masses, and were all disciples of the Venerable Ānanda. At that time, Yaśoda sent messengers to inform the various noble sages that they should all assemble in the city of Vaiśālī. There was still one person missing, and the number of seven hundred was not yet complete. At that time, Kubjashobhita, using his heavenly eye, saw the great noble sages gathering to discuss matters of the Dharma and employed his spiritual foot-power to arrive at the assembly. Then Sambhūta, in the midst of the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt on one knee, and proclaimed aloud: "Let the assembly be silent! Listen with reverence, attend with care! Long ago, the Great Sage, the Dharma King, skillfully and expediently entered *nirvāṇa*; although much time has passed, his verbal teachings still remain. The negligent *bhikṣus* of the city of Vaiśālī have erred regarding the disciplinary rules; ten matters have arisen that violate the teachings of Him who possesses the Ten Powers. Now, you noble ones, who deeply understand what is to be upheld and what is to be avoided, all having received the instructions of the great virtuous Ānanda, remember to repay the Buddha’s kindness and once again proclaim the holy decree." At that time, the great assembly was moved with grief; they immediately summoned the *bhikṣus* and, in accordance with the *Vinaya* (毘柰耶), reproached and restrained them, eliminated the erroneous practices, and clarified the holy teachings.

At that time, the Elder Yaśoda (耶舍陀) was residing in the country of Kosala (憍薩羅國), the Elder Sambhūta (三菩伽) was residing in the country of Mathurā (秣兔羅國), the Elder Revata (釐波多) was residing in the country of Sahajāti (韓若國), the Elder Sālha (沙羅) was residing in the country of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐國), and the Elder Kubjashobhita (富闍蘇彌羅) was residing in the country of Pāṭaliputra (娑羅梨弗國).

Traveling eighty or ninety li south from the place where the seven hundred sages and saints held their assembly, one arrives at the Śvetapura Monastery (濕吠多補羅僧伽藍), where the tiered terraces are magnificent and the multi-storied pavilions soar like birds in flight; the community of monks is pure and solemn, and they all study the Mahayana. Beside it are the sites of the traces where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation. Next to these is a stupa built by King Aśoka. This is the site where the Tathāgata, in the past, stopped to rest while traveling south to the kingdom of Magadha (摩揭陀國) and looking back north toward the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐城).

Traveling more than thirty li southeast from the Śvetapura (濕吠多補羅) Monastery, there is a stūpa on both the north and south banks of the Gaṅgā (殑伽) River; these are the places where the Venerable Ānanda divided his body between the two countries. Ānanda was the paternal cousin of the Tathāgata; he was learned and possessed of total retention, broad in his knowledge and strong in his memory. After the Buddha passed away, he succeeded Mahākāśyapa in upholding the True Dharma and guiding those who were advancing in their studies. While in the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國), he was walking in a forest when he saw a novice monk reciting a Buddhist scripture with erroneous chapters and sentences, and confused wording. Upon hearing this, Ānanda felt a growing sense of sympathy and longing; he slowly approached the novice and offered to correct and instruct him. The novice laughed and said, "The Great Virtuous one is senile; what you say is wrong! My teacher is brilliant and in the prime of his life; having received his instructions personally, there is certainly no error." Ānanda remained silent, withdrew, and sighed, saying, "Although I am aged, I have wished to remain in the world for a long time for the sake of all sentient beings, to uphold the True Dharma. However, the defilements of sentient beings are heavy, and it is difficult to instruct them with words; remaining for a long time is of no benefit, so I may as well quickly enter parinirvāṇa." Thereupon, he left the country of Magadha and headed for the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐城), crossing the Gaṅgā River and sailing in a boat midstream. When the King of Magadha heard that Ānanda was departing, his heart was filled with deep attachment to his virtue; he immediately prepared his military carriages and drove rapidly in pursuit to invite him back, with hundreds of thousands of people camping as an army on the southern bank. When the King of Vaiśālī heard that Ānanda was coming, his heart was filled with both grief and joy; he also mobilized his troops and raced to welcome him, with hundreds of thousands of people stationed as an army on the northern bank. The two armies faced each other, their banners and flags obscuring the sun. Ānanda, fearing that their troops would clash and kill one another, rose from the boat and ascended into the void. He manifested supernatural transformations and immediately entered into extinction (parinirvāṇa); he transformed into fire to consume his remains, and the remains then split in two, one part falling on the southern bank and one part falling on the northern bank. Thereupon, the two kings each obtained a portion; their entire armies wailed in grief, and they both returned to their respective countries to erect stūpas and perform offerings.
The capital city of the country is called Cañśuma (占戍挐), and it is mostly in ruins. Within the old palace city, there are still over three thousand households, living as if in a village or a town.

To the northeast of the great river there is a monastery (saṃghārāma) with few monks, whose academic pursuits are pure and lofty. Proceeding west from here along the riverbank, there is a stūpa over three *zhang* high; to its south flows a long stream, and this is the place where the Great Compassionate World-Honored One converted the fishermen.

Traveling more than one hundred *li* to the northeast of the Duyu (Fisherman) country, to the west of an old city, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), over one hundred feet high. It is the place where the Buddha in the past dwelt for six months, preaching the Dharma to save various gods and humans. One hundred forty or fifty paces to the north of this is a small stūpa where the Tathāgata in the past established the precepts for the bhikṣus. Not far to the west of this is a stūpa containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata. At this place, in the past, people from near and far towns would gather together, burning incense, scattering flowers, and keeping lamps and torches burning without interruption.

The country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) is over five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city has few inhabitants, but the towns have many registered households. The land is rich and fertile, nourishing crops; there is a unique variety of rice with large grains, an extraordinary fragrance, and a remarkable luster, which the local people call "rice for great personages." The land is low and damp, so the towns are built on high ground; from the end of early summer to the middle of autumn, the plains are covered with flowing water, allowing for the use of boats. The customs are honest and simple, and the climate is warm and hot. The people highly value the pursuit of learning and respect the Buddha-Dharma. There are over fifty monasteries and more than ten thousand monks, most of whom study the Mahayana teachings. There are several dozen *deva* temples, and followers of non-Buddhist paths are numerous.

Not far to the south of the hell is a stūpa. Its foundation is collapsed and sunken, leaving only the shape of an inverted bowl; it is adorned with precious substances and has stone railings. This is one of the eighty-four thousand. King Aśoka (無憂王) built it within the palace using human labor. Inside, there is one *dou* of the Tathāgata’s relics, and miraculous manifestations occasionally arise, with divine light shining from time to time.  After King Aśoka abolished the prison, he met the great arhat Upagupta (近護), who skillfully guided and transformed him according to his capacity. The king said to the arhat, "Fortunately, due to past merit, I occupy the position of the most honored among men, yet I lament these karmic obstructions that prevented me from encountering the Buddha’s teaching. Now, as the Tathāgata has left behind bodily relics, I wish to rebuild many stūpas." The arhat replied, "Great King, by the power of your merit, you can command all spirits, and with a heart of great vows, you protect the Three Jewels. This is a worthy wish, and now is the time." He then spoke extensively on the causes of offering earth and the Tathāgata’s prophecy regarding the merit of this construction.  Upon hearing this, King Aśoka was delighted. He summoned the spirits and commanded them, saying, "The Dharma King guides and benefits, and all sentient beings are fortunate. Relying on my past virtues, I have reached the pinnacle of honor among men. To honor the Tathāgata’s bodily relics, I am now rebuilding them for worship. You spirits must exert your strength and work with one heart! Throughout the borders of Jambudvīpa (贍部), wherever there are households numbering in the *koṭi*, you shall build stūpas using the Buddha’s relics. The intention originates with me, but the work is accomplished by you. I do not wish to possess the benefit of this supreme merit alone. You should each begin construction and await further orders." The spirits and deities received the command and set to work; once the work was completed, they all came to request further instructions. After King Aśoka (無憂王) had opened the various stūpas built by the eight kingdoms, divided their relics, and entrusted them to the spirits and deities, he said to the Arhat, "My desire is that the relics be enshrined in all these places at the same time. Although this is my wish, the matter has not yet gone according to my desire." The Arhat said, "Your Majesty should command the spirits and deities that on the appointed day, when the sun is obscured by a shape like a hand, that is the moment to enshrine the relics." The King accepted this instruction and proclaimed it to the spirits and deities. When the appointed day arrived, King Aśoka observed the sunlight; at high noon, the Arhat used his supernatural power to stretch out his hand and block the sun, which was witnessed by all at the construction sites, and at this very moment, the works were all completed.  Not far from the side of the stūpa, there is a large stone within a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) where the Tathāgata once stepped, and his twin footprints still remain; they are one foot eight inches long and over six inches wide. Both footprints possess the mark of a wheel, all ten toes are adorned with floral patterns, and the shape of a fish is clearly visible, emitting light from time to time. In the past, when the Tathāgata was about to attain extinction, he proceeded north toward the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸那城) and looked back south at the kingdom of Magadha (摩揭陀國); standing upon this stone, he told Ānanda, "I now leave these last footprints here as I am about to enter extinction, looking back at Magadha. One hundred years after my passing, there will be a King Aśoka who will rule the world, establish his capital in this land, protect the Three Jewels, and command the hundred spirits." When King Aśoka (無憂王) succeeded to the throne, he moved the capital and built a city, enclosing the stone with the footprints of the Buddha (周迹石) within it. As it was near the palace city, he constantly made offerings to it in person. Later, various kings competed to carry it away, but although the stone was not large, no one could move it. Recently, King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王) destroyed the Buddha-dharma and went to the site of the stone, intending to obliterate the holy relic; however, after he chiseled it, the surface became smooth again and the patterns remained as before, so he threw it into the Ganges River (殑伽河), but it soon returned to its original place. The stupa (窣堵波) beside it is the site of the traces where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.

More than two hundred *li* to the southwest of the city, there are the remains of a monastery. Beside it is a *stūpa* where divine light occasionally shines and miraculous signs appear from time to time; the masses, both near and far, never fail to offer their prayers there, for it is the site of the traces where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.

Traveling southwest from the aforementioned monastery for more than one hundred *li*, one arrives at the Tiladha-vihāra (鞮羅釋迦伽藍). Its courtyards comprise four precincts, with pavilions and towers of three stories; the elevated terraces rise to a height of many *ren*, and the heavy gates open wide. It was built by a descendant of King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王). It summons those of high talent and extends a broad invitation to those of eminent virtue; scholars from foreign lands and elites from distant regions, being of the same inclination, flock together, arriving one after another. The community of monks numbers in the thousands, all of whom study the Great Vehicle. Facing the path at the middle gate are three *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍), topped with wheel-symbols and hung with bells that sway in the air. Below, they are built on tiered foundations with railings surrounding them, while the doors, windows, beams, pillars, walls, and steps are all adorned with inlaid gold and copper reliefs. In the middle *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* is a standing statue of the Buddha thirty feet high, with a statue of Tārā Bodhisattva to the left and a statue of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to the right. All three of these statues are cast from brass; their majestic presence is awe-inspiring, and their spiritual insight reaches far. In each of the *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* there is one *sheng* of relics, which sometimes emit spiritual light and occasionally manifest miraculous omens.

More than ninety *li* southwest of the Tiladhaka Monastery (鞮羅釋迦伽藍), one reaches the great mountain of Pravaragiri (大山), where the clouds and rocks are dense and secluded, a dwelling place for spirits and immortals; venomous snakes and violent dragons nest in its marshes, and fierce beasts and birds of prey lurk in its forests. On the summit of the mountain is a large flat rock upon which a stūpa over ten feet high is built; this is the place where the Buddha entered into samādhi. In the past, the Tathāgata descended and stayed here, sitting upon this flat rock to enter the cessation samādhi (nirodha-samāpatti) for the duration of one night. The heavenly beings and holy spirits made offerings to the Tathāgata, playing heavenly music and raining down heavenly flowers. When the Tathāgata emerged from samādhi, the heavenly beings, moved by admiration, built a stūpa out of precious gems, gold, and silver. As the time since the Sage’s passing has grown more distant, the precious materials have turned into stone. From ancient times until the present, no human has ever reached it. Looking at the high mountain from afar, one sees strange phenomena: long snakes and fierce beasts moving in groups to the right, and heavenly immortals and holy spirits following shoulder to shoulder in praise and worship. On a ridge to the east of the mountain is a stūpa, marking the spot where the Tathāgata once stood to gaze at the land of Magadha (摩揭陀國) through which he had traveled.

Traveling forty or fifty li southwest from the Śīlabhadra Monastery (戒賢伽藍), one crosses the Nairañjanā River (尼連禪河) and reaches the city of Gayā (伽耶城). It is very rugged and well-fortified, but has few inhabitants, except for over a thousand families of Brahmins who are the descendants of a great rishi; the king does not treat them as subjects, and everyone holds them in high esteem. More than thirty li to the north of the city, there is a clear spring which Indian tradition calls holy water; for all who drink from or wash in it, the defilements of sin are eliminated.

To the east of the pool created by Śakra (帝釋), in a forest, is the pool of the Dragon King Mucilinda (目支隣陀); its water is clear and dark, and its taste is sweet and delicious. On the west bank is a small shrine (精舍; Skt. mūla-gandha-kuṭī) containing an image of the Buddha. Formerly, when the Tathāgata had first attained supreme enlightenment, he sat here in meditation for seven days. At that time, this dragon king guarded the Tathāgata by coiling his body around the Buddha seven times and manifesting many heads that bowed down to form a canopy; therefore, his dwelling is located on the east bank of the pool.  To the east of the Mucilinda Dragon Pool, in a forest shrine, there is an image of the Buddha in an emaciated state. Beside it is a place for walking meditation, more than seventy paces long, with a pippala (卑鉢羅) tree at both the north and south ends. Therefore, among the local people today, those who are afflicted with illness often apply scented oil to the image and frequently receive relief and recovery.  This is the place where the Bodhisattva practiced austerities. In order to subdue the non-Buddhists and also because he accepted the request of Māra, the Tathāgata practiced austerities for six years, eating one hemp seed and one grain of wheat per day. His appearance became haggard and his body became emaciated; when walking back and forth, he would grasp the trees to rise. Beside the pippala tree where the Bodhisattva practiced austerities, there is a stūpa; this is the place where Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya (阿若憍陳如) and the other four men resided. Initially, when the prince renounced his home, wandering through mountains and marshes and resting in forests and by springs, King Śuddhodana (淨飯王) ordered these five men to follow and attend to him. Once the prince practiced austerities, Kauṇḍinya and the others also diligently sought the way.

Southeast of the place where Kauṇḍinya and his companions resided, there is a stūpa marking the spot where the Bodhisattva entered the Nairañjanā River to bathe. Not far from the riverbank is the place where the Bodhisattva received the milk-rice. Beside that is a stūpa marking the place where the two elders offered parched grain and honey. The Buddha sat under a tree in the cross-legged position, silent and still, experiencing the joy of liberation; after seven days had passed, he finally arose from meditation.
