At that time, two merchant leaders were passing by the edge of the forest, and the deity of that forest told the merchant leaders, "The Prince of the Śākya clan is now within this wood; he has just attained the fruit of Buddhahood and his mind is concentrated in silent meditation. He has not eaten for forty-nine days; if you offer him whatever you have, you will obtain great and wholesome benefit." The two merchant leaders then each took their travel provisions of parched grain and honey to offer to him, and the World-Honored One accepted them. Beside the place where the elders offered the parched grain, there is a stūpa marking the spot where the Four Heavenly Kings offered alms bowls. After the merchant leaders had offered the parched grain and honey, the World-Honored One considered what vessel he should use to receive them. At that time, the four heavenly kings came from the four directions, each holding a golden bowl to offer to him. The World-Honored One remained silent and did not accept them, thinking that such vessels were not appropriate for one who has left the household life. The four heavenly kings set aside the golden bowls and offered silver ones, and even bowls of crystal, lapis lazuli, agate, musaragalva, and pearl, but the World-Honored One would not accept any of them. The four heavenly kings each returned to their palaces and brought back stone bowls, dark blue and translucent, which they presented again. To avoid favoring one over the others, the World-Honored One accepted them all, stacked them in sequence, and pressed them into a single bowl; therefore, on the outside, there are four ridges. Not far from the place where the four heavenly kings offered the bowls, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for his mother. After the Tathāgata had attained perfect enlightenment and was acclaimed as the teacher of gods and men, his mother, Māyā, descended from the heavenly palace to this place, and the World-Honored One, according to her capacity, manifested teachings to bring her benefit and joy. Beside it, on the bank of a dried-up pond, there is a stūpa; this is the place where, in the past, the Tathāgata witnessed various divine transformations and had karmic connections. Beside the place where he manifested divine transformations, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the Tathāgata converted the three brothers, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa (優樓頻螺迦葉波) and his followers, as well as their one thousand disciples. As the Tathāgata was setting forth the good path and subduing them according to their dispositions, the five hundred disciples of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa requested to receive the Buddha’s teaching. Kāśyapa said, "I shall also return from the path of delusion along with you." Thereupon, they followed one another and came to the place of the Buddha. The Tathāgata told them, "Discard your deer-skin garments and abandon your fire-worship implements." At that time, the Brahmins respectfully accepted the holy teaching and cast their robes and implements into the Nairañjanā River. Nadī-Kāśyapa (捺地迦葉波) saw the sacrificial vessels floating down the current and, together with his disciples, waited to see what his elder brother would do; having seen him change his course, he also followed suit and dyed his robes. The two hundred disciples of Gayā-Kāśyapa (伽耶迦葉波), hearing that their elder brother had abandoned his former practice, also came to the place of the Buddha and wished to practice the holy life. To the northwest of the place where the Kāśyapa brothers were converted is a stūpa; this is the place where the Tathāgata subdued the fire dragon that the Kāśyapas worshipped. When the Tathāgata was about to convert those people and overcome what they revered, he stayed in the chamber of the Brahmins' fire dragon. After midnight, the dragon exhaled smoke and flames. The Buddha, having entered into samādhi, also emitted a fiery light, so that the chamber was brightly illuminated with fierce and blazing flames. The Brahmin masters, fearing the fire would harm the Buddha, all rushed toward it, crying out in sorrow and pity. Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa (優樓頻螺迦葉波) said to his disciples, "Looking at it now, this may not be a fire; it must be that the Śramaṇa has subdued the fire dragon." The Tathāgata then placed the fire dragon into his alms bowl and, at dawn, held it up to show the disciples of the non-Buddhists. The stūpa beside this is the place where five hundred pratyekabuddhas (獨覺) entered nirvāṇa together. The stūpa to the south of the Mucilinda (目支隣陀) Dragon Pool is the place where Kāśyapa rescued the Tathāgata from drowning. At that time, the Kāśyapa brothers promoted their supernatural powers, and people from far and near admired their virtue, with the masses turning their hearts toward them. The World-honored One, intending to guide the deluded disciples, employed great skillful means to transform them; he raised dense clouds and caused a violent rain to fall, which surrounded the place where the Buddha resided, leaving it alone without water. Seeing this cloud and rain, Kāśyapa said to his disciples, "Will the Śramaṇa’s dwelling not be flooded?" He set out in a boat to rescue him, only to see the World-honored One walking on the water as if it were dry land; as he stepped into the middle of the river, the waters parted and the sand appeared. Having seen this, Kāśyapa’s heart was subdued and he withdrew.

Two or three li outside the east gate of the wall surrounding the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree is the cave of the blind dragon. This dragon, due to the accumulation of past misdeeds, was born blind as retribution. When the Tathāgata was traveling from Mount Prāgbodhi (正覺山) toward the Mahā-bodhi tree, he passed by the side of this cave, and the dragon’s eyes suddenly became clear. Seeing the Bodhisattva approaching the tree of the Buddha, he said to the Bodhisattva, "Kind sir, you shall soon attain Perfect Enlightenment. My eyes have been blind and dark for a long time; whenever a Buddha arises in the world, my eyes immediately become clear. During this Bhadrakalpa (賢劫), when the three past Buddhas arose in the world, I already gained clear vision. Now that you have come here, my eyes have suddenly opened; therefore I know that you shall surely become a Buddha."  Beside the east gate of the wall surrounding the Mahā-bodhi tree is a stūpa, the place where the King of Māras (魔王) frightened the Bodhisattva. At first, when the King of Māras knew that the Bodhisattva was about to attain Perfect Enlightenment, he tried to seduce and disturb him but failed. Worried and helpless, he gathered his divine hosts, marshaled his demonic army, and prepared his troops and equipment to threaten the Bodhisattva. Thereupon, wind and rain poured down, thunder and lightning darkened the sky, fires were set and smoke flew, and sand was raised and stones were hurled. They prepared spears and shields and made full use of bows and arrows. The Bodhisattva then entered the samādhi of great compassion, and all their weapons turned into lotus flowers. The demonic army was terrified and fled in a rout. Not far from there are two stūpas, which were built by Śakra (帝釋) and Brahmā (梵王).

East of the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree, crossing the Nairañjanā River, there is a stūpa in a great forest. To its north is a pond, which is the place where a fragrant elephant (gajendra) attended to his mother. In the past, when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path, he was a young fragrant elephant living in the northern mountains, who would roam by the side of this pond. His mother was blind, and he would gather lotus roots and draw clear water, respectfully performing his filial duties and adapting to the changing seasons. It happened that a man, wandering in the forest and losing his way, paced back and forth, wailing and crying in distress. The young elephant heard him and, feeling compassion, guided him to show him the way home. Once the man had returned, he reported to the king, saying, "I know of a fragrant elephant wandering in the forest thickets; this is a rare treasure, and you may go to capture it." The king accepted his words and raised an army to go hunting. The man acted as a guide, but the moment he pointed out the elephant to the king, both his arms fell off as if they had been severed. Although the king was startled by this strange event, he still bound the young elephant and brought him back. After the young elephant had been tied up for a long time, he would not eat grass or drink water. The stable keeper reported this to the king, who then went in person to question him. The young elephant said, "My mother is blind and has been starving for days; now that I am suffering in captivity, how could I find food sweet?" The king, feeling compassion for his situation, released him. Beside this is a stūpa, with a stone pillar erected in front, which is the place where the Buddha Kāśyapa (迦葉波佛) once sat in meditation. Nearby are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

To the east of where the four Buddhas sat, one crosses the Mahā (莫訶河) River and arrives in a great forest, where there is a stone pillar; this is the place where a non-Buddhist practitioner entered into meditation and made an evil vow. In the past, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Udraka Rāmaputra (欝頭藍子), whose aspirations transcended the mists and clouds, and whose body abandoned the marshes and thickets; he dwelt in this forest of the Dharma, hiding his spirit and concealing his traces. Having attained the five supernatural powers, he achieved the meditation of the peak of existence (bhavāgra). The King of Magadha (摩揭陀王) held him in particularly deep respect and, every day at noon, invited him to the palace for a meal. Udraka Rāmaputra would soar through the void and walk upon the air, coming and going without fail. The King of Magadha would watch and wait for the appointed time; once he arrived, the king would personally receive him and escort him to his seat.  When the king was about to depart on a tour and wished to entrust his affairs to someone, he examined those in the inner palace, but found no one capable of undertaking the command. He had a young daughter of virtuous and prudent character; she was both close to him and wise, with none surpassing her, so the King of Magadha summoned her and commanded: "I am about to travel far and have something to entrust to you; you should be diligent and see this matter through to the end with care. That immortal Udraka Rāmaputra is one whom I have long held in respect; when the time comes for him to arrive for his meal, treat him just as I have done."  Having given these instructions, the king departed on his tour. The young lady accepted the command and waited upon him according to the rites; when the great immortal arrived, she supported him and assisted him to his seat. Once Udraka Rāmaputra had touched the woman, desire for the realm of sense-objects arose, and he regressed, losing his supernatural powers. When he had finished his meal and spoke of returning, he was unable to soar through the void. Feeling ashamed and humiliated in his heart, he deceitfully said to the woman: "I have recently been cultivating the path, entering into meditation to soothe my spirit, and have been soaring through the void to come and go, having almost no leisure time. The people of the country have long wished to see this, and have heard of it for a long time." "However, the sages of old have left us instructions that benefiting others is our primary duty; how could I remain content with my own virtue and forget the need to assist others? I now wish to depart through the gate and travel by treading upon the ground, so that all those who see me may receive blessings and benefit." Having heard this, the king’s daughter made the announcement far and near. At that time, people rushed to compete, sweeping and cleaning the roads, and hundreds of thousands of people stood waiting to see his arrival. Udraka Rāmaputra (欝頭藍子) walked from the royal palace to that religious forest and sat in meditation, but his mind wandered to external environments; when he stayed in the forest, the birds chirped, and when he approached the pond, the fish and turtles made noise, so that his feelings were distracted and his mind disturbed, causing him to lose his concentration and abandon his meditation. He then gave rise to anger and immediately made an evil vow: "May I in the future become a fierce and wicked beast with the body of a leopard and the wings of a bird to seize and eat living creatures; let my body be three thousand li wide, with two wings each fifteen hundred li wide, so that I may enter the forests to devour the feathered tribes and enter the currents to eat the aquatic beings." Having made this vow, his anger gradually subsided, and after practicing diligently for a while, he regained his original concentration. Not long after, he passed away and was born in the Heaven of the First Existence (第一有天), with a lifespan of eighty thousand kalpas. The Tathāgata predicted that once his heavenly lifespan was exhausted, he would fulfill his former vow and obtain this wretched body. From that point on, he would wander through the evil paths, with no time set for his liberation.

To the east of the seats of the four Buddhas, one crosses the Mahā River and arrives in a great forest where there is a stone pillar; this is the place where a non-Buddhist entered into meditative concentration and made an evil vow.

Traveling more than one hundred li northeast from Kukkuṭapāda Mountain (鷄足山), one reaches the mountain of Buddhavana (佛陀伐那山). Its peaks and cliffs are lofty and steep, with jagged and towering ridges; among the rocks is a stone chamber where the Buddha once descended and stayed. Beside it is a flat rock where Śakra (帝釋) and the Brahmā King (梵王) ground ox-head sandalwood to anoint the Tathāgata; even now, a strong fragrance remains upon the stone. Five hundred arhats conceal their spirits here, and those who have a spiritual resonance may sometimes see them; they occasionally take the form of śrāmaṇeras to enter villages and beg for food, and their miraculous traces, appearing and disappearing, are truly difficult to describe.

More than ten *li* to the southwest of the Stick Wood (Yaṣṭivana), on the southern slope of a great mountain (Pravaragiri), there are two hot springs, the water of which is extremely hot. In the past, the Tathāgata manifested this water and bathed therein. They still exist today with their clear flow undiminished; people from near and far all come to bathe in them, and there are none among those with chronic illnesses or old ailments who are not cured. Beside them is a stūpa, which marks the place where the Tathāgata once walked.

Traveling six or seven li southeast from the Yaṣṭi Wood (杖林), one reaches the great mountain (Pravaragiri). In front of a transverse ridge stands a stone stupa where the Tathāgata once preached the Dharma to humans and devas for two or three months. At that time, King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王), wishing to come and hear the Dharma, cleared the mountain and piled up stones to build a staircase for his ascent, measuring over twenty paces in width and three or four li in length.

Three or four li to the north of the great mountain (Pravaragiri) is an isolated hill (Vyāsa), where in the past the Rishi Vyāsa (廣博仙人) lived in seclusion. He chiseled into the cliff to create a chamber, the remains of which still exist. He transmitted his teachings to his disciples, and his legacy still prevails.

On the western edge of the cliff stands a brick vihara (精舍), of lofty and spacious, extraordinary construction, with its door opening to the east. In the past, the Tathāgata often resided here to expound the Dharma; today, there is an image of him expounding the Dharma, equal in measure to the body of the Tathāgata. To the east of the vihara is a long stone, which is where the Tathāgata walked during his meditative perambulations. Beside it is a large stone, fourteen or fifteen feet high and over thirty paces in circumference; this is the place where Devadatta threw a rock from afar to strike the Buddha. Below the cliff to the south is a stūpa where, in the past, the Tathāgata expounded the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (法花經). On the side of the mountain cliff to the south of the vihara is a large stone chamber where the Tathāgata entered into meditative concentration in the past. To the northwest of the Buddha’s stone chamber, in front of a cave, is a large flat rock; this is the place where Ānanda was terrified by Māra. While the Venerable Ānanda was in meditative concentration here, the Demon King transformed himself into a vulture; during the dark phase of the moon, it perched upon the large rock, flapping its wings and shrieking to frighten the Venerable One. At that time, the Venerable One was terrified and at a loss. The Tathāgata, perceiving this, reached out his hand to comfort him, passing through the stone wall to stroke Ānanda’s head, and addressed him with words of great compassion: "This is a transformation by Māra; you should have no fear." Having received this comfort, Ānanda’s body and mind became peaceful and joyful. The bird’s tracks on the stone and the hole through the cliff, though much time has passed, still remain today. Beside the vihara are several stone chambers where Śāriputra and other great Arhats entered into meditative concentration. In front of Śāriputra’s stone chamber is a large well; though it is dried up and waterless, its ruins and hollow still remain. In the stony gully to the northeast of the vihara (mūla-gandha-kuṭī 根本香殿) is a large flat rock, which is the place where the Tathāgata dried his kaṣāya; the patterns of the robe are clear and distinct, as bright as if they were carved. Beside it, on the rock, are the footprints of the Buddha; although the wheel markings are faint, their shape and form can still be discerned. On the summit of the north mountain is a stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata gazed toward the city of Magadha (摩揭陀國) and preached the Dharma for seven days.

To the west of the north gate of the mountain city is Mount Vipula (毘布羅山). According to local tradition, on the shaded cliff to the southwest of the mountain, there were formerly five hundred hot springs; today, only several dozen remain, and they are still a mixture of cold and warm, not all of them being hot. The source of these springs originates from Lake Anavatapta (無熱惱池) to the south of the Snowy Mountains (雪山), flowing underground to this location; the water is exceptionally clear and fine, with a taste identical to that of the original lake. The water flows through five hundred branch minor hot hells, where the fiery heat rises upward, causing this warmth. The mouths of the springs are all carved from stone, some fashioned into the heads of lions or white elephants, others forming stone conduits for the cascading water, which flows down into pools constructed of layered stone. People from various regions and foreign lands all come here to bathe, and those who bathe often find their chronic illnesses cured. To the left and right of the hot springs, the foundations of various stūpas and monasteries (精舍) are arranged like fish scales; these are all sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation. Since this place is bordered by mountains and rivers, serving as a dwelling for the benevolent and the wise, there are indeed many recluses living here in seclusion.

To the west of the hot springs is the Pippala (卑鉢羅) stone cave, where the World-Honored One used to dwell constantly in the past. The cavern in the rear wall is the palace of the Asuras (阿素洛). Many bhikṣus who practice meditation reside in this chamber. At times, strange and monstrous forms of dragons, snakes, and lions appear; those who see them become mentally deranged. However, because this is a superior site where the holy and sagely have dwelt, those who follow in their footsteps and admire their influence forget the disasters and calamities associated with it. Recently, there was a bhikṣu of pure conduct who delighted in quiet seclusion and wished to hide away in this chamber to practice meditation. Someone cautioned him, saying, "Do not go there. It is full of disasters and strange occurrences, causing no small amount of harm. It is difficult to attain concentration there, and I fear you will lose your life. You should take warning from past events and not leave cause for later regret." The bhikṣu replied, "That is not so. I am determined to seek the fruit of Buddhahood and to subdue the heavenly demons; if this is the harm you speak of, how is it worth mentioning?" He then shook his khakkhara-staff and went to the chamber. There, he set up an altar and recited protective mantras. After ten days, a young woman emerged from the cavern and said to the bhikṣu, "Venerable one, you wear the dyed robes and keep the precepts, serving as a refuge for sentient beings; you cultivate wisdom and practice meditation, acting as a virtuous guide for living creatures. Yet now you dwell here and terrify us. Is this the teaching of the Tathāgata?" The bhikṣu replied, "I observe the pure precepts and follow the holy teachings. I hide my tracks in the mountain valleys to stay far from noise and confusion. Why do you suddenly reproach me for this?" She replied, "When you recite your mantras, the sound goes forth, and fire enters from outside, burning my dwelling and afflicting my kin." "I only pray that you have compassion and do not recite the mantras again." The bhikṣu said, "I recite the mantras for self-protection, not because I wish to harm living beings. In the past, when practitioners dwelt here to practice meditation, hoping to attain the holy fruit to save those in the dark paths, they saw your monstrosity and were terrified, losing their lives; this was your fault, so what excuse do you have?" She replied, "My karmic obstructions are heavy and my wisdom is shallow. From now on, I shall live in seclusion and keep to my place; I also hope that you, Venerable Sir, will not recite the divine mantras." The bhikṣu then practiced meditation as before, in peace and without harm. On Mount Vipula (毘布羅山) there is a stūpa, the place where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma in the past. Nowadays, many naked heretics (nirgrantha) reside here, practicing austerities without negligence day or night; from dawn until dusk, they turn around and observe the sun.

To the left of the north gate of the mountain city, on the shaded side of the southern cliff, traveling east for two or three li, one arrives at the Great Stone Chamber (Dakṣiṇagiri); in the past, Devadatta entered into meditation here. Not far to the east of the stone chamber, there are colored streaks on a flat rock that appear as if stained with blood, and beside it stands a stūpa built at the place where a bhikṣu practicing meditation took his own life and attained the fruit of sainthood. Formerly, there was a bhikṣu who exerted his mind and body, living in seclusion to practice meditation; as the years passed, he did not attain the holy fruit. Retiring and blaming himself, he sighed privately, saying: "The fruit of the non-learner (aśaikṣa) is not attained in time; what is the use of living in this body burdened with defilements!" He then went to this rock and stabbed his own neck; at that moment, he attained the fruit of Arhatship, rose into the void, manifested spiritual transformations, transformed into fire to consume his body, and entered into extinction (parinirvāṇa). Admiring his noble conduct, they built this to record his merit. On the cliff to the east of where the bhikṣu attained the fruit, there is a stone stūpa at the place where a bhikṣu practicing meditation threw himself from the cliff and attained the fruit of sainthood. Formerly, in the time of the Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who sat in the mountain forests practicing the meditation for attaining the fruit; though he had been diligent for a long time, he could not realize the fruit, yet he continued his contemplation day and night without forgetting his tranquil meditation. The Tathāgata, knowing that his faculties were about to ripen, went there to bring it to completion; he traveled from the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana) to the foot of the mountain cliff, snapped his fingers to summon him, and stood waiting. Seeing the Holy One from afar, the bhikṣu felt great joy in body and mind and threw himself from the cliff; because of his pure heart and his respectful faith in the Buddha's words, he attained the fruit of sainthood before reaching the ground. The World-Honored One said, "You should know that now is the time." He then ascended into the void and manifested miraculous transformations. This was to make manifest his pure faith, and therefore this memorial was established.

Traveling more than one *li* from the north gate of the mountain city, one arrives at the Kalandaka Bamboo Garden (迦蘭陀竹園; Skt. Veṇuvana-kalandakanivāpa). There is now a monastery (精舍; Skt. mūla-gandha-kuṭī) here with a stone foundation and brick chambers, with its entrance opening to the east. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he often resided here, expounding the Dharma and transforming beings, guiding the ordinary and rescuing the worldly. Now, an image of the Tathāgata’s body has been made.  Formerly, there was a great elder in this city named Kalandaka, who was renowned for his wealth and nobility at that time. He had donated a large bamboo grove to the non-Buddhists. When he saw the Tathāgata and heard the Dharma, he developed pure faith. He reflected on how he had previously allowed the bamboo grove to be occupied by those of other sects, while the Teacher of Gods and Men now had no place to lodge. At that time, various spirits and deities, moved by his sincerity, expelled the non-Buddhists and told them, "The elder Kalandaka intends to build a Buddhist monastery in the bamboo grove; you should depart quickly to avoid danger and calamity." The non-Buddhists were resentful and departed in anger. The elder then established the monastery here; once the work was completed, he went in person to invite the Buddha, and the Tathāgata thereupon accepted his offering.

Traveling more than twenty *li* west from the place where Ānanda attained the fruit, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is the site where the Mahāsāṃghika (大眾部) held their assembly. Hundreds of thousands of learners (*śaikṣa*) and non-learners (*aśaikṣa*), not having participated in the assembly of Mahākāśyapa, came to this place and said to one another: "When the Tathāgata was in the world, we studied under the same teacher. Now that the Dharma King has passed into extinction, they have excluded us. Wishing to repay the Buddha’s kindness, we must compile the Dharma-treasury." Thereupon, the ordinary and the saintly all gathered, and the wise and the virtuous fully assembled. They compiled the Sūtra Piṭaka, the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Abhidharma Piṭaka, the Miscellaneous Piṭaka (Saṃyukta Piṭaka), and the Dhāraṇī Piṭaka (禁呪藏), forming five separate collections. Because both ordinary people and sages assembled for this compilation, it was therefore called the Mahāsāṃghika (Great Assembly) school.

Going north from the Bamboo Grove Monastery (Veṇuvana-vihāra) for more than two hundred paces, one reaches the Kalandaka Pond (迦蘭陀池), where the Tathāgata often preached the Dharma in the past. Its waters were once clear and possessed the eight virtues, but after the Buddha’s Nirvāṇa, it dried up completely.

Traveling two or three li to the northwest of the Kalandaka Pond (迦蘭陀池), there is a stupa (窣堵波) built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is over sixty feet high. Beside it is a stone pillar, inscribed with an account of the construction of the stupa, standing over fifty feet high and topped with the figure of an elephant.

Not far to the west of the monastery (saṃghārāma) is a fragrant cell (mūla-gandha-kuṭī). In the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for three months, extensively expounding the wonderful Dharma for the devas and humans. More than one hundred paces to the south is a small stupa, the place where a bhikṣu from a distant land saw the Buddha. Long ago, a bhikṣu came from a distant land and, upon arriving here, encountered the Tathāgata and his holy assembly. Internally giving rise to a heart of reverence, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and immediately made a vow to seek the position of a wheel-turning king (cakravartin). Having seen this, the Tathāgata told the assembly: "That bhikṣu is truly to be pitied. His merit and virtue are deep and far-reaching, and his faith is firm; if he were to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, he would soon attain it. Now, however, he has made a vow to seek the position of a wheel-turning king, and in a future life, he will certainly receive this reward. From the place where his body touched the ground down to the golden wheel, the number of all the minute dust particles contained therein—each and every dust particle represents the reward of a wheel-turning king. Since he indulges in worldly pleasures, the holy fruit is far off." To the south of this is a standing statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. Sometimes he is seen holding an incense burner, going toward the Buddha’s fragrant cell, and circling it to the right. In the stupa to the south of the statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara are the hair and fingernails of the Tathāgata, shorn and clipped during those three months. Those who are afflicted with illness often recover by circumambulating it. The stupa by the side of the pond outside the western wall is where a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), holding a bird, questioned the Buddha about the matter of life and death. More than fifty paces to the southeast, within the enclosure, is a marvelous tree eight or nine feet high with its trunk divided into two; in the past, the Tathāgata chewed a willow twig and threw it on the ground, where it took root, and although a long time has passed, it has neither increased nor decreased. To the east is a great vihara, over two hundred feet high, where the Tathāgata in the past expounded the wonderful Dharma for four months. To the north, one hundred and some paces away, is a vihara containing an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩). Those of pure faith who come to make offerings see it differently, and its position cannot be fixed; sometimes it stands by the side of the door, and sometimes it appears before the eaves. The clergy and laity of various countries all come to make offerings. To the north of the Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva vihara is a great vihara, over three hundred feet high, built by King Bālāditya (婆羅阿迭多王); its ornamentation, dimensions, and the Buddha image within are the same as those of the great vihara under the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree. To its northeast is a stūpa where the Tathāgata in the past expounded the wonderful Dharma for seven days. To the northwest is the place where the four past Buddhas sat. To its south is a brass vihara built by King Śīlāditya (戒日王); although the work is not yet finished, according to its plans and measurements, it will be one hundred feet high when completed. To the east, two hundred and some paces outside the enclosure, is a standing copper Buddha image, over eighty feet high, which required a six-story pavilion to cover it; it was made in the past by King Pūrṇavarman (滿胄王). Two or three li north of the copper Buddha image of King Pūrṇavarman, inside a brick vihara, is an image of the Bodhisattva Tārā (多羅菩薩). Its stature is lofty, and its spiritual efficacy is very manifest. Every year on the first day of the year, grand offerings are made; kings of neighboring regions, ministers, and noble families bring wonderful incense and flowers, hold precious banners and canopies, play metal and stone instruments in succession, and harmonize them with string and bamboo instruments, holding this Dharma assembly for seven days. Inside the south gate of the enclosure, there is a large well. Formerly, in the time of the Buddha, a large company of merchants, pressed by heat and thirst, came to where the Buddha was. The World-Honored One pointed to the ground, indicating that water could be obtained there. The leader of the merchants then struck the ground with a cart axle; once the ground was indented, water gushed forth like a spring. Having drunk and heard the Dharma, they all realized the holy fruit.

Traveling eight or nine li southwest from the monastery, one reaches the town of Kolika (拘理迦邑), where there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; this is the native village of the Venerable Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子). Beside it is a stūpa marking the place where the Venerable One entered the nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa), and it contains his bodily relics. The Venerable One was of a great Brahmin lineage and had been a close friend of Śāriputra since youth. Śāriputra was esteemed for his brilliant talent, while the Venerable One was renowned for his profound discernment; they were equals in wisdom, always together in their movements, bound by a lifelong pact to share the same path, and together they grew weary of the secular world and sought to leave the householder's life, eventually taking Sañjaya as their teacher. Śāriputra encountered the arhat Aśvajit, heard the Dharma, and attained realization; he returned and recounted it to the Venerable One, who, upon hearing and realizing the Dharma, attained the first fruit. Together with his two hundred and fifty disciples, he went to the place of the Buddha. The World-Honored One saw them from afar and, pointing them out to the assembly, said: "Those who are coming are the foremost in supernatural powers among my disciples." Upon arriving at the place of the Buddha, they requested to enter the Dharma. The World-Honored One said: "Welcome, monks; practice the holy life purely to reach the end of suffering." Upon hearing these words, their hair and beards fell away, their secular garments changed, their precepts became pure, and their deportment became harmonious. After seven days, their defilements were exhausted, they attained the fruit of arhatship, and they gained supernatural powers. Three or four li to the east of the native village of Maudgalyāyana, there is a stūpa at the place where King Bimbisāra went to meet and see the Buddha. When the Tathāgata first realized the fruit of buddhahood, he knew that the hearts of the people in the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) were thirsting with longing. He accepted the invitation of King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) and, in the early morning, donned his robes and took up his alms bowl. Surrounded on all sides by a thousand bhikṣus—all of whom were elder brahmans with shell-shaped topknots who had donned dyed robes out of admiration for the Dharma, following him in his retinue—he entered the city of Rājagṛha (王舍城). At that time, the heavenly king Śakra (帝釋天王) transformed himself into a māṇava (摩那婆) with a shell-shaped topknot on his head. Holding a golden vase in his left hand and a precious staff in his right, his feet treading on empty space four finger-widths above the ground, he led the way for the Buddha amidst the assembly. Then King Bimbisāra of the country of Magadha, together with the various brahmans, elders, and laypeople of his kingdom—a multitude of hundreds of thousands—came out of the city of Rājagṛha in a procession to welcome the holy assembly.

Two or three li south of the Kapotaka monastery (迦布德迦伽藍), one arrives at the mountain of Vyāsa (孤山). The mountain is lofty and steep, with lush forests, famous flowers, and clear streams covering the cliffs and lining the ravines. Above, there are many vihāras (精舍) and sacred temples, which are extremely refined in their craftsmanship. In the central vihāra is a statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩); although small in size, its spiritual majesty inspires awe, as it holds a lotus in its hand and bears a Buddha figure upon its crown. There are often people who fast and focus their minds, seeking a vision of the Bodhisattva for seven days, fourteen days, or even a full month; those who receive a response see the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, in all his solemn and wondrous beauty and brilliant radiance, emerge from the statue to comfort and exhort them. Long ago, the king of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) in the South Sea looked into a mirror at dawn and saw not his own reflection, but rather this Bodhisattva statue atop a small hill in the Tāla forest of Magadha (摩揭陀國) in Jambudvīpa (贍部洲); the king, deeply moved and joyful, sought to find it. When he arrived at this hill, he found the statue to be exactly as he had seen, so he built a vihāra and established various offerings. Since then, subsequent kings, admiring this legacy, have built vihāras and sacred temples alongside it, and offerings of incense, flowers, and music have never ceased.

Traveling southeast for more than forty li from the statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩) on the isolated hill (Vyāsa 孤山), one reaches a monastery where there are more than fifty monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna. In front of the monastery is a great stūpa, which possesses many miraculous qualities; it is the place where the Buddha formerly preached the Dharma for seven days to the Brahmadeva-rāja and others. Beside it are the sites of the traces of the sitting and walking meditation of the three past Buddhas.

Traveling northeast from the monastery for more than seventy li, to the south of the Ganges (Gaṅgā) River, one arrives at a large settlement where the population is dense and prosperous. There are several deva temples, all of which are exquisitely carved and adorned. Not far to the southeast is a great stupa (stūpa), where the Buddha once stayed for one night and preached the Dharma.
Further to the southeast, at a corner of the great sea, is the country of Kāmalaṅkā (迦摩浪迦國).
Next, to the east, is the country of Dvāravatī (墮羅鉢底國).
To the east of this is the country of Īśānapura (伊賞那補羅國).
Further to the east is the country of Mahācampā (摩訶瞻波國), which is what is called Linyi (林邑) here.

To the southwest is the country of Yamanadvīpa (閻摩那洲國). Regarding these six countries, the routes are obstructed by mountains and rivers, and I did not enter their territories; however, their customs, lands, and boundaries are known through report.

In the great mountains on the southwestern border of the kingdom is the Puṣpagiri (補澁波祇釐) monastery. Its stone stūpa possesses many spiritual anomalies; sometimes, on fast days, it emits a bright light. Therefore, the pure-hearted faithful, from both near and far, all gather there, holding exquisite flower canopies and vying to perform offerings. Below the dew-receiving basin and above the inverted-bowl structure, if one places the handle of a flower canopy, it remains fixed there as if a magnet were attracting a needle.

In the monastery in the mountains to the northwest, there is a stūpa whose miraculous properties are the same as the former. These two stūpas were built by spirits and deities, and their spiritual wonders are of such a nature.

On the northern frontier of the country, atop the great mountain ridge (Pravaragiri), there is a stone stupa over a hundred feet high. It is the place where, at the beginning of the kalpa when the human lifespan was immeasurable, a Pratyekabuddha entered into extinction.

To the south of the country, bordering the sea, is Mount Malaya (秣剌耶山), with its lofty cliffs, steep ridges, deep caverns, and mountain torrents. Among them are white sandalwood trees and candaneva trees (栴檀儞婆樹). The latter resemble white sandalwood and cannot be distinguished from them, except in the height of summer, when one climbs to a high place and looks out from afar; those entwined by large snakes are known to be such. Because the nature of this wood is cool and cold, the snakes coil around it. Once they have been sighted, arrows are shot to mark them, and only after the snakes have hibernated in winter are the trees harvested. The camphor tree (羯布羅香樹; Skt. karpūra) has a trunk like a pine but different leaves, and its flowers and fruits are also distinct. When first harvested and still moist, it has no fragrance, but after the wood dries, it is split along the grain to reveal a fragrant substance within, shaped like mica and colored like ice or snow; this is what is called camphor (龍腦香).

To the east of the Malaya (秣剌耶) Mountains is Mount Potalaka (布呾洛迦山). The mountain paths are perilous, and the cliffs and valleys are precipitous. On the summit of the mountain is a lake with water as clear as a mirror, from which flows a great river that circles the mountain twenty times before entering the South Sea. Beside the lake is a stone celestial palace where the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩) comes and goes to dwell. Those who wish to see the Bodhisattva disregard their own lives, wading through waters and climbing the mountain, forgetting all hardships and dangers; yet those who are able to reach it are few indeed. As for the inhabitants at the foot of the mountain who pray with a sincere heart to see him, the Bodhisattva may appear in the form of Maheśvara (自在天) or as an ash-smearing ascetic (塗灰外道) to console them and fulfill their wishes.

The country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) is over 7,000 li in circumference. The capital city is over 40 li in circumference. The land is fertile, the climate is warm and hot, crops are sown in their proper seasons, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The population is prosperous, and the households are wealthy. The people are short and dark-skinned, and their temperaments are fierce and impetuous. They are fond of learning and value virtue, honoring goodness and diligently cultivating merit. This country was originally an island of gems; it contains many precious treasures and is inhabited by ghosts and spirits.  Later, there was a king in South India whose daughter was betrothed to a neighboring country. On an auspicious day, as she was being escorted there, they encountered a lion on the road. Her attendants abandoned the girl and fled to escape the danger, but the girl remained in her carriage, resigned to losing her life. At that time, the lion king carried the girl away, entering deep mountains and dwelling in secluded valleys. He hunted deer and gathered fruit to provide for her in due season. After many years had passed, she gave birth to a son and a daughter; their appearance was that of humans, but their nature was that of beasts.   As the son gradually grew up, he had the strength to wrestle with wild beasts. When he reached the age of twenty, his human intelligence began to manifest, and he said to his mother, "What am I? My father is a wild beast, and my mother is a human. Since we are not of the same species, how can we be mates?" His mother then recounted the past to her son, saying, "Humans and beasts follow different paths; we should flee at once." The mother said, "I tried to escape before, but I could not succeed on my own." The son subsequently followed his lion father, climbing mountains and crossing ridges to observe his movements so that they might escape the danger. Once he had waited for his father to leave, he carried his mother and sister on his back and descended toward human settlements. The mother said, "We must each be cautious and secretive; do not speak of the origin of these events, for if people should hear of them, they may look down upon us." Thereupon, they arrived at the father’s native country, but the country was not that of their kin, and their ancestral line had already been extinguished. They sought shelter with the townspeople, who asked them, "From what country are you?" They replied, "We are originally from this country, but we were scattered in foreign lands; mother and son have traveled together to return to our old home." The people all felt pity and compassion, and together they provided them with supplies.  When the lion king returned and saw nothing, he pined for his children. His fury erupted, and he left the mountain valleys to roam among the villages and towns, roaring and thundering, violently harming people and animals, and cruelly destroying living beings. Whenever the townspeople came out, he would seize and kill them. They beat drums and blew conch shells, shouldered crossbows and held spears, and followed in groups like an army; only then could they avoid harm.  The king, fearing that his benevolent influence was not reaching the people, released hunters, hoping to capture the beast. The king personally led the four divisions of the army, numbering in the tens of thousands, to surround the forests and thickets, spanning across the mountains and valleys. The lion roared, and both men and beasts fled in terror. Since he could not be captured, the king subsequently issued a recruitment call: whoever could seize the lion and rid the country of this menace would be rewarded with a great prize to honor their distinguished achievement.  Upon hearing the king’s order, the son said to his mother, "Our hunger and cold have become extreme; I should respond to the recruitment, for perhaps I may gain something with which to support you." The mother said, "You must not speak like this! Although he is a beast, he is still called your father; how could you, because of hardship, commit such an act of rebellion and harm?" The son replied, "Humans and beasts are of different species; where then is the place for ritual and righteousness? Since we are already obstructed and hindered, what hope is there for this heart?" He then hid a small knife in his sleeve and went out to answer the recruitment. At that time, thousands of people and ten thousand cavalry gathered like clouds and mist, but the lion sat in the forest, and no one dared to approach. The son went directly before him, and the father became tame and submissive. Thus, out of affection, he forgot his anger; the son then stabbed his blade into the father’s belly. The father still harbored loving kindness and remained without resentment or malice, even as his belly was ripped open, and he died enduring the pain. The king asked, "What kind of person is this, that he is so extraordinary?" He tempted him with benefits and threatened him with punishment, after which the son fully explained the beginning and the end, detailing the entire situation. The king said, "How rebellious! If he would even harm his own father, how much more so would he harm those who are not his kin? The beast species is difficult to tame, and their violent nature is easily stirred. To remove a menace to the people is a great merit, but to sever the life of one's father is a rebellious heart. I shall provide a heavy reward to compensate for his merit, but I shall banish him far away to punish his rebellion. In this way, the laws of the country will not be compromised, and the king’s word will not be inconsistent." Thereupon, he fitted out two large ships and stored them with plenty of provisions. The mother was left in the country and provided for with the reward for the merit, while the son and daughter were each placed on a ship and left to drift with the waves. The son’s ship drifted across the sea until it reached this island of treasures; seeing an abundance of precious gems, he settled there. Later, when merchants came to the island to collect treasures, he killed the merchant leader and kept his children. In this way they multiplied, and their descendants were numerous. They then established a ruler and ministers, assigned ranks of high and low, built a capital and cities, and occupied the territory. Because their ancestor had captured a lion (siṃha), they cited this original achievement to name the country. As for the ship carrying the daughter, it drifted to the west of Persia (Pārasī), where she was bewitched by spirits and gave birth to a group of daughters; this is the origin of the present-day Western Kingdom of Women. Therefore, the people of the country of the Lion (Siṃhala) have a base and dark appearance, with square chins and broad foreheads; their temperament is fierce and violent, and they are cruel and prone to poisoning. This is because they are the descendants of a wild beast, and thus the people are mostly brave and robust. This is one account.  What the Buddha’s teaching records is as follows: In the past, in the great iron city of this precious island, there dwelt five hundred rākṣasīs. Atop the city towers, two tall banners were erected to signify signs of good or ill fortune; the auspicious banner would move when there was a lucky event, and the inauspicious banner would move when there was a calamity. They would constantly lie in wait for merchants arriving at the precious island, whereupon they would transform into beautiful women, carrying fragrant flowers and playing music to welcome and console them, luring them into the iron city. After the festivities and banquets were over, they would place the merchants in an iron prison and gradually devour them.  At that time, in the continent of Jambudvīpa, there was a great merchant leader named Saṃgha; his son was named Saṃghala. His father being old, he took over the family business and set out with five hundred merchants to enter the sea to collect treasures. Blown about by wind and waves, they happened to reach the precious island. When the rākṣasīs saw the auspicious banner move, they brought fragrant flowers and played music, coming together to welcome the merchants and entice them into the iron city. The merchant leader then engaged in joyful entertainment with the rākṣasī queen, and the remaining merchants each paired off with one, and as the years passed, they all fathered children. The rākṣasīs, their affections for their old partners having grown distant, wished to imprison them in an iron jail to wait for other merchants. At that time, Saṃghala had a nightmare during the night and, knowing it was not an auspicious sign, secretly sought a path home. He happened upon the iron jail and heard the sound of piteous wailing, so he climbed a tall tree and asked, "Who is it that is bound and suffering such grief?" They replied, "Do you not know? The women in the city are all rākṣasīs. In the past, they enticed us into the city for entertainment. Once you had arrived, they imprisoned us and gradually consumed us as food; now more than half are gone, and before long, you too will suffer this same calamity." Saṃghala asked, "What plan can be devised to escape this danger?" They replied, "We have heard that there is a heavenly horse on the seashore; if one prays with utmost sincerity, it will surely ferry one across to safety." Having heard this, Saṃghala secretly informed the other merchants, and together they looked toward the seashore, focusing their minds on seeking salvation. At that time, the heavenly horse came and told the men, "If each of you grasps my mane and does not look back, I will ferry you across the sea to escape this peril and reach the continent of Jambudvīpa, returning to your home country." The merchants followed these instructions with single-minded devotion and gripped its mane; the heavenly horse then soared into the clouds and galloped across the seacoast. The rākṣasīs (羅剎女) suddenly realized their husbands had fled; they told one another, wondering where they had gone, and each carrying her young child, they flew through the air in search of them. Knowing the merchants were about to reach the seashore, they called out to one another and flew off to find them. Before long, they encountered the company of merchants; with mixed feelings of grief and joy, their tears flowed freely as they covered their faces, sobbing and saying: "I am grateful for our meeting and fortunate to have wed such a fine man; our home was full of joy and we have long shared deep affection, yet now you abandon us to go far away, leaving your wife and child desolate—how can anyone endure such a heart-wrenching fate? We pray you, look back and return with us to the city."  The hearts of the merchants remained unmoved. The rākṣasīs, finding their entreaties of no avail, resorted to their demonic charms and employed every manner of deception. The merchants, overcome by love and unable to bear the separation, felt their resolve waver, and they all fell back. The rākṣasīs congratulated one another and went away, holding the merchants by the hand.  Siṃhala (僧伽羅), however, possessed deep and firm wisdom; his mind was free from attachments, and he succeeded in crossing the great sea, escaping this peril. Meanwhile, the queen of the rākṣasīs returned alone to the Iron City. The other rākṣasīs said to her, "You lack wisdom and strategy, having been abandoned by your husband; since you are devoid of skill and ability, you should no longer dwell here."  The queen of the rākṣasīs then took the child she had borne, flew before Siṃhala, and, exerting her utmost charms, enticed and pleaded with him to return. Siṃhala recited a mantra and, brandishing his sharp sword, rebuked her, saying: "You are a rākṣasī, and I am a human; humans and ghosts follow different paths, and we are not a match." If you continue to harass me with your suffering, I shall end your life." The rākṣasī, knowing that her seduction had failed, flew through the air and arrived at the home of Siṃhala (僧伽羅). She deceived his father, Siṃha (僧伽), saying: "I am the daughter of a certain king. Siṃhala took me as his wife and we bore a son. We were carrying precious goods to return to his native country, but while crossing the sea, we encountered a storm and our ship was wrecked. Only my son, myself, and Siṃhala managed to survive. The mountains and rivers were difficult to traverse, and we suffered from cold, hunger, and hardship. Because of one word that displeased him, I was abandoned and cast aside, insulted with improper language, and reviled as a rākṣasī. To return home is to face a vast distance, and to stay here is to be a lonely, stranded traveler. With nowhere to turn, I dare to present my situation."  Siṃha said, "It is truly as you say; you should enter the house at once." Not long after, Siṃhala arrived. His father said to him, "Why do you value wealth and treasure while slighting your wife and child?" Siṃhala replied, "This is a rākṣasī." He then explained the previous events in detail to his parents, and his relatives and kin all joined in driving her away.  The rākṣasī then complained to the king, and the king wished to punish Siṃhala. Siṃhala said, "She is a rākṣasī, and her nature is full of seductive bewitchment." The king believed this was untrue, and being charmed by her beauty, he said to Siṃhala, "If you must abandon this woman, I shall keep her in my harem." Siṃhala replied, "I fear it will bring disaster. Since she is a rākṣasī, her only food is blood and flesh." The king did not listen to the words of Siṃhala and proceeded to take her as his wife. Later, in the middle of the night, she flew back to the precious island (Ratnadvīpa) and summoned the other five hundred rākṣasī demonesses to come together to the royal palace. Using poisonous incantations, they ravaged the palace; they ate the flesh and drank the blood of all the people and animals, then took the remaining corpses and returned to the precious island. At daybreak, the ministers and officials gathered for court, but the palace gates were closed and would not open. They waited and listened for a long time, but heard no human voices. Thereupon, they pushed against the doors and opened the gates, following one another as they hurried inside. When they reached the palace courtyard, it was silent and empty of people; there were only skeletons. The officials and aides looked at one another in dismay, wailing and weeping, unable to fathom the source of the disaster. Siṃhala recounted the entire story from beginning to end, and the ministers and subjects believed him, realizing that the king had brought this disaster upon himself.  Thereupon, the state assistants, veteran ministers, various officials, and senior generals inquired after those of illustrious virtue and sought out those of sublime character; all admired the merit and wisdom of Siṃhala, and they consulted together, saying: "How can the one who rules the people be chosen haphazardly? He must first possess merit and wisdom, and secondly embody sagacity and discernment; for without merit and wisdom, one cannot enjoy the precious throne, and without sagacity and discernment, how can one manage the affairs of state? Siṃhala is the very man. He perceived the hidden danger in a dream, was moved by the response of the heavenly horse, was loyal in remonstrating with his lord, and was wise enough to protect himself. The mandate of history is here; let us compose a new song of praise." The masses were happy to support him and honored him by establishing him as king. Siṃhala, unable to decline the offer, agreed to hold to the middle path, and after bowing respectfully to the assembled officials, he ascended the throne. Thereupon, he reformed the previous abuses and set an example of virtue. He then issued an order, saying: "Our former merchant companions are in the land of the Rākṣasas; their life or death is uncertain, and good and evil are indistinguishable. Now, to rescue them from their plight, we should prepare our arms and armor; to save those in peril and show compassion to those in distress is a blessing to the state; to recover precious goods and store up treasures is a benefit to the state." Thereupon, he organized his troops and traveled across the sea. At that time, the banners of ill omen atop the iron city began to shake; the Rākṣasīs, seeing this, were struck with terror and immediately unleashed their seductive charms, coming out to meet the men to entice and deceive them. The king, having long known of their deceit, ordered his soldiers to recite mantras with their mouths and exert their martial might with their bodies. The Rākṣasīs stumbled, fell, and were defeated; some fled to hide on isolated islands, while others drowned in the surging currents. Thereupon, he destroyed the iron city, broke the iron prisons, rescued the merchants, and obtained many jewels. He recruited the common people to move and settle on the treasure island, established a capital, built towns, and thus a kingdom was formed. He then used the king’s name as the name of the country.  Siṃhala (僧伽羅) is a matter from a previous life of Śākya Tathāgata. In earlier times, the kingdom of Siṃhala only honored licentious sacrifices. In the hundredth year after the Buddha passed away, Mahendra (摩醯因陀羅), the younger brother of King Aśoka (無憂王), abandoned worldly desires to seek the fruits of sainthood; having attained the six supernatural powers and the eight liberations, he traveled through the air to this country to propagate the true Dharma and spread the bequeathed teachings. From that time onward, the customs have been pure and faithful. There are several hundred saṃghārāmas and over twenty thousand monks, who follow the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. More than two hundred years after the arrival of Buddhism, each [group] specialized in its own field, dividing into two schools: the first is the Mahāvihāra (摩訶毘訶羅) school, which rejects the Mahāyāna and studies the Lesser Vehicle; the second is the Abhayagiri (阿跋耶祇釐) school, which studies both vehicles and propagates the Tripiṭaka. The monks are pure in their moral conduct, their concentration and wisdom are clear and bright, their deportment is exemplary, and they are numerous and flourishing.  Beside the royal palace is the Temple of the Buddha’s Tooth (mūla-gandha-kuṭī), several hundred feet high, shimmering with pearls and adorned with rare gems. A signal post is erected atop the temple, upon which is placed a large padmarāga jewel; its brilliant light shines resplendently, and when viewed from afar, it glitters like a bright star by day or night. Three times a day, the king bathes the Buddha’s tooth with scented water and powdered incense, either washing it or burning the incense, striving for the utmost rarity and splendor in his offerings.  Beside the Temple of the Buddha’s Tooth is a small temple, which is also adorned and polished with various precious gems. Inside is a golden Buddha statue, cast by a former king of this country to be of equal stature to himself, with the uṣṇīṣa adorned with precious jewels. Later, there was a thief who waited for an opportunity to steal it, but the heavy doors and surrounding railings were guarded with strict vigilance. The thief then dug a tunnel to enter the temple through a hole; when he attempted to take the jewel, the statue gradually grew taller and higher. Having failed in his quest, the thief retreated and sighed, saying: "In the past, the Tathāgata practiced the bodhisattva path, aroused a vast mind, and made great vows, offering up his own life and body, down to his cities and kingdoms, out of compassion for the four types of birth, bestowing everything upon all beings. Now, how could his bequeathed image be stingy with a jewel?" "Reflecting on this, I do not understand the past conduct." The image then bowed its head and bestowed the jewel. Having obtained it, the thief immediately took it to sell. Those who saw it all said to him, "This treasure is the jewel from the *uṣṇīṣa* (頂髻) of the golden Buddha image of the former king. Where did you obtain it to come here and sell it?" They then seized him and reported it to the king. The king asked where he had obtained it, and the thief said, "The Buddha gave it to me himself; I am not a thief." The king, thinking he was not being truthful, ordered an envoy to go and verify it, and the image was still bowing its head. Witnessing this sacred miracle, the king’s faith became pure and firm; he did not punish the man, but instead redeemed the jewel at a high price, adorned the image’s *uṣṇīṣa*, and replaced it on the crown. Because of this, the image has remained with its head bowed until the present day.  Beside the royal palace, a great kitchen was built, preparing food for eighteen thousand monks daily. When the time for the meal arrived, the assembly of monks would hold their alms bowls to receive the provisions, and having received their food, each would return to his own residence. Since the time the Buddha’s teaching spread to this land, this offering was established, and descendants inherited the succession, continuing the practice until the present. For the past ten or more years, the country has been in political turmoil without a stable ruler, and this practice has been abandoned. The country is situated on the edge of the sea and the land produces precious gems. When the king personally performs sacrifices, the spirits present rare treasures. The city’s inhabitants and scholars travel back and forth to seek and collect them, and according to their karmic rewards, what they obtain differs. Depending on the pearls and gems they acquire, there is a set tax.

More than two hundred years after the arrival of Buddhism, each [group] specialized in its own field, and they divided into two schools: the first is called the Mahāvihāra school (摩訶毘訶羅住部), which rejects the Mahāyāna and studies the Hīnayāna teachings.
The second is the Abhayagiri-vihāra school (阿跋耶祇釐住部), which studies both vehicles and propagates the Tripiṭaka.

Sailing several thousand li across the sea to the south of the country, one reaches the island of Nārikela (那羅稽羅洲). The inhabitants of the island are diminutive, being just over three feet tall; they have human bodies and bird-like beaks, and as they do not cultivate grain or crops, they subsist solely on coconuts.

Sailing several thousand *li* west across the sea from the country of Nārikela (那羅稽羅洲), on the eastern cliff of a solitary island, there is a stone Buddha statue over a hundred feet high, seated facing east. It has a moonstone (*candrakānta*) as its *uṣṇīṣa*; when the moon shines upon it, water flows down, drenching the cliffs and ridges and pouring into the mountain ravines. At one time, a group of merchants, having encountered a storm and drifted with the waves, arrived at this solitary island. The sea water was salty and undrinkable, and they suffered from thirst for a long time. It happened to be the fifteenth day of the month, and water flowed from the top of the statue, by which the entire group was saved; they believed that their utmost sincerity had moved the divine sage to rescue them. They remained there for several days, but whenever the moon was hidden behind the high cliffs, the water would not flow. The leader of the merchants then said, "It is not necessarily the case that it flows to save us. I have heard that when moonlight shines upon a moonstone, water will flow; could it be that there is such a gem atop the head of the Buddha statue?" They then climbed the cliff to look at it and found that the *uṣṇīṣa* of the image was indeed made of moonstone. When they met the people there, they told them the whole story from beginning to end.

To the west of the country, sailing several thousand li across the sea, one reaches the Great Treasure Island (Mahāratnadvīpa), which is uninhabited by humans and serves only as an abode for deities. In the quiet of the night, looking from afar, its light illuminates the mountains and waters. Many merchants have traveled there, but all have returned without obtaining anything.

Not far from the city is Mount Ujjanta (郁鄯多山). On its summit is a monastery, with rooms and corridors mostly carved out of the cliffs and ridges. The forests and trees are lush and dense, and streams flow across the landscape; it is a place where sages and saints wander and dwell, and where spirits and immortals gather.

On the eastern border of the country is the city of Hūma (鶴秣城); the inner city is not extensive, but the outer wall is more than sixty li in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous, and their households are wealthy.

To the northwest it borders the country of Hrom (拂懍國); its territory and customs are the same as those of Persia (波剌斯). Its physical appearance and language are slightly different; it possesses many rare treasures and is also very wealthy.

On an island in the sea to the southwest of the country of Fulin (拂懍國), there is the Western Women’s Country. It is inhabited entirely by women, and there are virtually no men. It possesses many precious goods and is a dependency of the country of Fulin; therefore, the King of Fulin sends men there every year to mate with them, and it is their custom not to raise any male children who are born.

According to local accounts, to the west of this country one reaches the country of Kaikanan (稽畺那國); it is situated among the valleys of the great mountains (Pravaragiri), and it has separate local chieftains but no sovereign ruler. It abounds in sheep and horses, and among the horses are those of excellent quality, whose forms are remarkably large; they are a rare breed among the nations and are prized by neighboring regions.

The great capital city of the country is called Ghasna (鶴悉那), which is over thirty li in circuit; sometimes the capital is at the city of Ghasala (鶴薩羅), which is also over thirty li in circuit, and both are steep, rugged, and well-fortified.

Or the capital is the city of Ghasala (鶴薩羅城), the city circuit is over thirty *li*, and it is both steep, rugged, and well-fortified. The mountains and rivers are undulating, and the fields and ridges are high and dry. Grain crops are sown in their proper seasons, winter wheat grows in abundance, vegetation is lush, and flowers and fruits are flourishing. It is suitable for turmeric (*kuṅkuma*), and produces the *hingu* herb; this herb grows in the Rāmēndu (羅摩印度) river valley. In the city of Ghasala, gushing springs flow in various directions, and the people of the country benefit from them to irrigate their fields.

Crops are sown in their proper seasons, winter wheat grows in abundance, vegetation is lush, and flowers and fruits are flourishing. The land is suitable for turmeric (kuṅkuma) and produces the hingu herb; this herb grows in the Rāmēndu (羅摩印度川) valley.

From here, traveling northward for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Vṛjiṣṭhāna (弗栗恃薩儻那國). The country of Vṛjiṣṭhāna is more than two thousand li from east to west and over one thousand li from north to south. The capital city of the country is named Hūbīnā (護苾那), and it is more than twenty li in circuit. The soil, products, and customs are the same as those of the country of Jaguḍa (漕矩吒國), though the language is different. The climate is cold and harsh, and the temperament of the people is fierce and impetuous. The king is of Turkic lineage; he has deep faith in the Three Jewels, values learning, and adheres to virtue.
The capital city of the country is called Hubina (護苾那), and it is over twenty li in circuit.

Proceeding northeast from this country, crossing mountains and fording rivers, and passing through several dozen small frontier towns of the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國), one reaches the Varasena (婆羅犀那) great range of the Great Snow Mountains. The range is extremely high and steep, with dangerous, precipitous slopes; the paths are winding and the cliffs and peaks interlock. Sometimes one enters deep valleys, and sometimes one ascends high precipices; even in the height of summer it is frozen over, and one must hack through the ice to cross. After traveling for three days, one finally reaches the top of the range. The cold wind is bitter and fierce, and accumulated snow fills the valleys; travelers passing through cannot find a place to stand. Soaring falcons cannot fly across it; they must walk on their feet before taking flight again. Looking down at the various mountains, they appear like small anthills. In the Jambudvīpa (贍部洲), this range is exceptionally high. Its summit has no trees, but only many stone peaks, clustered and leaning against one another, standing dense like a forest.

After traveling for three more days, I finally descended from the mountain range and reached the country of Antarava (安呾羅縛國). The country of Antarava is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is over three thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit. There is no great sovereign or leader, and it is subject to the Turks. The mountains and hills are connected, and the river valleys and fields are narrow and confined. The climate is cold and severe, and the wind and snow are biting and harsh. It is abundant in crops and suitable for flowers and fruits. The nature of the people is fierce and violent, and their customs lack order and discipline. They do not understand the concepts of sin or merit, and they do not value learning; they only maintain shrines to deities and have little faith in the Buddha-dharma. There are three monasteries with several dozen monks, all of whom follow the teachings of the Mahāsāṃghika school. There is one stūpa, which was built by King Aśoka.

From here, traveling northwest, entering valleys and crossing ridges, and passing through various small towns for over four hundred li, one reaches the country of Khost (闊悉多國). The country of Khost is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is less than one thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over ten li in circuit. There is no great monarch, and it is subject to the Turks (突厥). The mountains are numerous and the rivers narrow; it is windy and cold. The grain crops are abundant, and flowers and fruits are plentiful. The nature of the people is fierce and violent, and their customs lack laws and regulations. There are three saṃghārāmas (伽藍), and the number of monks is very small.

From here, going northwest across mountains and valleys and passing through various towns for over three hundred li, one arrives at the country of Huoh (活國). The country of Huoh is the ancient territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. It has no separate ruler, being subject to the Turks (突厥). The land is level and flat; grain is sown in its season, vegetation is lush and flourishing, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are simple and honest. The people are impetuous and fierce by nature, and they wear garments of felt and coarse wool. They mostly believe in the Three Jewels and rarely worship other gods. There are more than ten monasteries and several hundred monks, who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings. Their king is a Turk who governs the various small countries south of the Iron Gate (鐵門); he moves about like a bird and has no permanent seat of government.

From here, traveling east, one enters the Congling (Onion Mountains). The Congling are situated in the center of Jambudvīpa; they connect to the Great Snow Mountains (Mahāhimavat) in the south, reach the Hot Sea (Rēgistan/Issyk-Kul) and the Thousand Springs (Bing-gyul) in the north, border the country of Huo (Kunduz) in the west, and adjoin the country of Wusha (Usha) in the east. They extend for several thousand li in every direction. There are hundreds of layers of cliffs and ridges, with deep, precipitous valleys where ice and snow accumulate permanently and cold winds blow with great intensity. Because they produce many onions, they are called the Congling; furthermore, because the mountain cliffs are of an onion-green color, they are named accordingly.

Traveling east for more than a hundred li, one reaches the country of Mungan (瞢健國). The country of Mungan is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is more than four hundred li in circuit. The capital city of the country is fifteen or sixteen li in circuit. The soil, products, and customs are much the same as those of the country of Hu (活國). There is no great sovereign, and it is subject to the Turks.

To the north, one reaches the country of Alini (阿利尼國). The country of Alini is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It borders both banks of the Vaxšu River (縛芻河) and is over three hundred li in circuit. The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit. The suitability of the soil and the customs are much the same as those of the country of Hu (活國).

To the east, one reaches the country of Rāhu (曷邏胡國). The country of Rāhu is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). To the north, it borders the Vaxšu River (縛芻河), and it is more than two hundred li in circuit. The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit. The soil, products, and customs are much the same as those of the country of Hu (活國).

Going east from the country of Mungān (瞢健國), crossing steep mountain ranges, traversing deep valleys, and passing through several river cities for more than three hundred *li*, one reaches the country of Kṛṣma (訖栗瑟摩國). The country of Kṛṣma is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is more than ten *li* from east to west and three hundred *li* from north to south. The capital city of the country is fifteen or sixteen *li* in circumference. The native products and social customs are generally the same as those of the country of Mungān, but the people differ in being violent, foolish, and malicious in disposition.

To the north lies the country of Parighar (鉢利曷國). The country of Parighar is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is over one hundred li from east to west and over three hundred li from south to north. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circumference. The soil, products, and customs are much the same as those of the country of Kṛṣma (訖栗瑟摩國).

Going east from the country of Kṛṣma (訖栗瑟摩國), crossing mountains and traversing rivers for over three hundred li, one reaches the country of Himatala (呬摩呾羅國). The country of Himatala is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is over three thousand li in circumference. The mountains and rivers are winding and rugged, but the soil is fertile. It is suitable for grain crops, with an abundance of winter wheat; all kinds of plants grow luxuriantly, and various fruits are plentiful. The climate is cold and harsh. The people are violent and impetuous by nature, do not understand merit or sin, and their appearance is coarse and ugly. Their deportment and manners, as well as their clothing of felt and leather, are quite similar to those of the Turks. Their women wear wooden horns on their heads, over three feet high, with two branches in front representing their husband’s parents; the upper branch represents the father-in-law, and the lower branch represents the mother-in-law. As each passes away, the corresponding branch is removed; when both parents-in-law are deceased, the horn headdress is discarded entirely. In the past, this was a powerful kingdom, and the king was of the Śākya clan (釋種); to the west of the Onion Range (葱嶺), many states were subject to them. Because their borders neighbor the Turks, they have gradually adopted their customs; furthermore, due to being subjected to invasions and raids, they have had to defend their own territory. Consequently, the people of this country have been scattered into foreign lands, with dozens of fortified cities each having its own independent ruler, living in domed felt tents and moving about in search of pasture. To the west, it borders the country of Kṛṣma.

Traveling east through the valley for more than two hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Badakhshān (鉢鐸創那國). The country of Badakhshān is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is more than two thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country is situated upon a mountain cliff and is six or seven *li* in circuit. The mountains and rivers are winding and rugged, and the land is filled with sand and stone. The soil is suitable for pulse and wheat, and there is an abundance of fruits such as grapes, walnuts, pears, and crabapples. The climate is cold and harsh, and the people are fierce and impetuous by nature. Their customs lack propriety and law, and they have no knowledge of the arts. Their appearance is coarse and ugly, and they mostly wear garments of felt and coarse wool. There are three or four *saṃghārāmas* (monasteries), with very few monks. The king is simple and honest by nature and has deep faith in the Three Jewels.
The capital city of the country (Bada-chuangna 鉢鐸創那國; Skt. Badakhshān) is situated upon a mountain cliff and is six or seven li in circuit.

From here, traveling southeast through a mountain valley for more than two hundred li, one reaches the country of Yambagan (淫薄健國). The country of Yambagan is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is more than one thousand li in circumference. The capital city of the country is more than ten li in circumference. The mountain ranges are connected, and the river valleys and fields are narrow and confined. The native products, the climate, and the character of the people are the same as those of Badakshān (鉢鐸創那), though the language is slightly different. The king is harsh and violent by nature, and he does not distinguish between good and evil.

The city of Khaṇḍata (昏馱多城) is the capital of the country. Within it is a monastery established by a former king of this country, who hollowed out the cliffs and filled the valleys to construct its halls and chambers.
