In earlier times, this country had not been reached by Buddhism and only worshipped heretical deities; it was only a few hundred years ago that the transformation of the Dharma began to spread.  Initially, the king’s beloved son fell ill. He exhausted all medical arts, but the illness only worsened without any sign of recovery. The king then went in person to a temple of the gods to offer rites and pray for salvation. At that time, the priest of the temple spoke on behalf of the deity: "He will certainly recover; there is truly no cause for concern." The king, hearing this, was joyful and comforted, and turned his carriage to return home. On the road, he encountered a śramaṇa whose demeanor was remarkable. Struck by his appearance and attire, the king asked where he had come from. This śramaṇa had already attained the holy fruit and, wishing to propagate the Buddha’s Dharma, had assumed this form. He replied to the king, "I am a disciple of the Tathāgata, what is known as a bhikṣu."  The king, being full of anxiety, immediately asked, "My son is afflicted with illness, and it is not yet certain whether he will live or die." The śramaṇa said, "The king’s ancestors may be raised, but your beloved son is difficult to save." The king said, "The heavenly deity said he would not die, yet this śramaṇa says he shall perish; how can the words of such a deceptive and vulgar man be trusted?"  Upon arriving at the palace, he found his beloved son had already died. He concealed the death and did not hold a funeral, instead asking the priest of the deity again, who still said, "He will not die; the illness will surely be cured." The king then flew into a rage, bound the priest, and rebuked him, saying, "You and your kind live together to foster evil, wantonly exercising power and claiming blessings." "My son is already dead, yet you still claim he will recover; such deceit and delusion are truly unbearable! It is fitting to execute the spirit-master and destroy the spirit-temple." Thereupon, he killed the spirit-master, removed the spirit-images, and cast them into the Vaxšu River (縛芻河). As he turned his carriage to return, he encountered a śramaṇa. Seeing him, he felt respect and joy, bowed his head, and apologized, saying, "In the past, I lacked a bright guide and lingered on evil paths. Although the corruption has lasted long, the reform begins here. I hope you will deign to look upon me and descend to my residence." The śramaṇa accepted the invitation and followed him to the inner palace. Once the son had been buried, the king said to the śramaṇa, "The human world is full of entanglement, and birth and death are in constant flux. When my son fell ill, I asked the spirit whether he would stay or depart, and the spirit spoke falsely, saying he would surely recover. Having previously received your instructions, which indeed proved not to be false, I see that your Dharma is worthy of devotion; I only pray that you will show compassion and guide this deluded follower." He then requested the śramaṇa to survey the site for a monastery (伽藍) and establish it according to the proper rules. From that time on, the Buddha's teaching flourished. Therefore, the main hall (精舍; Skt. mūla-gandha-kuṭī) in the monastery was built for an arhat. In the great main hall of the monastery, there is a stone Buddha image, above which hangs a circular canopy of gilt bronze, adorned with various jewels. When people circumambulate, the canopy also rotates accordingly; when the people stop, the canopy stops. No one can fathom this spiritual manifestation. I heard from the elders that some say it is sustained by the power of a holy person's vow, while others say it is caused by secret mechanical arts. Observing the building, the stone walls are solid and steep. Examining all these opinions, no one knows the true account.

Crossing the great mountain (pravaragiri) of this country, one arrives north at the country of Šikni (尸棄尼國). The country of Šikni is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is five or six li in circuit. The mountains and rivers are connected, and the fields are covered with sand and stone. There is much pulse and wheat, but few cereal crops; trees are sparse, and flowers and fruits are scarce. The climate is bitterly cold. The customs of the people are fierce and brave; they are hardened to slaughter and devoted to theft. They do not know ritual or righteousness, and they do not distinguish between good and evil. They are confused about future misfortune or blessings, yet they fear the calamities of the present life. Their appearance is coarse and unsightly, and they wear skins and coarse wool for clothing. Their writing is the same as that of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨羅國), but their spoken language is different.
The country of Śiknī (尸棄尼國) is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is five or six li in circuit.

Crossing to the south of the great mountains of the country of Dharmasthiti (達摩悉鐵帝國), one arrives at the country of Śami (商彌國). The country of Śami is two thousand five or six hundred li in circumference. Mountains and rivers alternate, with high and low hills interspersed. All kinds of grain are planted, with pulse and wheat being particularly abundant; there are many grapes, and the land produces orpiment, which is obtained by splitting the rocks hewn from the cliffs. The mountain gods are fierce and malicious, repeatedly causing calamities; only after offering sacrifices can one enter, and then travel back and forth in safety. If one does not pray, winds and hail break out. The climate is cold, and the customs are impetuous. The people are simple and honest in disposition, but their customs lack etiquette and righteousness; their wisdom is limited, and their skills are superficial. Their script is the same as that of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國), but their spoken language is different. They mostly wear felt and coarse wool garments. Their king is of the Śākya clan and deeply reveres the Buddha's teachings; the people follow his example, and all are pure in their faith. There are two saṃghārāmas, with few monks.

To the northeast of the country, crossing mountains and traversing valleys, passing through dangerous terrain and treading over perilous paths for over seven hundred li, one arrives at the Pamir Valley (波謎羅川). It extends over one thousand li from east to west and over one hundred li from south to north, while at its narrowest point it is no more than ten li wide. It is situated between two snowy mountains, and therefore the cold winds are piercingly strong; snow falls during the spring and summer, and winds swirl day and night. The soil is saline and alkaline, with much gravel and stone; crops do not flourish, and vegetation is sparse, which leads to it being a desolate wilderness, entirely devoid of human habitation.

In the Pamir (波謎羅) Valley lies the Great Dragon Lake, extending over three hundred *li* from east to west and over fifty *li* from north to south. It is situated within the Great Onion Range (大葱嶺), lies at the center of Jambudvīpa (贍部洲), and occupies the highest elevation. The water is clear and bright as a mirror, its depth unfathomable, its color a dark blue-black, and its taste extremely sweet. Submerged within it dwell sharks, *chi*-dragons, fish, dragons, soft-shelled turtles, alligators, tortoises, and turtles. Floating and swimming upon it are mandarin ducks, wild geese, *jia*-geese, *su*-birds, and *hu*-birds. These birds lay large eggs, leaving their shells in the wilderness, either among the grassy marshes or upon the sandy islets. A large stream flows out from the west of the lake, running west to the eastern boundary of the Dharmasthiti (達摩悉鐵帝) country, where it joins the Vakṣu (縛芻) River and flows westward; therefore, to the right of this point, all waters flow to the west. A large stream flows out from the east of the lake, running northeast to the western boundary of the Khāsa (佉沙) country, where it joins the Sītā (徙多) River and flows eastward; therefore, to the left of this point, all waters flow to the east. South of the Pamir Valley, crossing the mountains, is the Balūra (鉢露羅) country, which abounds in gold and silver; the color of the gold is like fire.

Long ago, a king of Persia (波利剌斯國) married a wife from the land of Han. While escorting her back, they reached this place, but at that time there was a military rebellion, and the roads to the east and west were cut off. Consequently, they placed the king’s wife upon an isolated peak, which was extremely steep and precipitous; one had to use ladders to ascend or descend, and they established guards all around to keep watch day and night. Three months passed, and the bandits were finally pacified. They intended to proceed on the road home, but the woman was already pregnant. The envoy was terrified and said to his subordinates, "The King ordered us to welcome his bride, but we encountered this rebellion, camping in the wild barrens, unable to plan for the next morning. Through our King’s virtuous influence, the evil aura has been quelled, and now that we are about to return to our country, the King’s bride is pregnant. Considering this, it is a source of anxiety; we do not know if we will die here. We should identify the ringleader and perhaps execute him later." The questioning and clamor were loud, but they could not determine the truth. At that time, her maidservant said to the envoy, "Do not blame one another; it was a divine encounter. Every day at high noon, a man descends from the solar disc riding a horse to meet her here." The envoy said, "If that is the case, how can we clear ourselves of this guilt? If we return, we will surely be executed; if we stay, we will also be punished. With such a dilemma, what should we do?" They all agreed, "This matter is not trivial; who would willingly accept a severe execution? Let us await our punishment outside the borders and delay the matter for a while." Thereupon, they built a palace and quarters on the stone peak, with a circumference of more than three hundred paces. They built a city wall around the palace, established the woman as the ruler, and appointed officials to establish laws.

Traveling three hundred-odd *li* to the southeast of the city, one reaches a great rocky cliff where there are two stone chambers, in each of which an Arhat (阿羅漢) has entered the samādhi of extinction (滅盡定). They sit upright and are difficult to move; their forms resemble those of emaciated men, yet their skin and bones have not decayed, having already remained so for over seven hundred years. Their hair and beards grow constantly, and for this reason, the monks shave them and change their robes every year.

From this point, going eastward down the eastern ridges of the Pamir Mountains (葱嶺), climbing perilous peaks and crossing deep valleys, through dangerous mountain paths and amid continuous wind and snow, I traveled over eight hundred li, emerged from the Pamirs, and reached the kingdom of Wusha (烏鎩國). The kingdom of Wusha is over one thousand li in circuit. The capital city is over ten li in circuit and borders the Sītā River (徙多河) to the south. The soil is rich and fertile, crops are abundant, forests are lush, and flowers and fruits are plentiful. The land produces much variegated jade, including white jade, black jade, and green jade. The climate is temperate, and the wind and rain are timely. The customs lack propriety and righteousness; the people are by nature stubborn and fierce, prone to deceit, and lacking in shame. Their writing and language are somewhat similar to those of the kingdom of Khāsa (佉沙國). Their appearance is unsightly, and they wear garments of leather and wool. Nevertheless, they are able to revere and serve the Buddhadharma. There are more than ten saṃghārāmas, with fewer than one thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Small Vehicle according to the Sarvāstivāda school. For several hundred years, the royal line has been extinct, and having no separate ruler, they are subject to the kingdom of Kharbanda (朅盤陀國).

Two hundred or more *li* west of the city, one arrives at the Great Mountain (Pravaragiri). The mountain’s atmosphere is dense and swirling; clouds rise where it touches the rocks, and the cliffs and precipices are jagged and steep, as if about to collapse yet not falling. On its summit is a stūpa of imposing and extraordinary construction. According to local tradition, several hundred years ago, a mountain cliff collapsed, and within it was a bhikṣu sitting with eyes closed. His body was of great stature, his appearance emaciated, and his beard and hair hung down, covering his shoulders and face. A hunter saw him and reported it to the king, who went in person to pay his respects. The city’s inhabitants and scholars arrived without being summoned, burning incense and scattering flowers, vying to offer worship. The king asked, "Who is this person? He is so magnificent!" A bhikṣu replied, "This person with long, hanging hair and beard, clad in a kaṣāya robe, is an arhat who has entered the samādhi of mental extinction (nirodha-samāpatti). Those who enter the samādhi of mental extinction set a prior time limit; some say they will arise upon hearing the sound of a ghaṇṭā, others say they will wait for the sunlight to shine. With such an alert, they arise from their meditation; if there is no alert, they remain silent and motionless, the power of their meditation sustaining their body so that it does not decay. The physical body, sustained by morsel food, would perish upon emerging from meditation. It is proper to pour in ghee to provide nourishment and moisture, and only then strike the ghaṇṭā to awaken his meditative mind." The king said, "Is that so?" He then struck the ghaṇṭā. The sound had barely vibrated when the arhat suddenly opened his eyes and looked up. After a long while, he said, "Who are you people? Your appearance is base and inferior, yet you wear the kaṣāya robes?" They replied, "We are bhikṣus." He asked, "Is that so? Where is my teacher, Kāśyapa Tathāgata (迦葉波如來), now?" They replied, "He entered mahānirvāṇa a long time ago." Upon hearing this, he closed his eyes, looking dejected as if lost in thought. Shortly after, he asked again, "Has Śākya Tathāgata (釋迦如來) appeared in the world?" They replied, "The holy one who guided the world has already passed into extinction." Hearing this, he bowed his head again, and after a long while, he rose, ascended into the void, manifested supernatural transformations, and transformed into fire to consume his body, his remains falling to the ground. The king collected his bones and erected a stūpa (窣堵波) over them.

On the southern border of the country is a great mountain (Pravaragiri), with craggy cliffs and ridges and overlapping peaks. The vegetation defies the cold, presenting a singular sight in both spring and autumn. Deep ravines and rushing torrents flow in all directions, and cliff niches and stone chambers are scattered like chess pieces throughout the rocky forests. Many people from India who have attained the fruits of enlightenment employ their supernatural powers to travel far and alight here to dwell. Because many Arhats have entered nirvana here, there are numerous stupas. Even now, three Arhats remain in the mountain caves, having entered the samadhi of mental extinction; their forms appear like those of emaciated men, and their hair and beards grow continuously, so monks periodically go there to shave them. In this country, the number of Mahayana scriptures is particularly large; of all the places where the Buddha’s teachings have spread, none is more flourishing than this. There are over ten works consisting of one hundred thousand stanzas each, and from this size on down, their circulation is truly vast.

More than ten *li* to the southwest of the royal city, there is the Dīrghabhāvana Monastery (地迦婆縛那伽藍). Inside is a standing Buddha image made of hollow lacquer, which originally came here from the country of Kuci (屈支國). Formerly, a minister of this country was banished and lived in Kuci, where he constantly worshipped this image. Later, after he was allowed to return to his country, he continued to venerate it from afar with all his heart. After midnight, the image suddenly arrived of its own accord, and the man gave up his residence to build this monastery.

Traveling three hundred-odd *li* west from the royal city, one arrives at the city of Bhagai (勃伽夷城). Within it is a seated image of the Buddha, over seven feet high. Its physical marks are perfectly complete, and its majestic, solemn appearance is awe-inspiring. It wears a precious crown on its head, which emits light from time to time. According to local tradition, it was originally in the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) and was invited to be moved here. Long ago, there was an arhat whose *śrāmaṇera* (novice) disciple, when approaching the end of his life, asked for some sour rice cakes. The arhat used his heavenly eye to observe and saw that this delicacy existed in the country of Gostāna (瞿薩旦那國); he employed his supernatural powers to travel there and obtain it. After the *śrāmaṇera* had eaten it, he wished to be reborn in that country. His past aspiration was fulfilled, and he became the prince. Once he had succeeded to the throne, his might intimidated both near and far; he then crossed the Snow Mountains (Himālaya) to invade the country of Kaśmīra. The King of Kaśmīra mobilized his troops and horses, intending to resist the border invaders. At that time, the arhat admonished the king, saying, "Do not engage in battle; I can cause them to retreat." He then explained the essential teachings of the Dharma to the King of Gostāna. The king did not believe him at first and still wished to raise his army. The arhat then took the robe that this king had worn in his previous life as a *śrāmaṇera* and showed it to him. Once the king saw the robe, he attained the knowledge of past lives; he apologized to the King of Kaśmīra, reconciled with him, and released his troops to return home. He respectfully invited the Buddha image that he had worshipped when he was a *śrāmaṇera* to follow his army. When the image reached this place, it could not be moved further, so they built a monastery around it and invited monks to reside there. The king offered his precious crown and placed it upon the head of the image; the crown it wears today is the very one bestowed by the former king.

One hundred and fifty or sixty li to the west of the royal city, in the middle of the main road through the great desert, there are mounds which are all rat-earth hillocks (鼠壤墳). According to local tradition, in this desert there are rats as large as hedgehogs, whose fur is of various colors of gold and silver. They are the leaders of their groups, and whenever they emerge from their burrows to roam or rest, the other rats follow them.  In the past, the Xiongnu led several hundred thousand troops to invade and plunder the frontier cities, stationing their army beside these rat mounds. At that time, the King of Gostana (瞿薩旦那王) led several tens of thousands of soldiers, fearing that his strength was no match for the enemy. He had long known that the rats in the desert were remarkable, but he had not yet regarded them as divine. When the invaders arrived, there was nowhere to seek help, and the king and his ministers were terrified, not knowing what strategy to devise. In desperation, he set up offerings, burned incense, and petitioned the rats, hoping that they possessed spiritual power and would add a little to his military strength.  That night, the King of Gostana saw a giant rat in a dream. It said, "I wish to assist you. Prepare your troops early, and when you engage in battle at daybreak, you will surely be victorious." The King of Gostana, knowing he had received divine protection, immediately readied his horses and weapons and issued orders to his officers and men. Before dawn, they marched out and launched a surprise attack. When the Xiongnu heard of this, they were all struck with fear. Just as they were about to mount their horses and put on their armor, the rats gnawed through all their saddles, clothing, bowstrings, armor straps, and every kind of belt and fastening. When the enemy troops arrived, the Xiongnu stood with their hands bound behind their backs, waiting to be executed. Thereupon, the king killed their generals and captured their soldiers. The Xiongnu were terrified, believing that the king was protected by divine spirits. The King of Kustana (瞿薩旦那), moved by the great kindness of the rats, built a shrine and established sacrifices, a tradition of reverence followed for generations with profound and special esteem. Therefore, from the monarch above to the common people below, all perform sacrifices to seek blessings and protection. When passing by their burrows, people alight from their mounts and hurry forward, bowing to pay their respects and offering sacrifices to pray for good fortune. Whether offering clothing, bows, and arrows, or fragrant flowers and fine foods, once they have shown their sincerity, they mostly receive benefits and blessings. If they fail to offer sacrifices, they encounter disasters and calamities.

Five or six li to the west of the royal city is the Samājña Monastery (娑摩若僧伽藍). Within it is a stūpa over one hundred feet high, which possesses many miraculous signs and often illuminates with divine light. Formerly, there was an arhat who came from a distant land and stayed in this forest, manifesting great light through his supernatural powers. At that time, the king was in his multi-storied pavilion at night and saw from afar the light shining in the forest. He inquired about it, and everyone said, "There is a śramaṇa who has arrived from afar, sitting in meditation in the forest and manifesting supernatural powers." The king then ordered his carriage and went in person to observe. Having seen the wise and virtuous one, he felt deep respect and admiration for his character, and invited him to the royal palace. The śramaṇa said, "Things have their proper places, and one’s aspirations lie where they belong. Secluded forests and marshes are what my heart delights in; high halls and deep chambers are not what I am accustomed to." The king respected and revered him all the more, and for his sake built a monastery and erected a stūpa. The śramaṇa accepted the invitation and subsequently resided there. Shortly after, the king miraculously obtained several hundred grains of relics. He was extremely joyful and thought to himself, "Why did the relics come to respond so late? If I had obtained them earlier to place them under the stūpa, would that not have been a magnificent monument?" He immediately went to the monastery and told the śramaṇa in detail. The arhat said, "O King, do not worry; I shall place them for you now. You should use caskets of gold, silver, copper, iron, and large stone, one inside the other, to contain them." The king ordered the craftsmen, and in a few days the work was completed. He loaded them onto a precious carriage and sent them to the monastery. At that time, the king’s royal retinue and the various officials, numbering in the tens of thousands, came to witness the sending of the relics. The arhat then lifted the stūpa with his right hand, placed it in his palm, and said to the king, "You may now bury them beneath it." Thereupon, a pit was dug in the ground and the caskets were installed. When the task was finished, the stūpa was lowered back down without any tilting or damage. Those who witnessed it marveled that such a thing had never happened before; their faith in the Buddha became even more sincere, and their resolve to revere the Dharma grew more steadfast.  The king said to his officials, "I have heard that the power of the Buddha is inconceivable and his supernatural faculties are unfathomable. Sometimes he manifests billions of bodies, and sometimes he leaves traces of his presence among humans and devas. He can lift the entire world into the palm of his hand without the sentient beings within it having any sense of movement or stillness; he expounds the nature of the Dharma in a constant sound, and sentient beings attain understanding according to their own kind. This is the uncommon power of his supernatural faculties and wisdom that transcends words. Though his spiritual presence has vanished, his teachings are still transmitted. By consuming his harmony and drinking his grace, by savoring the Way and admiring his influence, we still obtain such spiritual efficacy and rely deeply upon his blessings. Exert yourselves, all of you! You should offer deep veneration; that the Buddha-dharma is abstruse and profound is evident from this."

Five or six li southeast of the royal city is the Ma-ża (麻射) Monastery, which was established by a former queen of this country. In ancient times, this country did not know of mulberry trees or silkworms. Hearing that they existed in the eastern country, the king sent an envoy to request them. At that time, the ruler of the eastern country kept them secret and would not bestow them, strictly ordering the frontier guards not to allow the seeds of mulberry or silkworms to pass out. The King of Gostana (瞿薩旦那國) then used humble words and low courtesies to request a marriage alliance with the eastern country. The ruler of that country, having a desire to extend his influence to distant lands, granted the request. The King of Gostana ordered an envoy to receive the bride and instructed him, saying: "Convey this message to the daughter of the eastern ruler: our country has never had silk, floss, or the seeds of mulberry and silkworms; she may bring them with her so that she may make her own garments." Upon hearing these words, the princess secretly sought the seeds and placed the silkworm eggs inside the padding of her hat. When she reached the frontier, the officials searched everywhere, but they did not dare to inspect the princess's hat. She then entered the country of Gostana and stopped at the former site of the Ma-ża Monastery. Only after the proper rites and ceremonies were prepared was she escorted into the palace, and the mulberry and silkworm seeds were left at this location. When the warmth of spring began, she planted the mulberry trees, and when the silkworm month arrived, she proceeded to gather and raise them. When they first arrived, she still fed them with various leaves, but from that time on, the mulberry trees grew in continuous shade. The queen then had a decree carved into stone, forbidding their injury or killing; only after the silkworm moths had flown away could the cocoons be processed. Anyone who dared to violate this would not be protected by the bright spirits. She then built this monastery for the first silkworms. Several withered mulberry trees are said to be the trees of the original stock. Therefore, in this country today, silkworms are not killed; if anyone stealthily takes their silk, the sericulture will surely be unsuccessful the following year.
The monastery beside the pond is deserted and in ruins, with no monks residing there.

More than a hundred li to the southeast of the city is a large river flowing northwest; the people of the country benefit from it, using it to irrigate their fields. Later, the flow ceased, and the king was deeply puzzled and alarmed. He then ordered his carriage and went to ask an Arhat (阿羅漢) monk, saying: "The water of the great river is what the people rely on for their needs; now that it has suddenly stopped flowing, where does the fault lie? Is my governance unjust, or is my virtue not in harmony? If not, why is this reprimand so severe?" The Arhat said: "Great King, your governance of the country is clear and harmonious. The river's flow has ceased because of the dragon. You should quickly offer sacrifices and pray, and the former benefits will return." The king then returned and offered sacrifices to the river dragon. Suddenly, a woman arrived, walking upon the waves, and said: "My husband died early, and I have no one to follow; this is why the river's flow has ceased and the farmers have lost their livelihood. If the King selects a noble minister from within the country to be my husband, the water will flow as before." The king said: "I respectfully hear your request; it is for you to choose whom you desire." The dragon then cast her eyes upon a high minister of the country. The king, having returned, said to his subordinates: "A high minister is the heavy pillar of the state; agricultural work is the life-sustaining food of the people. If the state loses its pillar, it is in danger; if the people are cut off from food, they die. Regarding these matters of danger and death, what is appropriate to do?" A minister stepped across his mat, knelt, and replied: "I have long been hollow and meager, yet I have mistakenly occupied a heavy responsibility. I have always thought of repaying the state, but have not yet encountered the time to do so. Now that I have been selected, how would I dare to refuse this profound duty? If it benefits the myriad people, why should I begrudge one minister?" "Ministers are the assistants of the state; the people are the foundation of the state. I hope the Great King will not hesitate further. I pray you cultivate merit and build a saṃghārāma." The King granted his request, and the work was completed in a few days. The minister then requested to enter the dragon palace early. Thereupon, the officials and commoners of the entire country played music and held a farewell feast. The minister donned plain white garments, mounted a white horse, bade farewell to the King, and respectfully thanked the people of the country. He urged his horse into the river, treading upon the water without sinking. Upon reaching midstream, he brandished his whip and traced a line on the water; the water parted in the middle, and he vanished from there. After a short while, the white horse floated to the surface, carrying a large sandalwood drum and a sealed letter. The letter said in brief: "Your Majesty did not overlook my humble status and allowed me to be mistakenly chosen by the divine; I hope you will perform many meritorious deeds to benefit the state and nourish your subjects. Take this large drum and hang it to the southeast of the city; if invaders approach, the drum will sound a warning first." The river water then flowed on, and it remains useful to this day. As the years and months have passed, the dragon drum has long been gone, but at the place where it was formerly hung, there is still a drum today.

Traveling more than thirty *li* east from the battlefield, one arrives at the city of Pimo (媲摩城). There is a standing sandalwood Buddha image over two *zhang* in height. It possesses many miraculous powers and at times emits a brilliant light. Whenever people have illnesses, they apply gold leaf to the part of the image corresponding to their own area of pain, and they are immediately cured. Those who make requests with a sincere heart often have their wishes fulfilled. I heard the local people say: "This image was made by King Udayana (鄔陀衍那王) of the country of Kauśāmbī (憍賞彌國) when the Buddha was still in the world. After the Buddha passed away, it traveled through the air from there to the city of Rauraka (曷勞落迦城) in the north of this country." When it first arrived, the people of the city were peaceful and prosperous, but they were deeply attached to erroneous views and did not treasure or respect it; although they heard it had come of its own accord, they considered it divine but did not value it. Later, an Arhat came to pay homage to this image. The people of the city were shocked, finding his appearance and clothing strange, and they rushed to inform the king. The king then issued an order that this strange man should be covered with sand and earth. At that time, the Arhat was covered in sand and earth, his mouth blocked and his food supply cut off. There was one man whose heart could not bear this; he had long held this image in reverent worship, and upon seeing the Arhat, he secretly provided him with food. When the Arhat was about to depart, he said to the man: "Seven days from now, it will rain sand and earth, filling this city until not a single soul remains. You should know this and plan your escape early. It is because they covered me with sand that they have brought this calamity upon themselves." Having spoken, he departed and suddenly vanished. The man entered the city and told his relatives and friends in detail, but those who heard him did nothing but laugh and mock him. On the second day, a great wind suddenly arose, blowing away the filth and soil, and it rained various treasures that filled the streets; the people then berated their informant even more. This man, knowing in his heart that it was inevitable, secretly opened a tunnel, exited the city, and took shelter outside. On the night of the seventh day, after midnight, sand and earth rained down and filled the city. The man emerged from the tunnel and went east to this country, staying in the city of Bhīmā (嫓摩城). No sooner had the man arrived than the image also arrived; he immediately worshipped it there and dared not move it. According to ancient records, when the Dharma of Śākyamuni comes to an end, the image will enter the dragon palace. Today, the city of Rauraka (曷勞落迦城) has become a great mound. Kings of various nations and powerful men from distant lands have often desired to excavate it to take its treasures, but as soon as they reach its vicinity, fierce winds suddenly arise, smoke and clouds gather from all sides, and the roads become lost.

After the Buddha had passed away, [the image] traveled through the air from that place to the city of Rauraka (曷勞落迦城) in the north of this country. When it first arrived, the people of the city were peaceful and prosperous, but they were deeply attached to wrong views and did not value or respect it; they passed on the story of its arrival, regarding it as a spirit but not holding it in high esteem. Later, an Arhat came to pay homage to this image. The people of the country were shocked, finding his appearance and robes strange, and they rushed to inform the king. The king then issued an order that this strange man should be covered with sand and earth. At that time, the Arhat’s body was covered in sand and earth, and he was deprived of food and drink. There was one man whose heart could not bear this; he had previously always respectfully honored this image, and upon seeing the Arhat, he secretly provided him with food. When the Arhat was about to depart, he said to the man, "Seven days from now, it shall rain sand and earth, filling this city until not a single soul remains. You should know this and plan your escape early. It is because they covered me with sand that they shall meet this calamity." Having spoken, he departed and suddenly vanished. The man entered the city and told his relatives and friends in detail, but those who heard him did nothing but laugh and mock him. On the second day, a great wind suddenly arose, blowing away the filth and raining down various treasures that filled the streets; the people then further scolded the one who had warned them. This man knew in his heart that it was inevitable, so he secretly opened a tunnel, went outside the city, and took shelter there. On the night of the seventh day, after midnight, sand and earth rained down and filled the city. The man emerged from the tunnel and went east to this country, staying in the city of Bhīmā (嫓摩城). No sooner had the man arrived than the image also came; he immediately made offerings to it there and dared not move it again. According to ancient records, when the Dharma of Śākyamuni comes to an end, the image will enter the palace of the dragons. Today, the city of Rauraka (曷勞落迦城) has become a great mound. Kings of various nations and powerful men from distant lands have often desired to excavate it to take its treasures. Yet, as soon as they reach its side, a violent gale suddenly breaks out, clouds and mist close in from all sides, and they lose their way.

Going east from the Bhīmā River (嫓摩川) into the sandy desert, one travels more than two hundred li and reaches the city of Niyang (尼攘城), which is three or four li in circuit and situated in the midst of a vast marsh. The marshy ground is hot and damp, making it difficult to walk or wade; the reeds and grasses are overgrown, and there are no longer any paths, so that only the road leading to the city is passable. Therefore, all those who come and go must pass through this city. The kingdom of Gostana (瞿薩旦那) considers it a strategic frontier post for its eastern border.

From here, traveling east, one enters the Great Quicksand (Taklamakan Desert), where the sands shift and flow, gathering and scattering with the wind. As human footsteps leave no trace, many people lose their way. The vast expanse stretches out in all directions with no landmarks to point the way, so travelers collect the bleached bones of the dead to serve as markers. There is a lack of water and vegetation, and there are many hot winds; when the wind rises, both people and animals become dazed and confused, thereby falling ill. At times, one hears singing and whistling, or hears wailing and crying. Amidst these sights and sounds, one becomes utterly bewildered and loses all sense of direction; this has led to frequent deaths, for it is surely the work of demons and malevolent spirits. Traveling more than four hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Tu-huo-lo (都邏故國; *Tukhāra*). The country has long been empty and vast, and its cities are all desolate and overgrown.

From here, traveling east for more than six hundred li, one reaches the old country of Calmadana (折摩馱那故國), which is the land of Jumo (涅末地). The city walls stand tall and solitary, but all signs of human habitation have vanished.

Traveling northeast from here for over a thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Navapa (納縛波故國), which is the land of Loulan (樓蘭). Regarding the mapping of mountains and rivers, the investigation of territories and soils, the detailing of the hard or soft nature of national customs, and the connection to the local climates and airs—since movement and stillness are impermanent and choices differ, these matters are difficult to verify exhaustively and cannot be explained merely by looking upward. Following where I have traveled, I have briefly written down the general outlines, citing what I have heard and seen, and recording those who admire the civilizing influence. Therefore, from the place where the sun sets, all are bathed in the grace and benevolence; wherever the wind of his influence reaches, all look up to his supreme virtue. He has unified the world and brought oneness to all within the universe; how could this be merely the act of a solitary envoy in a single carriage traveling ten thousand *li* through postal stations?

The Eastern Lord, taking advantage of his victory, comforted and gathered the people of the defeated state, moved the capital to the central region, and began to build city walls. He worried about the lack of soil and feared that the project might not succeed, so he made a proclamation far and near, asking who understood the geography of the land. At that time, there was an ash-smearing ascetic (pāśupata) carrying a large gourd filled with water who stepped forward and said, "I understand the geography." He then let the water flow out in winding curves, circling back to the beginning, after which he hurried away and suddenly vanished. Following those water marks, the foundations were raised and the construction was successfully undertaken; this became the seat of government, and the current king has established his capital in this city. The city is not high or steep, yet it is difficult to overcome in an attack; since ancient times, no one has ever been able to conquer it.

Thus, from the silver ox's mouth on the eastern side of the pond flows the Gaṅgā River (formerly called the Heng River, or also Hengjia, which are corruptions), which circles the pond once and enters the southeastern sea;
From the golden elephant's mouth on the southern side of the pond flows the Sindhu River (the old name Xintou is a corruption), which circles the pond once and enters the southwestern sea.
From the lapis lazuli horse's mouth on the western side of the pond flows the Vakṣu River (the old name Bocha is a corruption), which circles the pond once and enters the northwestern sea;

From the crystal lion’s mouth on the northern side of the pond flows the Sītā River (formerly called the Sida River, which is a corruption), which circles the pond once and enters the northeastern sea; or, it is said that it flows underground, emerges at Jishi Mountain, and is the current of the Sītā River, which is said to be the source of the river of China.

The central region of the continent of Jambudvīpa is the Anavatapta (阿那婆答多) Pond (in the language of the Tang, this means "without heat and affliction"; the old name, Anouda [阿耨達] Pond, is a corruption). It is situated to the south of the Fragrant Mountains (Gandhamādana-giri) and to the north of the Great Snow Mountains, with a circumference of eight hundred li.
Departing from the former territory of Gaochang (高昌), I begin with the nearest land, which is called the kingdom of Agni (阿耆尼國; formerly known as Wuqi 烏耆).

Traveling southwest from here for over two hundred li, crossing a small mountain and two large rivers, I reached a plain to the west; after traveling over seven hundred li, I arrived at the country of Kuci (屈支國) (formerly called Qiuci 龜茲). The country of Kuci is over one thousand li from east to west and over six hundred li from south to north. The capital city is seventeen or eighteen li in circuit. The soil is suitable for millet and wheat, and there is round-grained rice; it produces grapes and pomegranates, and abounds in pears, crabapples, peaches, and apricots. The land produces gold, copper, iron, lead, and tin. The climate is temperate, and the customs are simple. Their writing system is modeled on that of India, with slight modifications. In string and wind music, they are especially superior to other countries. Their clothing is made of brocade and felt, and they cut their hair and wear turbans and caps. For currency, they use gold coins, silver coins, and small copper coins. The king is of Kuci stock; he is of little wisdom and is constrained by powerful ministers. It is their custom that when a child is born, they press its head with a wooden board, wishing it to be flat. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas (伽藍) with more than five thousand monks, who study the Hīnayāna teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school. Their scriptural teachings and monastic regulations are modeled on those of India, and those who study them read the original texts. They still adhere to the gradual teachings and consume the three kinds of pure meat. They are devoted to cleanliness and purity, and the people compete in meritorious deeds.
